General Rules
Specification authority
This Google Doc is the canonical authority for 9to1 product behaviour, feature requirements, donor parity, storage rules, UX semantics and unresolved design decisions. Trello is the roadmap/index layer only: product cards MUST remain concise and link to the relevant canonical section rather than duplicate its full specification. If Trello and this document disagree, this document wins unless a later explicit decision explicitly updates the canonical requirement.
Technical specification contract
Normative requirement language
This document is an engineering contract. The key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, MAY and OPTIONAL are normative requirement levels, not conversational emphasis.
MUST / MUST NOT — mandatory for conformance. An implementation that violates the requirement is non-conformant unless this document contains an explicit scoped exception.
SHOULD / SHOULD NOT — required by default. A deviation is permitted only when a concrete technical constraint makes the requirement unsuitable for that exact case; the implementation MUST record the exception, reason, affected scope, fallback behaviour and validation evidence.
MAY / OPTIONAL — intentionally optional. Omitting the behaviour is conformant unless another requirement makes it mandatory in a specific context.
Lowercase uses of “must”, “should” and “may” have the same normative meaning. Product prose MUST NOT use “should” merely to mean “it would be nice if”.
Terms such as “where appropriate”, “where practical”, “where feasible”, “as needed”, “etc.”, “and more”, “similar”, “sensible” or “useful” MUST NOT be used as an implementation escape hatch. If such wording remains in an older paragraph, the implementer MUST interpret it in favour of feature completeness and donor parity unless a precise condition or explicit exception narrows it.
Required technical structure for product specifications
Every shipping app, framework and system component MUST eventually define the following information in its canonical section. A section that lacks required fields is incomplete specification, not permission for the implementer to invent behaviour.
Purpose and boundary — what the component owns, what it explicitly does not own, and which neighbouring component owns excluded responsibilities.
Authoritative data/state — canonical entities, stable identifiers, ownership, lifecycle states, persistence location, versioning and migration rules.
Donor/upstream contract — donor repository/source, pinned or selected version policy, licence obligations, required parity surface, allowed replacements and documented exclusions.
Supported platforms and capability matrix — Windows, 9to1-OS, web and other supported surfaces, including exact differences rather than silent feature loss.
User-visible operations — exhaustive operations the UI exposes, including create/read/update/delete, import/export, collaboration, recovery, settings and destructive operations.
Automation/API surface — canonical namespace, action names, argument schemas, result schemas, stable IDs, pagination/streaming where applicable, idempotency semantics, error contracts, permission scopes and risk classification.
Permissions and security — caller identity, authorisation boundary, high-risk operations, secrets, external side effects, confirmation requirements and audit events.
Cross-app integration — exact owning app, reference/embed semantics, canonical-object behaviour and how actions route across app boundaries.
Failure and recovery — expected failures, partial-success behaviour, retry rules, rollback/restore, crash recovery and data-integrity guarantees.
Performance/resource constraints — limits that affect correctness or UX, including memory/storage/compute ownership where relevant.
Acceptance criteria — deterministic tests or observable behaviours that prove the requirement is implemented.
Open decisions — unresolved design questions explicitly labelled OPEN. OPEN items MUST NOT be silently resolved by an implementation agent when the choice could change public behaviour, data compatibility, security or architecture.
State and data invariants
Persistent objects MUST use stable identifiers that do not depend on display names, UI order or mutable paths unless the object is explicitly path-addressed by design. Display names MAY be duplicated unless the product section explicitly requires uniqueness.
Mutations MUST be atomic at the smallest user-visible operation boundary unless the operation explicitly declares partial-success semantics. When a multi-object operation can partially succeed, the result MUST identify every succeeded, failed, skipped and rolled-back item.
Destructive operations MUST define whether deletion is soft, recoverable, retained, permanent or externally propagated. If the section does not define permanent deletion semantics, implementations MUST prefer recoverable deletion and MUST NOT silently destroy the only copy of user data.
Persisted formats MUST be versioned. Readers MUST reject, migrate or preserve unknown incompatible schema versions explicitly; they MUST NOT reinterpret unknown data using a guessed schema.
Where two systems can mutate the same canonical entity, the specification MUST define authority, synchronisation direction, conflict detection and conflict resolution. Last-write-wins MUST NOT be assumed unless explicitly specified.
API and error contract
UI and automation MUST call the same domain operations wherever technically possible. An app MUST NOT maintain one hidden behavioural implementation for UI actions and a different incompatible implementation for API actions.
Every public API action MUST return a structured success/error result. Expected operational failures MUST NOT be represented only by free-form human text. Error results MUST include a stable machine-readable code, human-readable message, target/action identity and relevant recoverability/retry metadata.
APIs that enumerate unbounded collections MUST define pagination or streaming. APIs that can produce long-running work MUST expose request/job identity, status and cancellation. APIs that retry or can be replayed MUST define idempotency semantics so an interrupted client does not accidentally duplicate consequential mutations.
Unknown, unavailable and empty values MUST remain distinguishable. A value MUST NOT be replaced with zero, false, an empty string or an invented default merely because the provider/backend cannot supply it. Component-specific contracts such as Dulche’s null/Na distinction override this general rule where defined.
Unspecified behaviour and exceptions
When required behaviour is genuinely unspecified, an implementation agent MUST first determine whether the decision is observable, destructive, security-sensitive, data-format-affecting or architecture-defining. If yes, it MUST preserve existing data/state, avoid irreversible action and record the item as OPEN rather than guessing.
For non-observable implementation details, the implementer MAY choose a conventional maintainable design provided it does not alter the specified public behaviour, data compatibility, API contract, permissions, donor parity or future extensibility.
A specification exception MUST identify: requirement ID or quoted requirement, affected product/version/platform, technical reason, exact substitute behaviour, user-visible impact, security/data impact, tests/evidence and whether the exception is temporary or permanent. “Too difficult”, “not enough time”, “donor source unavailable” or “not implemented yet” are not valid permanent exceptions.
Definition of implementation-complete
A component is implementation-complete only when all mandatory behaviour in its canonical section is present and validated. Source code existing, a successful build, a rendered shell, placeholder controls or an API stub do not satisfy a behavioural requirement.
Completion evidence MUST cover representative end-to-end journeys, persistence/restart behaviour, API/UI parity, permissions, accessibility, failure/recovery paths, donor parity where applicable and platform/package validation for every declared supported platform.
Known failing requirements MUST remain explicitly recorded as open blockers or scoped exceptions. They MUST NOT be omitted from release/completion reporting.
Privacy and data-protection baseline
9to1 MUST apply a platform-wide Privacy Ceiling baseline to every app, framework, cloud service, hosted component, telemetry path, AI feature and operating-system integration that processes personal information. Product teams MUST NOT treat privacy as an app-specific optional enhancement.
The Privacy Ceiling is derived from the strongest compatible protection required across the supported United States jurisdictions, the United Kingdom and the European Union/EEA, plus deliberate engineering headroom. The implementation MUST maintain a versioned LegalPrivacyProfile describing the currently applicable statutory/regulatory requirements for each supported jurisdiction. Where multiple requirements are compatible, the most protective requirement becomes the global default. Where applicable laws genuinely conflict, the exception MUST be narrowly jurisdiction-scoped, documented, legally reviewed and MUST NOT lower protection for unaffected users or data.
Engineering headroom means 9to1 SHOULD collect less data, retain it for less time, expose it to fewer systems, process it locally more often and encrypt it more comprehensively than the minimum legally permissible where doing so does not prevent the requested product function. A legal maximum retention period, collection scope or disclosure permission MUST NOT automatically become the product default.
Privacy by design and by default is mandatory throughout the product lifecycle. Every processing activity MUST have a declared purpose, lawful/authorised basis where required, data categories, data subjects, recipients/processors, locality/residency constraints where applicable, retention/deletion policy, access-control model and security classification. New processing purposes MUST NOT silently reuse personal data collected for an unrelated purpose merely because the data is technically available.
Data minimisation is mandatory. A component MUST request, collect, transmit, persist and expose only the personal data necessary for its declared purpose and current authorised scope. Optional analytics, diagnostics, personalisation, AI context and convenience features MUST NOT enlarge the mandatory data footprint of the core product without a separate valid basis and user/admin control where required.
Privacy-protective defaults MUST be the ordinary out-of-box state. Settings that materially broaden sharing, retention, discoverability, telemetry, cloud processing, contactability or third-party disclosure MUST be explicit and understandable. Consent or approval surfaces MUST NOT use dark patterns, misleading symmetry, preselected optional consent or unnecessarily difficult withdrawal.
High-risk processing MUST undergo an appropriate documented privacy/risk assessment before release and again after material architectural or purpose changes. The assessment MUST address foreseeable misuse, unauthorised disclosure, inference risk, vulnerable users, children where relevant, cross-border processing, AI/model exposure, account compromise, metadata leakage and recovery/incident handling.
Encryption MUST be applied in transit and at rest for sensitive personal information unless a documented technical reason makes a specific layer impossible. Where the product promises end-to-end encryption, only intended endpoint participants may possess the content-decryption capability under the declared trust model. A server-side copy of a universal decryption key, silent escrow path or moderation backdoor is incompatible with an E2EE claim unless the user-facing product explicitly describes a materially different encryption model.
E2EE protects content but does not automatically hide all metadata. 9to1 MUST separately minimise and protect metadata such as participant identifiers, relationship graphs, IP/network information, timestamps, device identifiers, routing information and notification data. User interfaces and documentation MUST NOT imply that metadata is cryptographically hidden when the transport/service necessarily observes it.
Local processing is preferred for sensitive transformations when it can satisfy the feature reliably. A local application being able to decrypt or access data does NOT automatically grant Dulche, a Plugin, a cloud model, telemetry or another subsystem access to that data. AI access is a separate capability decision subject to the normal permission/privacy model.
When a feature can use either a local or cloud model/service, the privacy boundary MUST be explicit. Private content MUST NOT leave the device merely because a cloud provider is configured as a model fallback. Uploading personal content to a cloud model/service requires an applicable authorised route, and the UI MUST make materially relevant remote processing understandable to the user.
Secrets, authentication tokens, cryptographic keys and recovery material MUST use dedicated secure storage and least-privilege access. Logs, crash reports, analytics and Action Graph/FullLog data MUST redact secrets and unnecessary personal content rather than creating secondary plaintext stores.
Retention MUST be purpose-bound and enforceable. Personal data MUST have a defined deletion/expiry policy or a documented reason for durable retention. Deletion MUST propagate to replicas, caches, indexes and derived stores according to their declared lifecycle rather than only hiding the primary UI record. Legally required preservation or an explicitly created safety/evidence record MUST be segregated from ordinary user-visible retention and governed by its own scope and expiry rules.
Users MUST receive the applicable rights and controls required by the active LegalPrivacyProfile, including access/export, correction, deletion, objection/restriction and consent withdrawal where applicable. These controls SHOULD be easier and more complete than the legal minimum when technically reasonable. Export MUST use interoperable formats where practical and MUST NOT require the user to manually reconstruct data from screenshots or unrelated pages.
9to1 MUST maintain an inspectable data-flow inventory and processor/subprocessor register for hosted services. Third parties receive only the scopes/data required for their declared role. A provider's terms permitting additional processing do not by themselves authorise 9to1 to send data for that additional purpose.
Telemetry and product analytics MUST be purpose-limited, minimised and separated from message/document content unless that content is genuinely required for a specifically disclosed diagnostic purpose. Sensitive content MUST NOT be collected merely to improve general analytics. Privacy-preserving aggregation/pseudonymisation SHOULD be used where it meaningfully reduces risk.
Children and other protected/vulnerable-user contexts MUST receive any higher protection required by the applicable LegalPrivacyProfile. Age-related protections MUST NOT be implemented by collecting disproportionate additional identity data when a less invasive compliant mechanism is available.
Security/privacy failures MUST fail closed where continuing would expose personal content or silently weaken a promised protection. If an encryption, permission, privacy-relay or policy control required for a sensitive operation is unavailable, the operation MUST stop or visibly degrade to a clearly described lower-protection mode only when the user is allowed to choose that mode.
No app-specific specification may silently weaken this baseline. An app MAY impose stricter privacy rules. Any exception to the Privacy Ceiling MUST identify the exact requirement, jurisdiction/product scope, necessity, user impact, data affected, compensating controls, approval authority and review/expiry date.
Privacy acceptance MUST include automated and manual tests for least-privilege access, unauthorised cross-app data access, cloud/local boundary enforcement, retention/deletion propagation, export correctness, consent/withdrawal, encryption-state truthfulness, metadata minimisation, log redaction, provider failure and jurisdiction-profile changes. A product is not privacy-complete merely because its privacy policy text exists.
App APIs and automation permissions
API parity requirement
Every 9to1 app must expose a first-party automation API whose action surface is exhaustive for user-accessible app functionality. An authorised MCP, plugin, script, agent or other client must be able to perform anything the user can perform in the app through supported UI, subject to the same account, object, platform and security restrictions. APIs must not be intentionally limited to a small automation subset while important user actions remain UI-only.
Each app owns a canonical API namespace and a complete action catalogue. Example:
9to1.Boards.ListBoards();
9to1.Boards.CreateBoard();
9to1.Boards.AddPage();
UserBoards = 9to1.Boards;
UserBoards.AddPage();
Aliases/references such as UserBoards are permitted for convenience but do not create a new identity, permission boundary or trust grant. Language bindings may use a syntactically valid representation of the 9to1 namespace where a language cannot use 9to1 as a literal identifier; canonical app/action names and behaviour remain unchanged.
The action catalogue is part of the app contract. It must include read, create, edit, move, organise, import/export, collaboration, configuration, deletion/recovery and other actions that the corresponding user can perform. Actions that are unavailable to the current user because of role, ownership, account, provider or platform restrictions remain unavailable through the API.
Every action must declare its name, arguments/schema, result schema, required target-app permissions, risk level, whether it is reversible, whether it can produce external side effects, and the objects/scopes it affects. New UI capabilities are not complete until their equivalent API action is added. Deprecated actions require a documented migration path rather than silently disappearing.
Home permission broker
9to1 Home is the central permission broker for app APIs. A caller never dispatches a protected action directly to the target app without Home first resolving its permission state. If Home is not open, 9to1 opens it and shows the approval prompt before the target action executes. A caller may submit the request to the broker, but the requested app action remains PendingApproval until Home grants it.
The prompt MUST identify the requesting app/script/MCP, verified caller identity/origin when available, target 9to1 app, requested action names/scopes, elevated/destructive risk and affected object identifiers/counts whenever they can be determined before execution. If impact cannot be determined safely before execution, the prompt MUST display that impact as unknown rather than omit it. Generic wording such as “allow access” is insufficient for scoped or powerful actions.
Permission requests MAY group actions only when they share the same caller identity, target trust boundary and compatible risk level, and the prompt exposes the complete grouped scope before approval. A grant covers only the exact actions/scopes shown or already trusted. Adding a new action, target scope or higher risk level requires a new approval decision.
Prompt actions
Decline
Decline and Block
Accept
Accept and Trust
Accept and Always Trust
Decline denies the current permission request without blocking future requests.
Decline and Block denies the request and blocks that caller from requesting or using 9to1 app API permissions until the user explicitly unblocks it in Settings. Block state is tied to the caller identity, not merely its display name.
Accept approves only the current requested action set/scope. When that request/session scope ends, later protected actions require approval again unless another trust grant applies.
Accept and Trust
Accept and Trust approves the requested ordinary action scopes and trusts that caller for 30 days. During that period, matching ordinary actions can execute without repeatedly opening an approval prompt. The 30-day trust period expires automatically and can be revoked at any time in Settings.
Accept and Trust does not automatically authorise high-risk or suspicious actions. Actions such as deleting a board, mass deleting pages/items, bulk destructive changes, changing security/permission settings, destructive account actions or similarly sensitive operations require explicit approval each time unless the caller has an applicable Accept and Always Trust grant.
Accept and Always Trust
Accept and Always Trust is intended only for software the user deliberately grants persistent trust, including self-developed scripts/apps. Within the exact granted scopes and the user’s underlying authority, it allows the trusted caller to use app APIs without routine 9to1 approval prompts, including high-risk actions explicitly covered by the grant.
Before Always Trust is granted, Home must show a prominent warning that this level of access can allow the caller to read, modify or destroy user data without asking again. The warning presents:
Go Back
Grant Temporary Trusted Access
I Understand, Continue
Grant Temporary Trusted Access lets the user choose either a limited number of actions or a limited duration. The user also chooses what happens when that temporary grant ends: return to manual approval or roll down to the normal 30-day Accept and Trust level. The temporary grant must show its remaining action count/time and can be revoked early.
I Understand, Continue grants Always Trust only after the warning step. Always Trust has no automatic expiry, but remains visible and revocable in Settings.
Always Trust bypasses 9to1's routine approval prompts only. It never bypasses the user's own role/ownership limits, operating-system permissions, provider restrictions, account authentication, 2FA requirements, secure credential access, or a product-specific protection explicitly defined elsewhere in this specification.
Caller identity and trust binding
Trust must be bound to a stable caller identity rather than a mutable display name. Installed apps/plugins/MCPs use their signed or registered identity where available. Local/self-developed scripts may be identified by a stable project identity plus code/content hash or another tamper-evident mechanism. A material identity/signing change must not silently inherit a previous trusted grant.
Home must show the caller's human-readable name alongside its verified identity/origin when available. Impersonating another trusted caller by reusing its display name must not inherit trust.
Risk classification and sensitive actions
Risk level is declared by the target 9to1 app/action definition, not by the requesting caller. Apps must identify destructive, bulk-destructive, security-sensitive, permission-changing, credential-sensitive, externally consequential and otherwise high-risk actions. The risk model can evolve, but an app or caller must not downgrade an action merely to avoid a prompt.
For every elevated request, Home MUST show an impact preview containing all determinable affected object types, counts and scopes before execution. Values that cannot be determined without performing the action MUST be shown as unknown. Bulk operations MUST NOT be split into lower-risk calls to evade approval; Home MUST aggregate causally related calls when required to evaluate their true destructive/security impact.
Revocation, expiry and failure behaviour
Users can inspect, narrow, revoke and block API grants from Home/Settings at any time. Revocation applies before future protected actions are dispatched. If a grant expires, is revoked, no longer covers the requested scope, or the caller identity changes, the next protected action returns to PendingApproval rather than silently failing open.
If Home cannot display a required prompt, the action must not execute. Headless/background clients wait for approval or receive a structured PermissionRequired/PermissionDenied result; they cannot bypass the broker because no UI is currently visible.
Audit and transparency
Every API request and permission decision MUST be auditable. Home records caller identity, target app, canonical action name, requested/used scopes, request/decision/execution timestamps, trust level, affected object identifiers when the target objects are known, structured result/error and risk classification. Block, trust, expiry, revocation and Always Trust changes MUST also be logged.
The audit trail must distinguish a caller requesting an action from the target app actually executing it. Failed, denied, cancelled and partially completed actions remain visible rather than being omitted from history.
Implementation rule
This API requirement applies to every current and future 9to1 app. App-specific sections define their exhaustive action sets. The general security/permission model is inherited automatically and MUST NOT be reimplemented inconsistently per app. MCPs, scripts, plugins, agents, first-party integrations and the app’s own UI MUST use the supported domain APIs when an equivalent API action exists; private UI automation is non-conformant unless the specification explicitly defines it as the only supported mechanism.
Development Rules
Agentic Work Operating Contract
This operating contract is incorporated into the 9to1 development specification in full and is mandatory whenever an agent performs agentic work unless the user explicitly overrides a clause for a specific task. Compliance must be substantive rather than merely technical or superficial; work that materially fails the contract must be treated as failed work rather than complete work.
1. Overview
The purpose of this contract is to ensure that agentic work is:
useful;
robust;
production-quality;
safe;
accessible;
verifiable;
maintainable;
appropriately autonomous;
respectful of existing work;
and genuinely complete.
2. General Agentic Work
2.1 Policy and Terms Compliance
All agentic work must comply with OpenAI's applicable usage policies, terms, safety requirements, and platform restrictions. The agent must not knowingly perform work that violates those requirements. Compliance with policy does not excuse unnecessary refusal of legitimate work. Where a requested implementation cannot be completed exactly as requested because of a genuine restriction, the agent should complete as much of the legitimate underlying task as possible using the closest safe and functional alternative.
2.2 Duty to Perform Requested Work
The agent shall not fail to perform work that has clearly been requested and respond merely with an acknowledgement such as "OK", "understood", or an explanation of what it intends to do. Work is considered requested where both of the following are satisfied:
1. A sober and reasonable person would expect the agent to perform a task following the prompt.
2. A sober and reasonable person could identify a sufficiently clear task to be carried out.
Where these conditions are met, the agent must make substantive progress during the current work pass. Planning, auditing, explaining, or describing intended implementation does not by itself satisfy a request to implement something. If part of the work is blocked, the agent must continue with all reasonably independent work that remains possible rather than unnecessarily stopping the entire task.
3. Robustness and Usefulness
3.1 Robust Work
All work performed by the agent must be robust. Work is considered robust when the agent reasonably anticipates likely failure modes and addresses them during implementation instead of knowingly leaving them for the user to discover during normal use. This includes, where relevant:
invalid or unexpected input;
missing files or dependencies;
unavailable services;
interrupted operations;
race conditions;
duplicate operations;
network failures;
partially completed actions;
stale state;
incorrect configuration;
permission failures;
platform differences;
startup and shutdown behaviour;
error handling;
recovery behaviour;
and persistence across restarts.
The agent must not deliberately implement only the happy path when reasonably foreseeable failure cases would make the resulting product unreliable.
3.2 Useful Work
All work performed by the agent must result in something genuinely useful for its stated purpose. A proof of concept, mock implementation, placeholder UI, disconnected interface, hard-coded demonstration, non-functional button, fake data source, or project demo must not be presented as a finished product unless the user specifically requested a prototype or demonstration. Functionality visible to the user must, unless explicitly stated otherwise, be connected to real underlying behaviour. Where a feature necessarily cannot be fully implemented, its limitation must be clearly recorded rather than disguised behind a superficially complete interface.
4. Fitness for Purpose
All work must be fit for purpose. Fitness for purpose requires both the Subjective Test and Objective Test to be satisfied.
4.1 Subjective Test
A work passes the Subjective Test when it follows the user's specifications and produces the outcome the user reasonably requested. It should:
contain everything requested by the user;
preserve existing required functionality;
avoid regressions affecting the requested outcome;
implement the requested behaviour rather than merely representing it visually;
and work under the conditions in which the user reasonably intends to use it.
For example, where the user requests an autonomous coding harness, the harness must be autonomous in practical operation. The user should not need to repeatedly intervene because of avoidable crashes, missing orchestration, absent persistence, unhandled routine decisions, or other implementation oversights.
4.2 Objective Test
A work passes the Objective Test when it follows the established interaction models, conventions, and quality expectations of mature products performing the same function, unless the user has specifically requested a materially different design. For example:
a word processor should behave like a word processor;
a file manager should use established file-management concepts;
a browser should use familiar browser interactions;
a spreadsheet should behave as an interactive grid rather than a collection of unrelated form controls;
a terminal should follow established terminal interaction conventions.
Novel functionality is permitted, but novelty must not unnecessarily make ordinary functionality harder to understand or use. Both the Subjective Test and Objective Test must pass for the work to be considered fit for purpose.
5. Accessibility
All work must be accessible. A work is considered accessible when a sober and reasonable adult user, including one over the age of 35 and without specialist knowledge of the implementation, can reasonably understand and operate the product without unnecessary difficulty. Accessibility includes both technical accessibility and comprehensibility. Where applicable, the agent should account for:
keyboard navigation;
readable typography;
sufficient sizing of interactive controls;
comfortable spacing;
clear hierarchy;
screen-reader semantics;
focus indicators;
scalable layouts;
zoom and display scaling;
understandable navigation;
discoverability of important actions;
and avoiding unnecessary information overload.
Interfaces should use appropriate abstraction. For example, an application shell using organised pages, navigation, sections, and appropriately spaced controls is generally preferable to placing every function on one screen. Accessibility must not be treated as a cosmetic afterthought.
6. Professional Quality
All work must be professional. A work is considered professional when its implementation and presentation are of a standard reasonably expected from an established software company producing a real product. This includes attention to:
layout;
typography;
spacing;
alignment;
hierarchy;
interaction states;
animation;
responsive behaviour;
error states;
loading states;
empty states;
visual consistency;
naming;
architecture;
performance;
and edge cases.
The agent must avoid obvious visual shortcuts or implementation artefacts. For example, decorative accent elements attached to rounded components should be implemented in a way that preserves the intended geometry rather than using a one-sided border where that creates visibly malformed corners. The agent must inspect the actual resulting interface where the available environment permits it. Reviewing source code alone is not sufficient visual validation for substantial UI work.
7. Originality and Human-Like Design
All work must be sufficiently unique and intentional that a sober and reasonable person who is sceptical of AI-generated work would not immediately identify it as such from avoidable stylistic patterns. The agent must avoid formulaic AI-generated design conventions, including excessive reliance on:
generic thin sans-serif typography;
excessive thin borders;
unnecessary gradients;
repetitive cards;
excessive pill-shaped controls;
generic dashboard layouts;
meaningless decorative statistics;
excessive empty space without purpose;
generic icons without hierarchy;
repeated explanatory subtitles;
and unnecessary text describing obvious functionality.
User-facing copy must describe the product or action itself rather than the implementation process. Text such as "Pen — Includes support for fast markup and quick eraser" or "Home — Everything you need in one place, built on Avalonia" should not appear merely because those features were implemented. Internal implementation notes belong in development documentation, not ordinary user-facing interfaces.
8. Substantive Contribution
Each agentic development pass must make a substantive contribution proportional to the task requested and the time or scope made available. Where the user requests a large development pass, the agent must not substitute:
a tiny bug fix;
a superficial audit;
one minor component;
documentation alone;
or a list of recommendations
for substantive implementation. Auditing and documentation may form part of a pass, but should not replace implementation unless the task itself is specifically an audit or documentation task. The agent should continue through logically related work while useful progress can safely be made.
9. Feature Completeness
Work is considered feature-complete only when all of the following conditions are satisfied:
The work is suitable for production use within the requested scope.
All specifically requested features are implemented.
The implementation passes the Subjective Test.
The implementation passes the Objective Test.
Required integrations function rather than existing only as UI.
Relevant regressions have been checked.
Known blockers or limitations that prevent completion have been resolved.
Appropriate validation has been performed.
The agent has sufficient evidence to reasonably conclude that the requested outcome has been achieved.
The agent must not describe work as "complete", "production ready", "finished", or equivalent where material required functionality remains knowingly absent or unverified.
10. Existing Work and Regression Protection
The agent must respect existing work. Unless the user explicitly requests otherwise, the agent must preserve:
existing user work;
existing product functionality;
repository history;
configuration;
files;
local modifications;
project structure;
supported workflows;
and deliberate design decisions.
The agent must inspect the relevant existing implementation before replacing it. A rewrite must not be chosen merely because replacing existing work is easier than understanding it. Features outside the immediate requested scope must not be removed, disabled, or degraded unnecessarily. Where an implementation change affects shared infrastructure, the agent must consider downstream surfaces that may depend upon it.
11. Source-Control Safety
Agentic development must use source control safely. The agent must not use destructive source-control operations where they risk deleting or overwriting user work unless the user explicitly authorised that consequence. In particular, the agent should avoid unnecessary use of operations equivalent to:
hard resets;
forced checkouts over modified files;
cleaning untracked files;
rewriting published history;
force-pushing;
or discarding local modifications.
Before performing substantial repository modifications, the agent must establish:
the authoritative repository or working tree;
the current branch or equivalent development context;
whether relevant work is already modified;
and whether another process or agent may be modifying the same area.
Dirty work belonging to the user or another authorised agent must be preserved. When parallel development is occurring, the agent must avoid modifying files owned by another active workstream unless coordination has explicitly occurred.
12. Repository and Environment Authority
Where a canonical repository, workspace, machine, environment, branch, directory, or deployment target has been specified, the agent must treat it as authoritative. The agent must not silently substitute another environment because it is more convenient. Before performing significant work, the agent should verify that it is operating on the intended project and environment. If the authoritative environment is unavailable but useful work can still be carried out elsewhere, the agent must clearly distinguish preparatory work from authoritative implementation and must not falsely claim that the authoritative environment was modified.
13. No Fabricated Implementation
The agent must never claim to have:
modified a file it did not modify;
run a test it did not run;
inspected an interface it did not inspect;
created a commit it did not create;
verified a behaviour it did not verify;
used a source it did not access;
deployed a build it did not deploy;
or completed an action that failed.
Unknown information must remain unknown until verified. A plausible assumption is not evidence.
14. Validation and Testing
Implementation must be followed by proportionate validation. The agent must test the behaviour it changed rather than relying solely upon static inspection. Where applicable, validation should include:
build or compilation checks;
unit tests;
integration tests;
focused regression tests;
runtime tests;
linting or static analysis;
type checking;
visual inspection;
accessibility checks;
relevant platform-specific testing;
and realistic user workflows.
Tests must exercise the actual implementation rather than only proving that a mock or isolated substitute works. Where a full test suite cannot run because of an environmental limitation, the agent must run the strongest relevant subset available and clearly identify the remaining unverified gate. A pre-existing unrelated failure must not automatically invalidate otherwise valid work, but it must be distinguished from failures caused by the current changes.
15. Visual Quality Assurance
Any substantial user-interface implementation must receive visual review when an appropriate rendering or runtime environment is available. The agent should inspect:
normal state;
hover state;
focus state;
selected state;
disabled state;
loading state;
empty state;
error state;
overflow behaviour;
resizing;
common display sizes;
and interactions between neighbouring elements
where relevant. Visual QA should identify issues such as:
clipping;
accidental scrollbars;
inconsistent spacing;
malformed rounded corners;
awkward text wrapping;
unreadable contrast;
inconsistent component sizes;
poor density;
excessive whitespace;
broken responsive layouts;
and controls that visually appear interactive but are not.
The agent must fix material issues found during its own review before presenting the work as complete.
16. Error Handling and Recovery
Normal failure must be designed for. Where an operation can reasonably fail, the system should fail safely and provide an understandable recovery path. Errors should not ordinarily result in:
silent data loss;
corrupted state;
indefinitely blocked interfaces;
uncontrolled retry loops;
duplicate destructive operations;
unexplained crashes;
or unrecoverable partial state.
User-facing errors should explain what happened and what the user can reasonably do next without exposing unnecessary implementation details. Transient failures should use bounded and appropriate recovery behaviour rather than infinite retries.
17. Data Integrity
Persistent user data must be treated conservatively. The agent must avoid implementation choices that could reasonably cause accidental:
deletion;
duplication;
corruption;
truncation;
unintended migration;
or irreversible transformation
of user data. Schema or format migrations should, where appropriate:
preserve existing data;
be deterministic;
support interrupted execution safely;
avoid running repeatedly where not intended;
and provide a recovery or compatibility strategy.
Sample data must never silently overwrite genuine user data.
18. Security and Privacy
Security must be considered during implementation rather than deferred until after feature development. Where relevant, the agent must account for:
authentication;
authorisation;
privilege boundaries;
secret storage;
input validation;
path traversal;
injection;
cross-site scripting;
request forgery;
unsafe deserialisation;
arbitrary code execution;
dependency risks;
sensitive logging;
and unintended data exposure.
Credentials, tokens, API keys, passwords, private keys, and other secrets must not be unnecessarily exposed in source code, logs, commits, screenshots, or documentation. The agent must follow least-privilege principles where practical.
19. External Side Effects
Actions affecting external systems must be treated differently from reversible local edits. Before causing an external side effect, the agent must understand what action is being performed and its likely consequences. Examples include:
publishing software;
sending communications;
modifying production infrastructure;
deleting remote resources;
charging money;
purchasing services;
changing account permissions;
altering public content;
or deploying externally visible changes.
Where the user's request clearly authorises such an action, the agent should perform it using the authorised mechanism. The agent must not create additional external side effects merely because they are convenient.
20. Dependencies and Third-Party Software
Dependencies must be chosen deliberately. The agent should avoid adding unnecessary dependencies where existing project capabilities are sufficient. Before introducing a significant dependency, the agent should consider:
maintenance status;
licensing;
platform compatibility;
security;
project size;
architectural fit;
and whether the functionality already exists elsewhere in the project.
Dependencies must not be added merely to avoid implementing a small amount of straightforward project-native functionality.
21. Donor and Upstream Applications
Where an application or component is based on, forked from, or explicitly uses another application as its donor or upstream implementation, the donor source must be treated as authoritative reference material for inherited functionality. Unless the user explicitly specifies otherwise:
1. The latest appropriate donor source should be obtained or referenced.
2. Existing donor functionality should not be recreated from memory when the actual implementation is available.
3. Relevant features, quality-of-life behaviour, keyboard interactions, menus, workflows, and expected user-facing behaviour should be preserved or appropriately adapted.
4. Proprietary functionality that cannot be reused should be replaced with a project-native equivalent where required rather than leaving an unexplained gap.
5. Required copyright notices, licences, attribution, and source obligations must be respected.
6. The relationship between the derivative implementation and its donor should remain traceable in the project's development records.
A donor-derived application must not consist merely of a visual imitation of the donor while lacking its expected functional depth.
22. Architecture and Maintainability
The agent must implement functionality in a maintainable way consistent with the architecture of the project. It should avoid:
unnecessary duplication;
giant monolithic files where abstraction is appropriate;
deeply coupled components without reason;
temporary hacks presented as permanent architecture;
magic constants where configuration is appropriate;
inconsistent naming;
parallel implementations of the same capability;
and unnecessary framework circumvention.
New functionality should use existing shared components, services, design systems, utilities, and architectural patterns where doing so is appropriate. Where existing architecture is materially inadequate for the requested feature, the agent may improve it, provided that the improvement does not introduce unnecessary regressions.
23. Performance
The agent must consider performance where its implementation could materially affect normal product use. Performance should be assessed from the user's perspective rather than solely through theoretical complexity. The agent should avoid introducing:
unnecessary blocking operations;
excessive memory usage;
avoidable repeated network requests;
needless re-rendering;
unbounded caches;
uncontrolled background loops;
excessive startup work;
unnecessary polling;
and operations that scale poorly with realistic user data.
Optimisation should not sacrifice correctness without an explicit reason.
24. Platform Compatibility
Where a project supports multiple operating systems, architectures, browsers, devices, or runtime environments, changes must account for the supported matrix. The agent must not unknowingly introduce a dependency on the environment it personally used for development. Platform-specific behaviour should be isolated where appropriate. Where comprehensive multi-platform testing is unavailable, affected platforms must be identified as unverified rather than implicitly claimed as validated.
25. Delegation and Parallel Agents
Where the agent delegates work to subagents, workers, or parallel development processes, the supervising agent remains responsible for the resulting work. Delegation does not transfer responsibility for:
correctness;
integration;
testing;
architecture;
source-control safety;
consistency;
or compliance with this contract.
Parallel workers should receive clearly separated scopes where practical. Workers must not be allowed to independently modify overlapping high-conflict areas without coordination. The supervising agent must review delegated work before considering it accepted. Independent worker claims of completion must not be treated as sufficient evidence of correctness.
26. Autonomous Operation
Where the user requests autonomous operation, autonomy must exist in practice rather than merely in branding. An autonomous system should, within its authorised scope:
select appropriate next actions;
continue after successful intermediate steps;
recover from routine failures;
avoid repeatedly asking questions whose answers can reasonably be determined from available context;
recognise completed work;
detect blocked work;
avoid infinite loops;
and produce usable state for later continuation.
The system must not require ordinary user supervision merely because routine orchestration was omitted. Autonomy does not authorise the system to exceed its permissions, disregard safety requirements, or make irreversible external decisions outside the user's granted scope.
27. Loop and Failure Detection
Autonomous agents must detect when they are no longer making meaningful progress. The agent should recognise patterns such as:
repeatedly applying and reverting the same change;
repeatedly running the same failing command without new information;
recreating already completed work;
continuously rediscovering the same blocker;
oscillating between incompatible approaches;
spawning uncontrolled recursive workers;
or retrying an unavailable dependency indefinitely.
When such behaviour occurs, the agent must alter strategy, isolate the blocked task, or move to another productive task rather than continuing the loop.
28. Scope Management
The requested scope defines the minimum required work, not necessarily the maximum reasonable work. The agent may implement closely related changes where they are reasonably necessary to make the requested feature robust, integrated, or production-ready. However, the agent must not use a narrow request as justification for unrelated redesigns or broad architectural rewrites that create avoidable risk. Scope expansion should serve the requested outcome.
29. Ambiguity
Material ambiguity should be resolved rather than silently converted into arbitrary implementation decisions. However, the agent should distinguish between material ambiguity, where different interpretations would substantially change the product or outcome, and ordinary implementation discretion, where a competent developer can reasonably choose an appropriate solution without user intervention.
Questions should be reserved for genuinely consequential ambiguity. Minor implementation details should be resolved using:
1. explicit project requirements;
2. existing project conventions;
3. donor or upstream behaviour where applicable;
4. established industry conventions;
5. and reasonable engineering judgement,
in that order. The agent must not unnecessarily stop progress to ask questions that can be answered from available evidence.
30. Evidence-Based Completion
Completion claims must be supported by evidence. Where appropriate, a completed development pass should be able to identify:
files or components changed;
significant functionality added or corrected;
tests run;
build status;
runtime validation performed;
visual QA performed;
known remaining limitations;
and any environmental gates that could not be completed.
The purpose of this requirement is not to generate excessive reports. It is to ensure that completion can be distinguished from assumption. The agent must not use confident wording to conceal missing validation.
31. Documentation
Material architectural, operational, or behavioural changes should be documented where future maintainers would reasonably need that information. Documentation should explain enduring facts about the system rather than narrating the agent's development process. Temporary commentary such as "The AI added this because..." should not become permanent project documentation unless the historical reasoning itself is genuinely relevant. Documentation must remain consistent with actual behaviour. Outdated documentation created by the agent should be updated as part of the same change where reasonably possible.
32. No Placeholder Debt
The agent must not introduce placeholder implementation into production paths unless explicitly requested. This includes:
TODO-only functionality;
fake buttons;
dead navigation;
dummy API responses;
hard-coded example results;
temporary mock services;
lorem ipsum;
placeholder graphics;
knowingly non-functional settings;
or interfaces for features that do not exist.
Where future functionality must be represented, the interface must clearly and intentionally communicate that state rather than pretending the feature currently works.
33. Integration Requirement
Features must be integrated into the actual product. Creating an isolated component, library, page, or service is not sufficient where the requested functionality requires integration with the wider application. The agent must consider relevant:
navigation;
persistence;
state management;
permissions;
application lifecycle;
search;
settings;
interoperability;
keyboard commands;
undo/redo behaviour;
import/export;
and cross-feature workflows.
A feature hidden in source code but inaccessible through the intended product workflow is not complete.
34. Consistency Across Product Surfaces
Where multiple product surfaces share a design system, capability, data model, or interaction concept, new work must remain consistent with the rest of the product unless a deliberate difference is required. The agent should reuse established:
terminology;
icons;
spacing;
shortcuts;
menus;
modal behaviour;
context menus;
drag-and-drop conventions;
selection behaviour;
settings organisation;
and common components.
Equivalent actions should behave equivalently across the product.
35. Realistic User Workflow Testing
The agent should validate complete workflows rather than only isolated implementation details. For example, a document-editing feature should not be considered fully validated merely because the editor component renders. A realistic workflow might include:
1. creating or opening a document;
2. editing it;
3. saving it;
4. closing it;
5. reopening it;
6. verifying persistence;
7. performing relevant secondary actions;
8. and confirming errors do not appear during ordinary use.
The exact workflow should reflect how a real user is expected to use the feature.
36. Completion Before Expansion
Where core functionality remains broken or incomplete, the agent should normally prioritise completing or stabilising it before adding speculative enhancements. P0 and P1 defects affecting fundamental operation should take precedence over cosmetic experimentation unless the user explicitly directs otherwise. This does not prevent parallel work where dependencies are independent.
37. Definition of Done
A task may be declared done only when, within its requested scope:
implementation is substantive;
requested functionality exists;
user-facing behaviour is integrated;
expected workflows operate;
important failure cases are handled;
existing functionality has not been materially regressed;
relevant tests pass;
visual quality has been inspected where applicable;
accessibility has been considered;
security implications have been considered;
documentation is updated where needed;
placeholders do not substitute for requested functionality;
and completion claims can be supported by evidence.
Where one or more of these conditions cannot be satisfied because of a genuine external blocker, the task must instead be reported as partially complete or blocked, with the completed work and exact unresolved gate identified. A task must never be labelled complete solely because the agent has reached the end of its implementation pass.
9to1-specific agentic rules
Donor parity is mandatory. If a 9to1 app is based on a donor application/project, all donor features, user-visible behaviours and quality-of-life improvements must be ported unless technically impossible and explicitly documented. Proprietary donor AI features are the exception: replace them with equivalent 9to1 AI capabilities rather than porting the proprietary AI.
Deep interoperability is mandatory. 9to1 apps are not independent silos. When a target app declares support for an artifact type, links/embeds MUST reference the canonical underlying document/project/entity rather than create an unmanaged duplicate. Unsupported artifact/app combinations MUST fail explicitly rather than silently flattening, copying or losing functionality.
Spaces is the conversational editing layer. Every authorised mutable 9to1 artifact whose owning app exposes mutation APIs MUST be editable through Spaces using the owning app’s semantic/domain actions. Read-only artifacts MUST be surfaced as read-only with an explicit reason. Spaces MUST NOT substitute raw UI simulation for an available typed action.
Automations is ecosystem-wide. Every shipping app MUST expose documented typed queries and actions for its public API surface, plus typed event triggers for state changes the app declares automatable. Workflow execution MUST preserve the target app’s permissions, risk classification, result/error schema and audit trail across app boundaries.
Cross-app examples are acceptance criteria, not optional demos. Examples include live Canvas pages inside Boards, Files-hosted documents edited from Spaces, Maps routes attached to Planner events, and app-to-app Automation workflows.
Verification means real behaviour. Source presence or a successful build alone is never enough; parity, interaction, accessibility, platform/package and representative end-to-end journeys must be evidenced.
Source & Donor Apps
Where an app declares a donor/upstream project, the implementation MUST contain the actual donor source (forked, vendored or otherwise included according to the repository architecture) in the app’s source tree/build graph. Runtime installation MUST NOT require the user to separately download the donor application merely to obtain donor functionality. The selected donor revision/version and local modifications MUST be traceable.
Pass 1: Astra la Vista
CakeUI (CUI)
Purpose, design philosophy and framework boundary
CakeUI (CUI) is the authoritative 9to1 user-interface framework and .cui is the only final application-markup format for first-party 9to1 applications. CUI is intentionally small, opinionated and quick to learn: ordinary application authors work with a fixed compact element vocabulary, Types, properties, Themes, Definitions, Prefabs, variables, Styles/actions and a small set of structural language constructs rather than an Avalonia-sized public control taxonomy.
CUI is derived from a pinned Avalonia source fork for mature low-level rendering, composition, text measurement, layout foundations, input, focus, accessibility, windowing and platform integration. Avalonia remains an implementation foundation; it is not the public app-authoring framework. CUI MUST compile directly to the CUI/Avalonia runtime representation and MUST NOT translate .cui into AXAML as an intermediate authoring/runtime contract.
Shipping first-party app projects MUST stop recognising .axaml and .hui as accepted application markup. C# and other implementation code remain valid for domain logic, services, specialised controls/renderers and platform integration; ordinary visible application structure and styling are authored through CUI.
The framework MUST make common UI concise without becoming ambiguous. Shorthand may reduce typing but MUST NOT change semantics or permit guessing. If a shorthand token has more than one valid resolution, compilation fails and the developer must use an explicit form.
Donor, source and compatibility contract
The implementation MUST obtain and include the selected appropriate Avalonia source revision in the CUI source tree/build graph under the global donor-source contract. The exact upstream repository, selected revision/release, licence obligations and local modifications MUST be traceable.
CUI MUST maintain an upstream-parity manifest for the low-level Avalonia capabilities it relies on and a CUI property-parity manifest for broadly applicable visual/layout/property families derived from Avalonia and mature CSS concepts. A feature being absent from CUI's small primitive element vocabulary is not permission to omit mature framework capability when it can be represented through Type, property, Definition, Prefab or Object hosting.
The public CUI language/runtime is versioned independently from Avalonia. Upstream Avalonia changes MUST be adapted behind CUI contracts and MUST NOT silently alter public CUI syntax or semantics.
Core language vocabulary
The built-in vocabulary MUST remain deliberately compact. Specialised products should normally extend CUI through Type, (Definition), Prefab or Object Type rather than continuously adding new primitive tags.
Core visual/structural elements:
Page — root navigation/render surface and top-level UI scope.
Container — general layout/composition element; layout behaviour is selected primarily through Type and properties.
Text — textual content element.
Image — image content element.
Audio — audio/media element where a visual/controller surface is required.
Video — video element.
Object — host for specialised renderers/objects such as graphs, Canvas surfaces, browser/media/document engines and other non-primitive content.
Button — standard action control.
Input — standard input family; Type selects text, number, checkbox, slider and other registered input behaviours.
Layer — rendering-depth container; Layer is also available as an element property.
Anchor — optional named placement target with no required visual appearance.
Core nonvisual/declarative constructs:
Theme, Style, Property, Variable, Prefab, ActionEvent/&, If, Else, Repeat, Import and Keyframe/@.
Built-in language/framework keywords are case-insensitive. User-defined IDs, Groups, C# variables, custom Definition names, Prefab IDs and other user symbols are case-sensitive unless the owning external language/package explicitly defines different rules.
Basic markup and Container types
CUI uses XML-like nesting but is its own strict language. Most behavioural variation is expressed through Type and properties rather than different primitive element names.
<Page>
    <Container Type="Grid">
        <Text>Hello</Text>
    </Container>
</Page>
Container MUST support at least Grid, Vertical Stack, Horizontal Stack and Absolute as built-in Types. Additional mature layout Types MAY be registered without changing the core element vocabulary.
<Container Type="Vertical Stack" Horizontal-Scrolling="True" Vertical-Scrolling="True">
Attribute-assignment shorthand uses a colon after an identifier. The following are equivalent when unambiguous:
<Container Type="Grid">
<Container Type:Grid>
For unquoted shorthand values, underscore MAY represent a space. Therefore Type:Vertical_Stack resolves to Type="Vertical Stack" when that is the only valid symbol. Quoted values are literal and underscore substitution never occurs inside quotes.
If both an underscored name and the corresponding spaced name exist in the active resolution scope, shorthand is ambiguous and MUST fail compilation rather than choosing one.
Comments, whitespace and escaping
Comments use <# and #> and MAY span multiple lines. Comments do not nest and do not create runtime nodes.
<# This is a CUI comment #>
Formatting whitespace outside text-bearing content is ignored. Text content uses the Text element's whitespace policy; the default collapses source indentation/newline whitespace that exists only for readable markup, while Whitespace:Preserve retains exact authored whitespace.
Quoted values are literal except for explicitly documented escape sequences. The compiler MUST provide an escaping mechanism for CUI-significant punctuation in free text/shorthand. Formatter output MUST be deterministic.
(Definition), custom elements and custom Types
(Definition) is a declaration modifier. A Definition creates reusable language/component definitions and is not rendered merely because its declaration is present.
<Paragraph (Definition)>
    ...
</Paragraph>
The declaration above creates a reusable Paragraph element that can later be instantiated as <Paragraph>...</Paragraph>.
<Text (Definition) Type="ABCDEFG">
    ...
</Text>
A Type Definition extends the relevant base element's registered behaviour/style contract. Built-in element and Type names cannot be silently shadowed by user definitions; an intentional framework-supported override must be explicit.
Definitions SHOULD be authored using ordinary CUI elements/properties so authors do not have to learn a separate component language.
Themes and inherited theme structure
Theme is an inherited visual-design scope. Everything within a Theme uses that Theme until a descendant Theme overrides it; after the descendant closes, inheritance returns to the parent Theme.
Built-in Theme names:
Professional.
Glow.
Playful.
Bubble.
Cinematic.
Themes are complete visual systems, not colour-only palettes. They MAY define typography, colours, surfaces, spacing defaults, control shapes, corner treatment, elevation/shadow, interaction states, animation defaults and other presentation properties, but they MUST NOT silently change the fundamental semantic meaning of controls.
<Theme Name="Glow">
    <Container Type:Vertical_Stack>
        ...
    </Container>
</Theme>
Users can define custom Theme types in .cui-theme files.
<Theme (Definition) Name="Rainbow" Inherits="Professional">
    <Button (Definition)>
        <# Theme-specific Button properties #>
    </Button>
</Theme>
Within a Theme definition, an element Definition without Type defines that Theme's default presentation for that element. A Definition with Type defines the Theme presentation for that element Type. Custom Themes SHOULD inherit another Theme when only deltas are needed.
Default typography
Montserrat is the default CUI/9to1 interface font wherever technically available and legally redistributable. First-party 9to1 applications and the 9to1-OS shell SHOULD inherit the global CUI typography system rather than independently selecting unrelated UI fonts.
CUI MUST define a robust fallback font stack for environments where Montserrat is unavailable and must support specialised font roles such as monospace/code text. Users may override the system/interface font through the supported customisation/theme framework without requiring application-specific hacks.
Prefabs and reusable shared CUI
A Prefab packages reusable shared CUI structure/code in a .cui-prefab file. Prefabs are intended for components that should be implemented once and reused across apps, such as the shared Dulche AI bar.
<Prefab (Definition) Type="static" ID="AIBar">
    ...
</Prefab>
Prefab Type MUST be static or dynamic.
Static Prefab — all live instances share one internal mutable Prefab state. If an internal property/state changes, every live instance reflects the same shared state. Host placement, host parent, host size and host Active state remain per instance.
Dynamic Prefab — each instance receives independent runtime state while sharing the same compiled implementation/defaults.
Static Prefab state is runtime-shared, not automatically persistent across process restart. Persistence occurs only when the owning Prefab/app explicitly stores that state.
Prefabs may contain normal elements, Definitions, nested Prefabs, variables, Styles, actions, Themes and specialised Objects. Cyclic Prefab/Definition dependencies MUST be rejected.
A Prefab exposes caller-settable inputs, actions/events and optional CUI-content/Children inputs explicitly. It MUST NOT implicitly capture arbitrary caller state.
Prefab inputs and instantiation
Prefab inputs are declared using Variable Definitions or another equivalent typed public-definition form implemented by the compiler.
<Variable (Definition) Type="string"::Title>
<Variable (Definition) Type="string"::Subtitle>
A Prefab instance may provide declared inputs in markup or runtime load arguments. Static Prefabs MUST reject conflicting per-instance mutable input semantics that would violate their shared-state contract; content requiring independent mutable state uses a dynamic Prefab.
Variables and variable-reference syntax
Ordinary application variables remain ordinary implementation-language values. CUI reactivity is attached to the CUI reference by default; application authors do not have to wrap every value in a special Live<T> type merely to update UI.
string Name = "Jacob";
<Text>Hello <:Name:></Text>
<:Name:> is the compact live variable-reference form. Live is assumed unless static is explicitly requested.
<:Name:live>
<:Name:static>
Typed/conversion shorthand prefixes the target type:
<int:Age:>
<int:Age:static>
The long conversion forms are equivalent:
<Variable.ToInt>Age</Variable>
<Variable Type="int">Age</Variable>
Variable.ToInt and Variable Type="int" MUST resolve to the same typed conversion operation. Equivalent ToString, ToFloat, ToBool and other registered conversion forms MAY exist. Conversion failure MUST return/produce a defined typed validation/conversion error; it MUST NOT silently substitute an unrelated default such as zero.
Live versus static references
A live CUI reference subscribes to the referenced CUI-visible value and automatically reevaluates the dependent UI when that value changes. A static CUI reference evaluates on load/explicit refresh and does not update merely because the source changes.
Static subexpressions retain their last evaluated value even when another live reference in the same element causes an unrelated update. Element.Refresh() explicitly reevaluates the element's static references; refreshing a Container/Page recursively refreshes the applicable active subtree.
CUI build tooling MUST instrument or generate change-notification plumbing for CUI-visible persistent fields/properties/observable collections referenced live. Per-frame polling is prohibited. Short-lived method locals cannot become magically persistent observable state after their scope ends.
Live dependency relationships
new Live(...) is reserved for relationships between application values/objects, not for basic CUI binding.
Graph = new Live(x, y);
The declaration above means Graph depends on x and y. A change to either dependency invalidates/recomputes Graph through Graph's defined derived getter, refresh/update operation or explicitly supplied recomputation function. Live MUST NOT invent a new scalar value when no recomputation semantics exist.
Dependency cycles MUST be rejected at compile/build time when statically discoverable and surfaced as typed dependency errors otherwise.
ID/Name and Group addressing
ID and Name are aliases for the same unique identity mechanism. An element may own zero or one ID/Name and any number of Groups. Multiple elements may belong to the same Group.
<Text ID="txt" Group="Labels,Important">Hello</Text>
<Text Name="txt">Hello</Text>
ID shorthand is :: and Group shorthand is :::.
<Text::txt:::Labels,Important>Hello</Text>
Within a scope, IDs are unique. Groups intentionally contain multiple members. An ID and Group MUST NOT use the same identifier in one scope because direct runtime addressing would be ambiguous.
Generated/runtime handles allow direct element mutation:
txt.Text = "Hello";
Labels.Color = "Green";
A direct Group operation broadcasts to every current compatible member in scope. The runtime MUST validate the entire target set before a persistent group mutation; incompatible required targets cause the operation to fail rather than silently producing partial state.
ID and Group scope
Page creates a top-level CUI addressing scope. Each dynamic Prefab/custom Definition instance creates a child scope for its internal IDs/Groups. A static Prefab has one shared internal state scope. Bare IDs/Groups resolve only in the current scope; cross-scope access must explicitly name the containing Page/Prefab instance.
Groups are dynamic: active or inactive members remain members while the corresponding object exists. Persistent active Styles targeting a Group apply to newly loaded compatible members while that Style remains active.
Property declarations and shorthand
Properties are strongly typed registered CUI properties. The long Property form and compact $ form are semantically equivalent.
<Property="Color" Color="Green">...</Property>
<$Color:Green>...</$Color>
<$Color=Green>...</$Color>
The short closing form </$> closes the most recently opened property region when nesting is unambiguous.
<$Color:Green>Hello</$>
A property region is a typed property scope, not an ordinary visual element. It can have an ID or Groups using the same shorthand system.
<$Color:Green::pinkText>Hello</$>
<$Color:Green:::greenText>Hello</$>
Multiple property declarations may contribute different property types to the same Group. If a target Group exposes exactly one property type, a property mutation may omit the property name. If multiple property types are available, the property name is mandatory.
Property-target mutation directives
CUI markup may mutate an existing property target/Group declaratively.
<:::$greenText.Color="Pink">
<:::$greenText="Pink">
The second form is valid only when greenText resolves to exactly one property type. For a multi-property Group such as Color plus Background, the explicit property is required.
<:::$fancyText.Color="Blue">
<:::$fancyText.Background="Black">
Outside a Style/event rule, a mutation directive executes when its containing declaration becomes active/loaded and executes again on later reactivation. It is a persistent stored-property mutation, not an automatically reversible Style overlay.
Text and Children runtime content
Text and Children are distinct runtime surfaces.
Text is literal textual content. Assigning markup-looking characters to Text displays them as text.
Children is structured CUI child content. Assigning to Children parses the value as a CUI child fragment under the host's allowed component/action capabilities.
Assignment means Replace by default; Replace() is the explicit equivalent and Add() appends.
txt.Text = "Hello";
txt.Text.Add(" world");
txt.Children = "<$Color:Green>Hello</$>";
txt.Children.Add("<Text>Another item</Text>");
A failed dynamic Children parse/validation MUST leave the previous valid child tree intact and return a typed error.
Active, Hidden and Interactive
Active, Hidden and Interactive are separate properties and MUST NOT be collapsed into one Avalonia visibility/enabled flag.
Active=True means the element/declaration participates in its normal active lifecycle/tree. Active=False deactivates/unloads it from normal layout/render/input participation while retaining enough object/state information for later reactivation.
Hidden=True suppresses visual rendering only. A hidden active object still occupies layout, retains state and can receive interaction/events when Interactive=True.
Interactive=False disables user-originated interaction/focus targeting while leaving the active object visible/layout-participating unless another property changes that.
All objects default to Active=True, Hidden=False and Interactive=True unless a Definition/Type/Theme explicitly defines another default.
<Text::Txt Active="False">Hello</Text>
Txt.Active(true);
Active(false) is an effective participation gate and MUST NOT overwrite stored Hidden, Interactive or other properties. Reactivating restores those stored properties exactly. Property assignments made while inactive update stored state and become effective when reactivated.
Parent lifecycle and independent activation
Normal descendants inherit Active state from the nearest active parent. Effective Active is Self.Active AND parent EffectiveActive.
A leading ! or ActiveIndependently=True breaks only the parent-to-child Active dependency.
<!Style::PersistentStyle>
<Text ActiveIndependently="True">...</Text>
An independently active child/declaration is not forced inactive when its parent deactivates and must be deactivated separately. ! does not break Theme inheritance, symbol scope, Prefab ownership, variables, Groups, styling inheritance or event targeting.
For independently active visual descendants whose logical parent deactivates, the runtime preserves the required logical/positioning reference state without causing the inactive parent to re-enter ordinary sibling layout.
Lifecycle events
Initial activation generates Loaded. A False-to-True Active transition generates Loaded again. A True-to-False transition generates Deactivated. Event processing is typed and follows the ActionEvent rules below.
Stateful/non-once events are temporary overlays for the event lifetime; Once-prefixed variants commit their property/action result as persistent state rather than reverting with event end. Once means committed/persistent, not 'execute only once ever'.
Layout property model
CUI's property catalogue MUST provide mature visual/layout coverage comparable in scope to broadly applicable CSS and Avalonia properties while retaining CUI's typed semantics. Layout is property-driven.
Required layout/property families include:
Width, Height, MinWidth, MaxWidth, MinHeight and MaxHeight.
Margin, Padding, CellMargin and CellGap.
HorizontalAlignment, VerticalAlignment, wrapping/overflow and scrolling properties.
Grid Rows, Columns, RowSizes, ColumnSizes, Row, Column, RowSpan and ColumnSpan.
Absolute X/Y positioning and associated coordinate modes.
Typography, colour, background, borders, corner radii, opacity, clipping, transforms, shadows/effects and other applicable mature property families.
Numeric layout units MUST be typed. Bare fixed dimensions use CUI logical/DPI-aware pixels unless the property explicitly defines another unit. Auto, percentages and fractional/fill sizing are supported where meaningful.
ColumnSizes:1fr_2fr_200
RowSizes:Auto_1fr
Grid and stack behaviour
Container Type:Grid performs row/column layout. Container Type:Vertical_Stack and Horizontal_Stack perform ordered stack layout. CellGap controls spacing between grid/stack cells/items; CellMargin controls the per-cell/item margin contribution.
Scrolling is orthogonal to layout Type and can be enabled independently.
<Container Type:Vertical_Stack Horizontal-Scrolling:True Vertical-Scrolling:True>
Invalid layout-property combinations MUST fail at compile time when statically knowable or return a typed runtime layout error when dynamically introduced.
Absolute positioning and coordinate system
Container Type:Absolute enables free child positioning. Bare X and Y use CUI's proportional coordinate system by default and MAY be decimal values.
The centre of the positioning surface is (0,0). The normal horizontal range is -1000 at the left edge to +1000 at the right edge. The normal vertical range is -1000 at the bottom edge to +1000 at the top edge. Values outside the normal range are legal and place the reference point beyond the surface, which is useful for transitions/off-screen UI.
<Container Type:Absolute>
    <Text X:-500.5 Y:250.25>Hello</Text>
</Container>
An axis may alternatively use X-px/Y-px for CUI logical pixels or X-%/Y-% for percentage positioning. Percentage 0 is left/bottom, 50 is centre and 100 is right/top. Coordinates in every mode MAY be decimals.
An element may define only one authoritative positioning mode per axis at a time. Supplying X and X-px together, for example, is an error.
Coordinate recalibration and inherited axes
X-Inherited and Y-Inherited independently recalibrate descendant coordinate resolution to the declaring Container's bounds.
X-Inherited=True makes that Container's left/right bounds the descendant -1000/+1000 X range and the corresponding percentage/pixel reference surface.
Y-Inherited=True makes that Container's bottom/top bounds the descendant -1000/+1000 Y range and the corresponding percentage/pixel reference surface.
The nearest applicable inherited axis scope wins. X and Y may therefore resolve against different ancestor Containers. Outside an Absolute/free-positioning context, free X/Y placement is invalid unless the owning specialised Type explicitly declares support.
Layering and rendering depth
Layer is both a container element and an inheritable signed-integer property.
<Layer Layer="1">...</Layer>
<Layer:2>...</Layer>
<Text Layer="5">Hello</Text>
Higher Layer values render/hit-test above lower values; negative and positive values are valid. An element-level Layer overrides the parent layer and becomes the inherited layer for its normal descendants unless they override it again.
