9to1.Mail.Rules.Create(rule);
9to1.Mail.Changes.Subscribe(accountID?, cursor?);
These are minimum canonical entry points. Every additional user-visible Mail operation and preserved donor capability MUST have an equivalent typed API/domain action under the global API-parity rule.
Failure behaviour
Mail MUST return structured failures including AccountNotFound, AuthenticationRequired, ProviderUnavailable, ProviderCapabilityUnsupported, Offline, SyncFailed, MessageNotFound, ThreadNotFound, DraftConflict, SendFailed, SendRejected, AttachmentUnavailable, MailboxQuotaExceeded, RateLimited, PermissionDenied, InvalidRecipient, EncryptionKeyUnavailable, CertificateError and structured partial bulk outcomes in addition to the global error contract.
Platform behaviour
Native Windows/9to1-OS Mail MUST support configured local caching/offline behaviour and Home-integrated notifications/files/model services. Web Mail uses authenticated server/provider APIs and the same canonical account/message identities where available, but browser storage/offline capabilities MUST be capability-negotiated rather than assumed identical to native.
Acceptance requirements
Mail is implementation-complete only when acceptance coverage verifies at least:
The final UI passes dedicated visual QA for a cohesive modern 9to1 CUI shell with responsive pane behaviour, clean message/compose surfaces, consistent spacing/typography and no exposed legacy donor UI.
Applicable mature donor email capabilities are accounted for in the donor-parity manifest independently from visual design.
At least Gmail/Google, Outlook/Microsoft and generic IMAP+SMTP accounts can coexist with Unified Inbox without provider-semantics loss.
Gmail-style label semantics and generic IMAP folder semantics remain distinguishable and correct.
Incremental push/IDLE/provider sync updates a connected mailbox without complete rescans for ordinary changes.
Offline cached mail is readable and queued mutations survive app/device restart then reconcile on reconnect.
Draft autosave/recovery preserves content and surfaces provider/local conflicts rather than overwriting silently.
Offline send enters Outbox/Queued and send failure remains visible/retryable rather than being reported Sent.
Client-side Undo Send cancels before provider submission and stops presenting undo once sending is irreversible.
Scheduled send accurately identifies provider/cloud/device execution semantics and does not imply guarantees the selected executor cannot provide.
Attachments can be opened/saved through Files and Attach from Files works with authorised local/9to1 Drive content.
Search works across the defined fields and saved smart views do not duplicate messages.
Remote email HTML/script cannot execute trusted app code and remote-image tracking obeys privacy controls.
OpenPGP/S/MIME donor-supported behaviour works or has an explicit scoped parity exception.
The AI bar can summarise/draft against explicit context while respecting local/cloud privacy policy.
AI cannot bypass Mail.Send permission simply because it drafted a message.
Provider reauthentication/revocation does not erase valid cached messages/drafts.
Home notification deep links open the exact intended message/thread/account.
Home/Dulche service restart produces a recoverable/degraded state without mailbox database corruption.
Core UI operations and provider actions have equivalent typed API coverage.
Games
Product role and ambition
9to1 Games is the native CUI game-development, real-time 3D creation, modelling and rendering environment. It is not merely a launcher and it is not the same product as Play. Games is where users build games, interactive worlds, real-time experiences, 2D/3D scenes, models, materials, animations and rendered content. Play remains the structured human/Agent game framework.
Games MUST be based on a maintained fork of Godot as its primary game-engine donor and MUST preserve mature applicable engine functionality unless this specification explicitly replaces it with a 9to1-native equivalent. Donor parity is a floor rather than a ceiling: the purpose of the fork is to produce a materially more capable, more intuitive and more integrated creation environment rather than only re-skinning Godot.
Games MUST also integrate a maintained Blender-derived modelling/rendering toolset deeply enough that modelling feels like part of the same product rather than an external export/import workflow. Because 9to1 is substantially open source, implementation MAY integrate Blender-derived code as deeply as is technically useful while preserving all applicable licence/source-distribution obligations. The donor-parity/source manifest MUST identify the exact Godot and Blender revisions, licences, modified components and redistribution obligations used by a release.
Games MUST expose at least two first-class workspaces over the same canonical project/assets: Development and Creation/Rendering. Development prioritises scene graph, gameplay, scripts, debugging, profiling, networking, UI and build/export. Creation/Rendering prioritises modelling, sculpting, UV, materials, texture work, rigging, animation, simulations, lighting, cameras, high-quality rendering and related asset workflows. A user MUST be able to use Creation/Rendering without building a game.
CUI-native editor
The user-facing editor MUST be rebuilt as a coherent 9to1 CUI experience rather than exposing donor-native editor chrome as the final interface. Existing mature donor capability MAY remain behind the shell, but navigation, inspector, asset browser, scene graph, editors, dialogs, settings, errors and workflows MUST follow 9to1 interaction conventions.
Games MUST host the normal persistent floating Dulche AI bar. The AI bar receives only authorised project/editor state and MUST be able to reason over semantic scene, script, component, material, animation, profiler and error data through typed Games APIs. It MUST NOT rely on generic Computer Use to manipulate the Games editor when a typed Games action exists.
The Godot UI authoring workflow MUST be upgraded/rebuilt around the canonical CUI Visual Builder. Game HUDs, menus, overlays, dialogue, inventories, maps, settings, responsive layouts and other game UI MUST use the same high-quality visual layout concepts and reusable components as CUI while compiling/running efficiently inside Games. Game UI remains part of the canonical game scene/component model and MUST NOT become a disconnected design-only artifact.
Canonical scene graph and purposeful components
Games MUST preserve a powerful scene/node graph foundation while providing higher-level purposeful components for common game concepts. Stable SceneID, EntityID, NodeID, ComponentID, ResourceID, AssetID and ProjectID identities MUST be used; mutable names/paths are not canonical identity.
The scene graph MUST support ordinary low-level engine nodes for expert use and high-level purpose-built entities/components for rapid development. Examples include Player Character, Vehicle, Camera Rig, Door, Interactive Object, Collectible, Spawn Point, Checkpoint, Trigger Volume, Dialogue Actor, NPC, Enemy, Weapon, Inventory, Quest, Save Point, Water Body, Landscape, Foliage, Destructible Object, Audio Zone, Lighting Rig, UI Screen/HUD, Multiplayer Spawn and Navigation Area.
Purposeful components MUST have real runtime semantics, typed APIs, inspectors, events, extension points and Dulche understanding. They MUST NOT be decorative prefab labels over unrelated scripts.
Games MUST favour composition. Complex built-ins such as Player Character or Car SHOULD be composed from inspectable native primitives plus first-party C# gameplay components rather than implemented as one opaque monolithic class.
Shared graph infrastructure with Automations
Games and Automations MUST share the same canonical node-graph editor/data infrastructure and backend concepts for GraphID, NodeID, typed ports, typed connections, groups, comments, subgraphs, search, selection, snapping, minimap, copy/paste, undo/redo, versioning, validation, keyboard accessibility, semantic API access and execution/debug visualisation.
Sharing the graph infrastructure MUST NOT force all graphs through one execution runtime. Each GraphType registers its own legal node families, compiler/runtime adapter and semantics. Automation graphs execute through the automation runtime; gameplay visual scripts through the Games runtime; material/shader graphs through the rendering compiler; animation/state graphs through the animation runtime; procedural world graphs through the generation runtime.
Games MUST expose only context-relevant nodes by default. A shader graph MUST NOT show Send Email merely because Automations uses the same graph infrastructure. Cross-domain nodes require an explicit compatible bridge.
Visual gameplay graphs MUST interoperate with C# and C++. Eligible C# or C++ functions/events explicitly exposed to Games SHOULD be callable/observable as graph nodes/events without requiring hand-written graph wrappers.
C# first-class language and mixed-language projects
C# is the canonical first-class scripting/gameplay language for Games. Documentation, templates, autocomplete, refactoring, debugging, profiler integration, hot-reload support where safe, generated APIs, examples and Dulche coding assistance MUST default to C#.
GDScript MUST NOT be exposed as a supported public Games development language. Donor language infrastructure MAY remain internally where unavoidable during migration, but user projects and canonical Games documentation MUST NOT require or promote GDScript.
C++ MUST remain available for low-level, engine-extension, rendering, platform, performance-critical, unusual memory/layout or other systems work where C# is inappropriate. The engine SHOULD continually minimise the amount of low-level work developers need to write themselves.
A Games project MUST support C# and C++ simultaneously. The user MUST NOT have to choose one project language. C# and C++ MUST operate over the same canonical scene/entity/component/resource model and may call deliberately exposed functionality across the language boundary.
Games SHOULD generate routine interop/binding glue. Normal developers MUST NOT be expected to hand-write P/Invoke declarations, ABI wrappers, pointer-marshalling layers, lifetime glue or duplicated type conversions merely to call a supported exposed C++ component from C#.
Common engine types such as vectors, transforms, entities, components, assets, materials, textures and scenes MUST have canonical interoperable representations. Native/managed ownership and lifetime rules MUST be explicit at the runtime level while remaining safely automatic for ordinary high-level use.
Intuitive API design contract
The public Games API MUST describe game intent rather than mirror internal engine plumbing. Where an operation has a clear domain action, the high-level API MUST expose that action directly.
For example, a user-facing API such as Object.SetX(value) is preferred over requiring a developer to traverse a chain such as Object.X.Position.Persistent(). Similar simple verbs SHOULD include SetPosition, MoveTo, Rotate, Show, Hide, Enable, Disable, Open, Close, Play, Stop, Spawn, Destroy, Give, Take, Attach and Detach where semantically appropriate.
Public APIs MUST use consistent names, strong typing, sensible defaults, concise parameters and direct discoverability. Internally complex operations such as replication, authority resolution, component traversal or persistence SHOULD be handled by Games when the desired intent is unambiguous.
Advanced low-level APIs MAY expose explicit replication, authority, memory, rendering and engine primitives for expert use. Their existence MUST NOT make low-level plumbing the normal or documented path for ordinary game logic.
API design quality MUST include human and AI interpretability: a competent developer or model SHOULD normally be able to infer the purpose of a high-level operation from its name, target type and typed parameters without reading engine implementation details.
Shared and individual state semantics
Games MUST use shared and individual as the canonical high-level state/replication qualifiers. The aliases shar and indiv MUST be accepted as equivalent shorthand where the Games language/parser supports these declarations.
shared/shar means one canonical state is shared across the relevant game/session audience and replicated according to the object's authority policy. individual/indiv means the state is resolved independently for the relevant player/entity.
The shared/individual model applies consistently where meaningful, including UI state, gameplay variables, progression, objectives, settings and keybind definitions. It MUST replace the earlier public/private naming for Games state scope.
Example intent: GetEntity(Player) { UI.Show(ui, individual); } updates only that player's corresponding UI state. GetEntity(Player) { UI.Show(ui, shared); } updates the shared state seen by the applicable audience. The runtime handles the required identity, replication and join/reconciliation plumbing.
The API SHOULD infer natural scope when it is unambiguous so developers do not repeatedly specify individual for obviously per-player state. Explicit qualifiers remain available when the developer needs to override/default the behaviour.
The high-level model MUST avoid forcing developers to maintain maps keyed by PlayerID merely to represent ordinary per-player state. Games retains stable internal identities and advanced maps/collections remain available for genuinely custom logic.
Multiplayer/replication intent
For ordinary gameplay, developers SHOULD specify desired state, ownership and visibility rather than manually implement RPC direction, player-ID dictionaries, replication callbacks, joining-player reconstruction, local/server copies and reconciliation.
High-level operations such as Door.Open(shared), UI.Show(LevelComplete, individual), Inventory.Give(Key, individual) or a shared world-state update SHOULD compile/route into the appropriate authoritative replication mechanism.
Games MUST still expose advanced networking primitives for specialised games, but high-level APIs are authoritative for common development and MUST remain deterministic, inspectable and debuggable.
Declarative keybind system
Games MUST provide a canonical human-readable keybinding definition file, provisionally named keybinds.csmap, that is understood by the editor, runtime, C# APIs, visual graphs, Dulche and generated settings UI.
Keybind definitions MUST be semantic rather than hard-wired gameplay code. A developer defines an action such as Jump, Crouch or Movement and then maps supported keyboard/controller/touch inputs to it.
shared Keybind means the declared binding is common for the applicable game/profile scope. individual Keybind means each player may have a separately resolved/remappable binding. shar and indiv are accepted shorthand.
Games SHOULD support readable controller-layout names rather than forcing numeric button indices, including semantic/positional forms such as Controller.Letters.Down, Controller.Letters.Left, bumpers, triggers, D-pad, LeftStick and RightStick. Platform-specific glyph/display mapping is handled by the engine.
Composite input shorthand MUST be supported. A declaration equivalent to shared Keybind Movement { Keyboard(WASD); Controller(LeftStick); } MUST produce one typed movement input rather than four unrelated actions. Digital WASD and analogue stick values resolve through one semantic Movement binding.
Keybind consumption MUST be simple. Event.KeyPress(BindingName) { ... } is the canonical intent for listening to a binding press. Corresponding release/hold/value-change/input events SHOULD follow the same readable event family.
The input subsystem MUST resolve device hot-swap, keyboard/controller/touch source, player ownership, remapping, persistence and appropriate input value types without requiring ordinary gameplay code to poll physical devices.
Individual/remappable bindings MUST have ready-made CUI settings components for rebinding, conflict detection, reset-to-default, clearing, device-specific display and per-player persistence. Duplicate bindings MAY be legal; conflicts in the same active context should warn rather than be silently rejected.
The system SHOULD support input contexts, chords/combinations and typed analogue/gesture inputs without requiring developers to build timing/device-selection infrastructure from scratch.
Prebuilt object and gameplay library
Games MUST ship an optional, substantial first-party library of production-usable drag-and-drop entities, components and complete gameplay systems so creators can begin with working mechanics rather than blank scenes.
The library MUST include at least a configurable basic/stick-man-style player character with full movement, crouch, jump, sprint and swimming support; starter vehicles including a car, plane, boat and submarine; environmental systems including water and lava; and common interactive/world primitives.
Starter content MUST be fully usable without opening its implementation, while remaining inspectable, extensible and replaceable. It MUST NOT be a set of disconnected demos or opaque sample projects.
The standard Player Character inspector MUST expose substantial high-level configuration rather than only speed/jump toggles. It SHOULD expose at least Movement Speed, Acceleration, Sprint Speed, Limited Stamina, Stamina Level/Maximum, per-action stamina consumption for walking/sprinting/jumping/crouching/swimming where applicable, Stamina Replenish Delay, Stamina Replenish rate, Crouch Speed, Jump Height, Air Control, Can Sprint, Can Crouch, Can Jump and Can Swim, plus appropriate advanced movement/collision settings.
Inspector sections MUST progressively reveal dependent settings. Disabling Limited Stamina SHOULD hide/de-emphasise irrelevant stamina controls; disabling Crouch SHOULD collapse crouch-only parameters. An Advanced disclosure SHOULD expose expert parameters without turning the default inspector into an unstructured wall of fields.
Starter vehicles MUST similarly expose meaningful tuning such as acceleration, maximum speed, braking, steering response, traction, suspension/buoyancy/aerodynamic values and feature toggles appropriate to the vehicle type.
Water SHOULD expose working swimming/buoyancy/current/wave/underwater behaviour and integrate automatically with compatible Player/vehicle components. Lava SHOULD expose fluid-like behaviour where desired plus damage/ignition/heat/visual properties. Built-in environment systems MUST interoperate through shared typed contracts rather than custom one-off scripts.
The library SHOULD also include reusable systems such as health/damage, inventory, interaction, quests, dialogue, checkpoints, save/load, respawning, teams, rounds, scoring, racing, pickups, simple AI/navigation and common multiplayer/lobby/spectator features.
Optional first-party C# feature components
Each applicable built-in entity MUST expose a contextual catalogue of optional first-party C# feature components that the creator can enable through simple checkboxes/toggles. These are normal editable C# components built on the same public Games component API, not privileged hidden native features.
For Player Character, examples MUST include optional components such as Double Jump and Ragdoll Properties/behaviour, and SHOULD include other appropriate features such as Fall Damage, Mantling, Climbing, Sliding, Wall Running, Dash, Stamina, Oxygen, Footsteps, Head Bob, Camera Shake, Interaction, Inventory, Health, Regeneration, Knockback, Swimming and other mature starter behaviours.
Enabling an optional component MUST add/activate the corresponding C# component and reveal its configurable properties. Double Jump, for example, SHOULD be able to expose maximum jumps, second-jump height, reset rules, stamina cost and contextual restrictions without requiring the creator to open code.
Ragdoll SHOULD be able to expose activation conditions, body/joint behaviour, collision, recovery and replication-related settings while relying on native skeleton/physics primitives underneath.
Native engine components SHOULD be reserved for fundamental high-performance primitives and engine facilities such as transforms, identity, core rendering, low-level physics/collision, audio primitives, input routing, replication primitives, navigation and animation/runtime infrastructure. Higher-level gameplay behaviours SHOULD prefer editable C# when performance/architecture permits.
First-party C# components MUST expose source code to the project/user according to the 9to1 open-source distribution model and MUST be usable unchanged, parameter-tuned, extended, duplicated/forked or replaced by developer code.
Custom developer C# components MUST participate in the same inspector and discovery model as first-party components. A developer-defined component compatible with Player SHOULD be able to appear in the same contextual component picker with automatically generated CUI settings for eligible exposed properties.
Component metadata MUST support dependencies, compatibility, stable identity/version, display name/category, exposed settings, events/actions and migration information. When enabling a component requires another component, Games SHOULD offer to enable the dependency rather than leave a silently broken configuration.
Disabling an optional component SHOULD preserve its configuration by default so re-enabling restores it. Removing/deleting the component is a separate explicit operation.
Component inspector generation
C# components MUST be able to declare user-editable settings through concise metadata/attributes. Games MUST generate a polished CUI inspector automatically for standard supported property types rather than requiring every component author to build a bespoke editor panel.
Metadata SHOULD support user-facing name, description/help, units, numeric ranges/steps, enum choices, grouping, advanced disclosure, conditional visibility, asset/entity pickers, validation and safe defaults.
Auto-generated inspectors MUST remain overrideable/extensible when a component genuinely requires a specialised editor.
Component events and state
Reusable components MUST publish semantic typed events and inspectable state. For example, a character component SHOULD be able to expose events such as Jump, SprintStart, SprintEnd, StaminaEmpty, EnterWater and LeaveWater plus readable state such as IsSprinting, IsCrouching, IsSwimming and Stamina.
Consumers MUST be able to subscribe through C#, visual graphs and Dulche-compatible typed actions without inspecting private implementation fields.
Component versioning and project safety
First-party library components MUST be versioned. Existing projects MUST NOT silently change behaviour merely because the globally installed library was updated. Projects MAY pin component versions and receive explicit migration/upgrade flows with change previews where practical.
Creators MUST be able to fork a first-party component into project-owned code. Once forked, it becomes project-owned and MUST NOT be overwritten by later library updates.
Rendering and graphics engine
Games MUST invest in a high-end modern rendering stack capable of producing visually exceptional games and rendered scenes rather than treating rendering as donor parity only.
The engine SHOULD independently implement capabilities comparable in outcome to modern virtualised-geometry and dynamic-global-illumination systems without copying proprietary source code, algorithms that are not legally available, trademarks as product features or confidential implementation detail.
Rendering goals SHOULD include highly scalable detailed geometry, automated/low-touch LOD handling, GPU-driven rendering where beneficial, visibility/occlusion systems, geometry streaming/clustering as appropriate, dynamic global illumination, indirect lighting, reflections, modern shadows, temporal reconstruction/upscaling, large-world rendering, physically based materials and predictable profiling/quality controls.
Creators SHOULD be able to achieve high geometric detail with much less manual LOD authoring than conventional pipelines while retaining explicit expert control when needed.
Every advanced renderer feature MUST expose truthful hardware/platform capability detection, quality fallbacks, performance diagnostics and deterministic project settings. Unsupported hardware MUST degrade gracefully rather than silently producing broken scenes.
Landscape, world and procedural tools
Games MUST provide first-class landscape/world creation rather than requiring an external terrain package for normal use.
Landscape tooling SHOULD include sculpting, smoothing, erosion-style operations, heightmaps, layers, splines, roads, rivers, lakes/oceans, biome painting, foliage, procedural scattering, world/region streaming, large-world coordinates, landscape collision/navigation generation and runtime deformation where supported.
Procedural world generation MUST be able to use the shared graph editor infrastructure through a dedicated generation GraphType with terrain/foliage/geometry/scatter/environment nodes and a specialised generation runtime.
World tools MUST integrate with the canonical scene graph, materials, physics, navigation, Files/assets, Dulche and build/export pipeline.
Material and shader tools
Games MUST provide a strong native material/shader authoring environment using the shared graph infrastructure with a dedicated material/shader GraphType and renderer/compiler backend.
The material system SHOULD support reusable functions/subgraphs, instances, parameters, layers, procedural inputs, normal/displacement workflows, physically based shading, transparency, subsurface/clearcoat/anisotropy where the renderer supports them, decals, terrain materials, preview scenes and performance/complexity diagnostics.
The beginner path MUST support high-quality materials without requiring shader source code. Experts MUST retain access to lower-level shader code and advanced render hooks where supported.
Integrated Blender-derived modelling
Games MUST provide built-in professional modelling tools derived from Blender and redesigned/integrated for the Games workflow rather than behaving as a loosely launched external application.
The modelling environment SHOULD cover mesh modelling, selection modes, transform/extrude/bevel/inset workflows, modifiers, sculpting, retopology, UV editing, texture/vertex painting, rigging, weight painting, animation, procedural/geometry workflows, simulations and high-quality rendering/compositing capabilities where appropriate.
CUI interaction and contextual tooling SHOULD make common modelling tasks substantially easier to discover and perform than raw donor workflows while preserving advanced depth for expert users.
A selected scene asset SHOULD be editable in the modelling workspace and returned to the same canonical asset/scene relationship without manual export/import round trips. Changes MUST flow through the normal asset revision/undo/source-control model.
Creation/Rendering mode MUST be useful as a standalone modelling/rendering application. A user MUST be able to create, model, light, animate and render an asset/scene even when the project contains no playable game logic.
Asset pipeline and cross-app integration
Games MUST integrate with Files as the canonical 9to1 file/project substrate where applicable and SHOULD integrate cleanly with Picture, Wave and other media/creation apps for textures, images, audio/video and generated assets without unnecessary duplicate exports.
Assets MUST have stable identity, source/import settings, derived/cache state and dependency tracking. Reimport MUST preserve intentional scene/component references wherever possible.
Stack/Dev integration SHOULD provide source-control-aware project workflows, diffs where semantically possible, branches and code review without corrupting binary/derived asset state. Terminal MUST expose supported Godot/Games CLI/build/export workflows.
Dulche in Games
Dulche MUST operate semantically through Games APIs and project data. It SHOULD be able to answer questions such as why a character falls through a floor, create or modify typed scene components, tune exposed parameters, create scripts, diagnose errors, analyse profiler output, modify materials/graphs, assemble starter systems and perform authorised project edits.
Dulche MUST prefer existing first-party/native components over generating redundant custom implementations when they satisfy the user's request. If a user asks for a third-person character that can sprint, crouch and swim, Dulche SHOULD assemble/configure the applicable existing components rather than reinventing those systems in new code.
AI-generated Games changes MUST remain inspectable through normal scene/script/graph diffs and undo/revision mechanisms. AI assistance MUST NOT create hidden state that cannot be reproduced through supported project structures.
Build, run, debug and export
Games MUST preserve mature Godot-derived project run/debug/export capability and improve it where required for the 9to1 workflow. Running a game, running the current scene, attaching a debugger, breakpoints, errors, remote scene inspection, profiler data and platform export MUST remain first-class.
The editor MUST clearly separate editor state from running-game state while allowing safe live inspection and supported hot-edit/hot-reload behaviour.
Export targets SHOULD preserve applicable mature donor platform coverage subject to the selected donor revision, platform SDK/licence availability and 9to1 release support. Unsupported export targets MUST be reported truthfully rather than exposed as fake buttons.
Relationship with Play
Games and Play are separate. Games builds and runs normal games/interactive content. Play governs structured human/Dulche-Agent matches, contestants, scoring, judging, visibility and game actions.
A Games project MAY explicitly expose a typed Play-compatible interface so Dulche Agents can participate through purpose-built game actions/state. Generic Computer Use MUST NOT be used as a hidden fallback for controlling arbitrary game executables, anti-cheat surfaces or unsupported games.
Games API families
Games MUST expose typed API families for projects, scenes/entities/nodes/components, resources/assets, transforms, gameplay state, input/keybinds, graphs, UI/CUI Visual Builder, materials, animation, physics, navigation, audio, rendering, landscapes/worlds, modelling integration, build/run/debug/export and component-library discovery/installation/configuration.
High-level APIs and advanced APIs MUST remain clearly layered. The existence of a low-level API MUST NOT allow implementation agents to omit the intuitive high-level operation required by this specification.
Every mutation MUST use stable identities, structured results, revision/conflict semantics and the global Home permission/audit model where actions cross normal trust boundaries.
Failure and recovery
Games MUST preserve project integrity across editor crashes, failed imports, failed builds, hot-reload errors, graph compilation errors, component upgrade failures and interrupted modelling/render operations. Autosave/recovery MUST NOT silently overwrite a newer valid source revision.
Errors MUST identify the relevant ProjectID/SceneID/EntityID/ComponentID/GraphID/AssetID and provide actionable context. High-level APIs MUST return structured errors rather than swallowing engine exceptions.
Component/library upgrades, donor migrations and project format migrations MUST be transactional or recoverable. A failed migration MUST leave the previous valid project state recoverable.
Acceptance requirements
Games is implementation-complete only when acceptance coverage proves at least: a real maintained Godot-derived engine/editor; native CUI rebuild; Development and standalone Creation/Rendering workflows; deeply integrated Blender-derived modelling; CUI Visual Builder game UI; canonical scene graph and purposeful components; shared node infrastructure with Automations plus specialised graph runtimes; first-class C#; absence of public GDScript dependency; simultaneous C#/C++ interoperability; intuitive high-level APIs; shared/individual plus shar/indiv semantics; declarative keybinds and Event.KeyPress-style semantic input; robust per-player remapping; configurable starter Player with detailed movement/stamina/swim controls; contextual optional C# components including Double Jump and Ragdoll; custom C# component inspector integration; starter car/plane/boat/submarine; water/lava environment systems; reusable gameplay systems; high-end rendering; strong landscape/procedural tools; strong materials/shaders; semantic Dulche operation; safe project/version migration; mature run/debug/export; and explicit separation from Play.
AI Apps
Spaces
Product role
9-1 Spaces is the conversational, research, study and agentic-work environment across the 9to1 ecosystem. A Space is a persistent context and behaviour container with stable identity, conversations, sources, model policy, memory policy, connected capabilities and permissions. Spaces operate on canonical app entities through their owning typed APIs and MUST NOT duplicate mutable 9to1 artifacts merely to make them conversational.
Spaces MUST support cross-app actions including Write document mutation, Board/embedded-Canvas editing, Data updates, Planner mutation, Maps route creation, media/project-file actions, Stack operations and Automation coordination whenever the target app exposes the corresponding API. Consequential mutations inherit the target action’s permission/review contract. Spaces MUST NOT fall back to raw UI automation when a typed action exists.
Built-in Space types
The built-in first-party Space types are Chat, Study, Tasks, Agent, Shopping, Research, Translate and Experiences. These are distinct product environments with protected first-party behaviour and UI; they are not merely system-prompt presets.
Chat is the broad general-purpose conversational environment for ordinary questions, app actions, files, web research where enabled, shared objects, tools and agentic work.
Study is the learning environment and MUST support source-backed explanation, topics, practice questions, quizzes, flashcards, progress/weak-area tracking and review scheduling. Study progress MUST be based on recorded interactions/answers rather than inferred solely because material was shown to the user.
Tasks is the goal-oriented work environment and MUST expose structured objective, plan/steps, current step, dependencies, blockers, approvals, outputs, status and run state. Tasks are individual work items/runs and are distinct from Automations, which own recurring/event-triggered execution.
Agent is the environment for interacting with and supervising persistent 9to1 Agents. It MUST surface the selected Agent identity, state, runs, relevant memory/tools and Action Graph access while preserving the Agent definition and permissions owned by the Agents/AI Studio/Dulche contracts.
Shopping is a product-discovery/comparison environment for requirements, candidates, research, saved items and purchase-related context. It MUST preserve source/provenance and MUST NOT treat generated claims as product facts.
Research is the deeper source-oriented research environment for research plans, source sets, citations/provenance, findings, notes and structured outputs. It MUST make source scope and outside-web access explicit.
Translate is the conversational translation/localisation environment backed by Dulche Translate. It uses the normal Space conversation, context, sources, Plugins, Skills, Agents, memory, model policy and permissions rather than a special two-box translator UI. Its translation-specific persistent control is the selected target-language set shown immediately above the standard Space chatbar; there is no separate Translate-specific context row because current artifact/selection/files/sources and semantic app context use the normal Spaces context architecture. Translate supports one or many target languages, conversational refinement, structured Translation Sets/variants, artifact-aware translation and authorised agentic follow-up actions through normal typed owning-app APIs.
For conversational translation into multiple target languages, each language variant MUST render as its own assistant speech bubble rather than being collapsed into one combined multi-language response card. The language/locale name is shown directly above the corresponding bubble, for example French above the French translation bubble, Spanish above the Spanish bubble and German above the German bubble. The bubbles remain siblings of the same TranslationSetID/request so retry, edit, regenerate, apply or publish operations may target one language without losing the others.
Experiences is the conversational stateful environment for open-ended interactive experiences such as roleplay, simulations, interactive stories, mysteries, fictional worlds, scenario training and other AI-driven experiences that do not require the formal contestant/scoring structure of Play. It uses the normal Space conversation, context, Agents, Skills, Plugins, model policy, permissions, memory and Generative UI architecture.
Every active Experience MUST maintain canonical structured experience state rather than treating generated narrative prose as the sole source of truth. Experience state MAY include world/scene/time, characters, relationships, inventory/resources, objectives, flags, timeline, hidden information, rules and typed domain-specific state. When the narrative says a state-changing event occurred, the corresponding canonical state transition MUST be committed before future turns rely on it.
Experiences MAY use persistent Dulche Agents for autonomous characters/roles that genuinely benefit from independent identity, memory or goals, while lightweight characters MAY remain scoped experience actors/state rather than becoming permanent Den Agents. Agent knowledge and private/hidden state MUST be filtered by the Experience visibility policy so one character cannot access information it has not learned.
Experiences SHOULD support checkpoints, rewind and branching. A branch combines the conversation branch with the matching Experience-state revision so trying a different decision does not mutate the original timeline. Rewind/branch of simulated state MUST NOT pretend to undo real external side effects that already occurred through authorised Plugins/actions.
Experiences MAY expose maps, inventories, evidence, character panels, timelines, objectives, cards or other interactive elements through safe CUI/Generative UI. The normal conversation remains the primary interaction surface; generated UI is a structured representation of canonical Experience state, not a separate hidden game runtime.
Experiences MAY launch or embed a formal Play Match when the scenario requires a structured competition, and Play MAY offer Continue in Experiences for an open-ended continuation. Experience state and Play Match state remain distinct canonical entities rather than being silently merged.
User-created Spaces and nesting
The sidebar does not expose a ninth Custom type. Users create user-defined Spaces through + New Space and manage the hierarchy through Edit Spaces. User-created Spaces have SpaceOrigin = UserCreated and receive the full Space graph editor described below; built-in first-party Spaces have SpaceOrigin = BuiltIn and expose only the protected Events & Extensions editor.
Spaces MAY be nested through ParentSpaceID to create logical hierarchies. Nesting MUST preserve each Space’s stable identity and MUST NOT imply permission escalation. Child inheritance of sources, connected apps, model policy, memory, Skills, Plugins or Agents must be explicit/inspectable; a child cannot regain a capability or permission explicitly denied by a parent/security policy.
Edit Spaces MUST support reorder, nest/unnest, rename, icon, sharing, inheritance configuration, duplicate, archive/delete/recover and other structural management without exposing protected first-party internal implementation.
Sidebar and navigation
The Spaces sidebar is scoped around the currently selected Space. Its top control MUST display the currently selected Space and provide a Space switcher when activated; an adjacent overflow control provides quick actions for that Space.
Immediately below, the sidebar MUST expose the built-in Space destinations Chat, Study, Tasks, Agent, Shopping, Research, Translate and Experiences, followed by New Chat, then Space-relevant options. A divider separates the persistent + New Space and Edit Spaces controls.
Space-relevant options are typed capabilities/surfaces appropriate to the selected Space and may include Sources, Files/context, Topics, Progress, Runs, Findings, Tools, Agents, Approvals, Settings or custom sidebar items. The set is context-sensitive but MUST be deterministic and inspectable, not arbitrary hidden AI-generated navigation.
New Chat creates a new conversation inside the currently selected Space. It MUST NOT create another Space. Recent/pinned conversations may appear within the selected Space’s Chat/conversation surface without turning the global sidebar into an unbounded cross-Space history list.
Plugins — custom sidebar elements and per-Space visibility
Plugins MUST support contributing custom sidebar elements. An element MUST be able to open an arbitrary configured page/URL, an authorised app surface, an authored CUI page or a generative page, or invoke an Automation or another declared authorised action. Navigation and action-triggering behaviour MUST be explicit. Arbitrary pages remain subject to the existing safe rendering, origin, permissions and external-navigation rules; this capability does not authorise unrestricted code execution.
For each Plugin, the user MUST be able to select which Spaces display its sidebar elements. This selection MUST be inspectable, editable and persisted using stable Plugin, Space and SidebarItem identities. An excluded Space MUST NOT display that Plugin's sidebar contributions merely because the Plugin is installed globally. Sidebar visibility is distinct from permission to execute the Plugin or access Space data; it MUST NOT silently change either.
Attaching a Plugin MUST now be the primary method of supplying custom sidebar elements in custom Spaces. Ordinary Plugin-provided sidebar elements MUST NOT require users to construct a built-in Automation or Space lifecycle graph solely to load the element.
The existing built-in automation/Events & Extensions/full Space graph mechanisms for loading, showing and controlling custom sidebar elements MUST remain supported for enhanced and combined workflows. Plugin and graph routes MUST share the existing sidebar identity, ownership, lifecycle and rendering contracts, preserving AppSurface, CUI and GenerativeUI support. They MUST NOT duplicate the same contribution or replace protected first-party sidebar items. Disabling or detaching a Plugin MUST stop its active contributions without leaving executable orphan actions or deleting unrelated Space content.
Plugin sidebar — supplied concept mockup clarification
The supplied sidebar concept mockup is the applicable visual reference. The relevant example is the My Homework row immediately below New chat and above the divider; the earlier expanded-composer screenshot is not the sidebar reference.
Plugin-contributed sidebar elements MUST support this ordinary navigation-row presentation: an icon on the left, a readable text label beside it, and alignment, spacing and interaction treatment consistent with neighbouring sidebar items. A custom entry can sit directly beneath New Chat within the selected Space's permitted custom-sidebar area; it MUST NOT require opening a separate Plugin panel simply to reach the entry.
The screenshot is a concept reference for the custom entry's presentation and placement, not a requirement to copy its project names, conversation history, colours or complete sidebar structure. Existing protected navigation and Space-scoping requirements remain in force. The Plugin's per-Space visibility selection still determines where its entries appear, and the existing automation/Space-graph route remains supported.
Plugin sidebar API and acceptance
Extend the canonical Plugin and Spaces APIs for contribution registration, configuration, removal, per-Space visibility and authorised action dispatch; UI and API MUST use the same stable SidebarItemID and ownership/lifecycle rules. Test Plugin-defined URL/page, authored CUI, generative-page and Automation actions; persistence after restart; visibility only in selected Spaces; keyboard navigation and accessible names; and safe disable/detach without orphan actions or deletion of unrelated content. The original automation/Events & Extensions/Space-graph contribution route MUST continue to work, including combined workflows without duplicate contributions. The Plugin manifest and Builder MUST expose these contribution contracts rather than creating a second sidebar registry.
Canonical Space and conversation model
Space MUST contain at least SpaceID, SpaceOrigin, built-in type where applicable, Name, Icon?, ParentSpaceID?, owner/scope, instructions/configuration, model policy, context/source policy, memory policy, capability bindings, permissions, created/modified timestamps and revision metadata. SpaceID is stable across rename, nesting and UI ordering.
Conversation MUST contain at least ConversationID, SpaceID, Title, CreatedAt, ModifiedAt, ActiveBranchID, optional model override and revision metadata. Messages MUST have stable MessageID, author principal/role, branch/parent relationship, timestamp, content blocks, model/provider provenance where AI-generated and tool/action references where applicable.
Conversation branching and history
Editing an earlier message, regenerating a response or branching from a message MUST preserve prior history as a conversation branch rather than silently destroying descendants. Users MUST be able to return to earlier branches and identify which branch is active.
Tool calls and consequential actions already executed remain historical facts attached to their original run/branch and MUST NOT be retroactively undone merely because text was regenerated. New branches start from the selected historical conversational state but respect current external entity revisions/permissions.
Stop and resume
While a response/run is active, Spaces MUST expose Stop. After the user stops a resumable response, the stopped response remains in place and its primary control becomes a Play/Resume button. Resume continues the same user-visible RequestID/run from persisted execution state rather than behaving like Regenerate.
Request states MUST distinguish at least Queued, Running, Stopping, Stopped, Completed, Failed, Cancelled and Blocked. Stopped is resumable when the underlying run/checkpoint supports continuation; Cancelled is terminal unless a new/restarted run is explicitly created.
A stopped run MUST retain RequestID, conversation/message linkage, selected model/provider policy, context references/snapshot metadata, completed tool/action records, Action Graph, Subagent state/checkpoints and remaining budget/limits where applicable. Resume MUST NOT repeat already-completed consequential actions. If the provider cannot literally resume a token stream, Dulche may continue from persisted checkpoint/context while preserving the same user-visible continuation semantics.
Regenerate and Retry remain distinct from Resume: Regenerate creates a new response branch; Retry re-attempts a failed operation/run with idempotency and side-effect safeguards.
Model selection
Spaces MUST use the Universal Model Picker. Effective model policy resolves explicit request override, conversation override, Space default, app/default policy and global default in that order, subject to capability/privacy/entitlement restrictions.
Switching model mid-conversation MUST NOT rewrite provenance of prior responses. Every AI response/run must retain effective model/provider identity and relevant policy provenance.
Sources and context
Spaces context MUST be represented as explicit typed references rather than opaque prompt stuffing. Supported reference families include Files/folders, Boards/pages, Write/Present/Canvas/Data artifacts, Mail threads/messages, Planner items, Map routes, Stack projects, Sites/projects, connected-app entities, conversations and uploaded sources.
Each context/source reference MUST retain stable source identity, revision/change token where applicable, permission state and ingestion/index state where required. Spaces must be able to detect that a referenced source has changed rather than treating an old snapshot as current.
A Sources/Context surface MUST let the user inspect what is attached, where it came from, current revision/availability, whether it is included automatically, ingestion/index status and remove/disable controls. Spaces MUST NOT rely on mysterious hidden context for ordinary operation.
Dragging/adding a folder SHOULD create a folder reference plus scope/filter configuration rather than eagerly duplicating every contained file. Spaces can retrieve authorised current files on demand through Files APIs.
Context budgeting and retrieval
When available material exceeds the selected model’s context, Dulche/Spaces MUST use deterministic context selection/retrieval. Required/current selection and explicit attached sources take priority over optional historical context. Retrieval/summarisation/omission decisions MUST be represented in run logs/Action Graph sufficiently for inspection.
Spaces MUST NOT claim that an answer considered an entire source set when only a subset was retrieved. Source-grounded modes must retain provenance for the chunks/entities actually used.
Canonical artifact editing
Any authorised mutable 9to1 document/project/entity whose owning app exposes domain APIs MUST be openable/editable from Spaces without creating a duplicate canonical copy. Spaces MAY host an embedded artifact surface alongside conversation, but the artifact retains its owning app identity, revision history and permissions.
Spaces MUST support direct low-risk edits when clearly requested and reviewable proposed-change workflows for larger/ambiguous mutations. Review UI MUST correspond to actual typed target-app actions/diffs and MUST NOT present a fabricated text-only diff disconnected from the canonical artifact.
Shared Productivity Engine
Spaces MUST use Home’s Shared Productivity Engine for supported rich content/object rendering and editing. Pasted or embedded tables, code blocks, images, drawings, graphs and other shared objects MUST preserve shared schema/formatting and remain editable through the same object actions used by Write, Present, Canvas and Boards.
AI-generated shared-engine objects SHOULD be directly transferable to supporting apps without reconstructing them from rendered text/images.
Plugins, Skills and Agents
Every Space has its own capability bindings for Dulche Plugins, Skills and persistent Agents. By default, a newly created Space inherits all currently installed/enabled Dulche Plugins and Skills and all available Agents unless restricted by policy.
Space capability bindings MUST support inherited availability plus explicit per-Space enable/disable/exclusion and optional version pinning where the underlying package/Agent contract supports it. Installing a new globally enabled Plugin/Skill or making a new Agent available automatically makes it available to Spaces that still inherit that category.
Space bindings reference canonical Dulche package IDs/versions and Agent IDs; they MUST NOT clone package/Agent definitions into the Space. Availability does not grant permission: a Space may see a Plugin/Skill/Agent while still requiring the normal permission/trust decision before protected actions execute.
Shared node-editor framework
All Space graph editing uses the Home-owned Node Graph Framework also used by Automations. Home owns graph data structures, node registry, typed ports/connections, renderer, pan/zoom/selection, grouping, validation, clipboard/duplicate, undo/redo, graph versioning, execution visualisation hooks and contextual AI-bar integration. Spaces owns Space-specific event/action nodes and graph semantics; Dulche executes AI/model/Agent/tool portions; owning apps execute their typed actions.
Graph connections MUST be typed. Incompatible connections MUST be rejected or require an explicit conversion node. Graph nodes MUST reference stable canonical app/capability IDs rather than UI coordinates or screen controls.
Built-in Space Events & Extensions editor
Built-in Chat, Study, Tasks, Agent, Shopping, Research, Translate and Experiences Spaces expose a limited Events & Extensions graph editor attached only through published safe extension hooks. The protected first-party core graph/behaviour is not editable, disconnectable or replaceable.
Allowed extension hooks may include Space loaded/activated/deactivated/closed, conversation created/opened, response started/stopped/resumed/completed and relevant type-specific events such as Study session started/completed, Task started/blocked/completed, Research run completed, Translate Translation Set/job completed, Experience started/checkpointed/branched/completed or Agent run state changed.
Allowed extension actions may include Set Do Not Disturb, send Home notification, add/remove allowed context, open app/entity, create Planner item, invoke Automation/Agent/Skill/Plugin/permitted MCP capability, update extension-owned Space variables and add/show custom sidebar surfaces.
The built-in extension editor MUST NOT allow removal/replacement of protected sidebar items, suppression of required first-party events, replacement of the Space’s conversation/runtime behaviour, bypass of permissions, mutation of protected first-party graph internals, disabling required recovery/safety behaviour or creation of unbounded loops.
Published extension hooks are versioned. After a 9to1 update, incompatible/retired hooks MUST produce a needs-attention/repair state rather than silently breaking the whole Space.
User-created Space full graph editor
User-created Spaces created through + New Space may use the full Space graph editor. Their graph may define lifecycle behaviour, conversation routing, source retrieval, model/Agent selection, logic/branching, state, app actions, Generative UI, custom sidebar surfaces and other authorised Space behaviour.
Full graphs MAY use bounded logic nodes such as If, Switch, Filter, Merge, Wait, bounded Loop, variables, compare/transform plus typed AI/runtime nodes such as Prompt model, Choose model, Run Agent, invoke Skill/Plugin/MCP, retrieve/search sources and Generate UI.
Full graphs MUST still obey Home permissions, Dulche runtime limits, package/Agent availability, target-app contracts and loop/budget safeguards. A graph is not a permission escalation mechanism.
Custom graph edits MUST use Draft versus Active revision semantics. Changes are validated before Apply/Publish; invalid drafts do not replace the last valid active graph. Prior active revisions SHOULD be rollback-capable.
Graph-editor AI bar
Both the built-in Events & Extensions editor and the full user-created Space graph editor MUST host the persistent contextual AI bar. The bar receives graph-semantic context and modifies graphs only through typed Node Graph APIs, never by mouse/keyboard simulation.
A user MUST be able to request behaviour in natural language such as turning on Do Not Disturb when Study activates or adding a Planner sidebar surface. AI-generated graph changes MUST be presented as valid graph mutations and the assistant SHOULD explain the resulting behaviour in plain language, with relevant nodes highlightable from the explanation.
If a request would modify protected built-in behaviour, the editor/AI MUST reject that mutation and direct the user toward a user-created Space/full graph instead of attempting an unsafe override.
Custom sidebar surfaces
Space extension graphs MAY add custom sidebar items without replacing protected built-in items. Every custom SidebarItem MUST have stable SidebarItemID, title, icon, order/placement, visibility condition where supported, InterfaceType, interface reference/definition and required permissions.
Supported InterfaceType families MUST include AppSurface, CUI and GenerativeUI. AppSurface embeds an authorised surface from another 9to1 app such as Planner, Files, Boards, Maps, Stack or another declared embeddable surface while preserving canonical owning-app behaviour. CUI renders an explicitly authored safe interface backed by typed state/actions. GenerativeUI renders a Dulche-generated interface constrained by the Generative UI schema/component/action rules.
Generative sidebar interfaces MAY be Dynamic (regenerated/refreshed from current authorised context) or Persisted (stored definition until explicitly regenerated/edited). Generated UI MUST NOT execute arbitrary code or gain permissions merely because it is displayed.
Protected built-in sidebar IDs/namespaces cannot be shadowed/overwritten by extensions. Custom entries use extension-owned stable IDs.
Long-running work and Action Graph
Long-running requests/tasks MUST expose run status, current objective/step, elapsed state, Subagents/tool activity summaries, blockers, approvals and outputs where applicable, with Pause/Resume/Stop/Open Action Graph controls supported by the underlying run.
Closing/navigating away from Spaces MUST NOT automatically kill a run that was explicitly started with background-capable semantics. Home/Dulche retains durable run state and may notify through Home when work completes, blocks, needs approval or fails.
Tool/action rendering may be collapsed in conversation but MUST remain inspectable. Action Graph opens the actual Dulche execution graph; Spaces MUST NOT fabricate a second independent action history.
Agents and Subagents
Persistent Agents may be invoked inside any Space where available/authorised. The Space contributes authorised context but MUST NOT expand the Agent’s own effective permissions, tool scopes or memory policy.
Dulche Subagents remain runtime child-execution primitives and MUST NOT be conflated with persistent user-facing Agents. Spaces may show concise worker counts/status while detailed execution remains inspectable in Action Graph.
Memory and Dulche Den
Spaces MUST support explicit memory/context scopes including conversation-local, Space-level and permitted broader personal/team/organisation scopes. Space-level persistent memory/context lives through Dulche Den under stable Space identity and applicable permissions.
Shared Spaces MUST NOT implicitly expose a participant’s private personal Den context or private connected accounts. Caller-specific private context remains private unless deliberately shared through an authorised shared/team mechanism.
Web access and source provenance
Web access MUST be an explicit Space/tool policy with at least Allowed, Ask and Disabled semantics where applicable. Source-only/closed-corpus workflows MUST be able to disable outside web retrieval completely.
When an answer materially relies on identifiable source material, Spaces MUST preserve clickable provenance/citations back to the underlying file/page/message/web source/entity where supported. It MUST distinguish source-derived claims from generated reasoning and must not claim support that the retrieved sources do not provide.
Search, organisation and sharing
Spaces MUST support search across authorised Space/conversation titles, messages, source names and applicable run/tool metadata. Search respects Space sharing/permissions.
Conversations MUST support rename, pin, archive, delete/recover, move to another compatible Space, duplicate/fork and export. Moving a conversation changes future Space environment/policy but MUST preserve historical provenance/model/action records.
Spaces MAY be shared at Space or conversation level with explicit roles such as Viewer, Participant and Editor/Admin or equivalent typed scopes. Multi-human conversations MUST record AuthorPrincipalID per human message. Sharing a Space MUST NOT automatically share private external-account credentials or personal Den state.
Study structured state
Study MUST persist structured learning state such as course/topic/concept, attempts, recorded confidence/proficiency evidence, last reviewed, next review and source references. It MUST support source-only versus broader-information policy and clearly distinguish supplied-source content from outside knowledge when both are permitted.
Tasks structured state
Task MUST contain at least TaskID, Objective, Status, Plan, ordered Steps, CurrentStep, Dependencies, Inputs, Outputs, Blockers, Approvals and associated RunID(s). Required states include Draft, Ready, Running, Waiting, Blocked, Paused, Completed, Failed and Cancelled.
A Task may invoke persistent Agents, Dulche Subagents and tools, and may itself be launched by an Automation, but Task identity remains the user-level work item rather than becoming an Agent or Automation.

9to1.Spaces.Capabilities.List(spaceID);
