Automation and Spaces integration
Automations, Spaces and Dulche can invoke the exhaustive Picture action catalogue subject to permissions/capabilities. Long-running generation/render/export operations return job/run state with progress, cancellation and typed errors.
Picture publishes typed events for meaningful document/revision/generation/export changes without flooding Automations with raw pointer/stroke-move events.
Collaboration and conflict handling
Picture mutations are revision-aware. Independent edits may merge where the canonical object graph proves them non-conflicting; concurrent incompatible edits to the same element/mask/layer/revision MUST surface a conflict rather than blind last-write-wins.
AI-generated edits are attributable to a revision/action actor and are undoable/reviewable through the same history system as manual changes.
Security and generated content
AI/image generation/editing follows configured model/tool permissions, content controls, privacy/local-cloud routing policy and source-asset access permissions. Picture MUST NOT upload local/private images to a remote model/provider when the effective privacy policy forbids it.
Generated/imported external content is treated as content, not executable code. Embedded metadata/scripts MUST NOT acquire application execution privileges.
Accessibility
Picture's Create/Edit/Generate/Browse surfaces MUST be keyboard-operable for required workflows. Sliders/controls expose names, values and keyboard adjustment. Layer/object lists, tools, masks and selection state expose meaningful semantic accessibility information.
Image descriptions/alt text MAY be stored/edited where applicable. Colour-only indicators require textual/semantic equivalents. Zoom/crop/transform handles have keyboard-accessible alternatives.
Platform capability behaviour
Picture MUST provide useful Windows, 9to1-OS and web editing/creation experiences over the same PictureDocument model. Codec, RAW, HDR, GPU effect, pen/tilt and local/remote AI capability differences are explicit and queryable.
The web app MUST NOT degrade into a read-only image viewer. Unsupported platform features are disabled with a capability reason while preserving the canonical document so another capable client can continue editing.
Performance and resource behaviour
Picture MUST use resolution-appropriate decode, GPU acceleration where suitable, incremental/tiled rendering for very large images, bounded preview/thumbnail caches, background full-quality rendering and cancellable long-running jobs.
Interactive edit previews may use reduced-resolution proxies, but final save/export renders from canonical source content at requested quality. Large layer/vector graphs should avoid full-document rerenders when only a bounded element/region changes.
AI-generated previews/variants and caches are bounded and revision-addressed. Closing or cancelling generation does not corrupt the last valid document.
Failure behaviour
Picture MUST return structured failures including DocumentNotFound, ElementNotFound, InvalidSelection, InvalidMask, UnsupportedFormat, UnsupportedCodecFeature, ColourProfileUnsupported, HDRUnsupported, RevisionConflict, LinkedAssetUnavailable, GenerationUnavailable, GenerationFailed, InvalidGenerationRegion, ExportUnsupportedFeature, RenderFailed, PermissionDenied and CapabilityUnavailable in addition to shared engine/model errors.
A failed edit/generation/export leaves the prior valid document revision intact. Unsupported export features are reported before destructive flattening/conversion.
Acceptance requirements
Picture is implementation-complete only when acceptance coverage verifies at least:
A real Raster, Vector and Hybrid PictureDocument can be created, saved, closed and reopened with editable structure intact.
Automatic composition mode allows ordinary users to create/edit complex images without manual layer management, while Manual Layer mode exposes the same underlying canonical structure without conversion.
Shared Write/Present/Canvas/Boards productivity, text, shape, selection/transform and Rnote-derived drawing engines are actually reused rather than reimplemented as Picture-private equivalents.
Raster editing covers crop/transform, light/colour, blur/sharpen/repair and masks with non-destructive/revision-aware behaviour.
Vector editing covers path/anchor/Bézier editing, fills/strokes, boolean operations, snapping/alignment, text/path integration and raster/vector conversion workflows.
A user can circle/smart-select a subject, freely move/resize/delete/replace it, and Picture reconstructs exposed background while preserving revisioned editable state.
Generative fill/erase/replace/extend and background replacement operate on explicit selections/objects and preserve source/revision provenance.
Text-to-image, reference-guided creation and sketch-to-image create normal editable Picture assets/documents rather than opaque temporary results.
Sketch-to-image can use shared drawing-engine strokes and supports iterative region refinement.
Manual drawing/painting/markup uses the shared Rnote-derived drawing engine and retains editable stroke semantics.
Before/after comparison, variants, undo/redo and persistent revision history survive restart.
Raster, vector, text, generated objects, masks and linked assets coexist correctly in a Hybrid document.
Save, Save Copy and export preserve the editable source while producing interoperable rendered/vector outputs with explicit flattening where required.
Files identity survives rename/move/hydration and live cross-app references remain canonical.
The persistent AI bar performs semantic typed edits against selected objects/regions and never requires raw UI simulation.
Windows, 9to1-OS and web preserve the same canonical document model while capability-negotiating codecs/GPU/AI/pen differences.
Large source images/layer graphs remain interactive through tiling/proxy rendering/bounded caches and final export renders at requested source quality.
When Home is absent at process start, Picture follows the global Install Home/bootstrap contract rather than launching an incompatible private runtime.
Wave
Product role and native-generation principle
9-1 Wave is the native CUI audio recording, editing, mixing, sequencing and sound-creation app. It combines an approachable multitrack editor with professional waveform/spectral editing, mixing, effects, music sequencing, sound-effect construction, text-to-speech and AI-assisted production.
All generated audio components MUST be native, structured Wave components whenever the requested result can be represented by Wave's own sequencer, synthesis, effect, speech or clip systems. AI MUST NOT normally return an opaque arbitrary waveform as the canonical result for music, sound effects, speech or other structured generative workflows. Rendering to audio is a derived/export/playback result; the editable native component remains canonical.
Example: asking AI to create a song produces editable sequencer/instrument/pattern/arrangement data; asking for a laser sound creates an editable Sound Effect Builder patch; asking for narration creates a native Text-to-Speech object retaining its text/voice/prosody settings.
Shared media/audio engine
Wave MUST share its core audio/media primitives with Motion, Present and other eligible 9to1 surfaces rather than creating incompatible per-app audio engines. The shared media/audio layer owns canonical audio assets, clips, time ranges, transport/playback, waveform/spectrogram analysis, effect descriptors, rendering/export primitives and realtime-safe audio processing where applicable.
Motion uses the same compatible audio clip/effect/timeline primitives for video projects. Present recording/narration uses compatible Wave/shared-media assets. Vision & Voice contributes shared microphone/device discovery, OS audio permissions and applicable capture primitives, while Wave remains the persistent production editor. Dulche Audio/Voice supplies model-backed transcription, analysis and speech capability without becoming a second project model.
GStreamer is an approved maintained media backend and GStreamer Editing Services or an explicitly documented equivalent may be used where appropriate. Backend choice MUST preserve the public Wave project/action contracts.
Canonical project model
WaveProject has stable ProjectID, sample-rate/channel configuration, timeline/timebase, tempo map where used, Tracks[], Markers/Regions[], native generated components, project settings, CreatedAt/ModifiedAt and Revision.
AudioTrack has stable TrackID, name, ordered Clips[], Gain, Pan, Mute, Solo, RecordArm, Effects[], AutomationLanes[], routing/bus state where supported and Revision.
AudioClip has stable ClipID, SourceAssetID or native GeneratedComponentID, source range, TimelineStart, Duration, Gain, fades, stretch/pitch settings, effects/automation references and Revision. Timeline editing MUST be non-destructive by default.
Generated native components receive stable IDs and can be inserted on tracks like other sources while retaining their editable structured source. Rendering a component for playback/export does not replace that structured source.
Main workspace and transport
Wave's primary workspace is a multitrack timeline with transport, track controls, selected clip/component inspector and optional mixer/effects/sequencer/spectral panels. Record, Edit, Mix and Generate are workflow emphases over one project rather than incompatible document modes.
Transport MUST include:
Play, Pause, Stop and Record.
Seek to start/end and previous/next marker or region.
Loop playback/recording.
Timeline position display with time/timecode and musical bars/beats where enabled.
Playback speed and metronome/count-in where relevant.
Keyboard-first editing shortcuts are required for repetitive timeline operations.
Recording
Wave MUST support robust microphone/device recording including input-device selection, mono/stereo/multichannel where available, input monitoring, level meters/clipping indication, record-arm per track, count-in/pre-roll/post-roll, punch-in/punch-out, overdub, loop/take recording and pause/resume.
Recording is written incrementally/crash-safely so a process or device failure does not discard an entire long recording. Incomplete recoverable takes remain clearly marked until finalised.
Waveform and clip editing
Required clip/waveform operations include:
Select time range, move, duplicate, copy/paste, split and join/compose where semantically valid.
Trim, slip/source-range edit, delete, ripple delete and insert/ripple move.
Fade in/out and crossfade.
Gain/normalise, silence, reverse, resample, time-stretch and pitch-shift.
Snap to grid, markers, transients, clips or musical timing where enabled.
Ordinary clip edits change clip/source-range/timeline metadata rather than destructively rewriting source bytes. A destructive source edit, where explicitly requested, creates a recoverable revision/new source asset.
Multitrack, mixer, routing and buses
Wave MUST support multiple simultaneous audio tracks for voice, music, sound effects, ambience, generated content, imported media and multiple takes. Track grouping and multi-selection allow coherent edits across related clips.
The mixer provides per-track and master gain, pan, mute/solo, meters, insert effects and supported sends/buses/routing. Advanced routing may be hidden by default but the canonical project supports it where exposed.
Master processing is explicit and non-destructive. Export rendering follows the current routing/effect graph.
Effects and parameter automation
Core non-AI effect families include at least:
EQ/filtering including high/low-pass and parametric EQ.
Compressor, limiter, gate/expander and de-esser.
Reverb and delay.
Chorus/flanger/phaser and modulation effects where supported.
Distortion/saturation.
Pitch shift/time stretch.
Stereo width, gain/normalisation and utility processing.
Effects are non-destructive insert/processing nodes by default and can be reordered, bypassed, edited and removed.
Effect/track/instrument parameters may be automated over time using native automation lanes/curves. Automation data is structured and editable rather than baked into a rendered waveform.
Spectral editing and repair
Wave MUST provide Waveform, Spectrogram and combined Waveform+Spectrogram views. Time/frequency selections can drive attenuation, filtering, silence, repair and model-assisted cleanup operations.
Native/manual repair includes where supported:
Click/pop removal.
DC offset correction.
Hum/notch filtering.
Noise reduction and gating.
Clipping repair where technically possible.
Silence trimming and loudness normalisation.
AI-assisted cleanup MAY isolate speech, remove/reduce noise, reverb, clicks, breaths/coughs, restore damaged recordings and perform other model-backed repair, but outputs remain represented as native derived clips/effect operations/revisions rather than silently overwriting the source.
Audio enhancement and denoising tools
Wave MUST expose first-class Enhance Audio and Denoise tools for selected clips, tracks, time ranges and imported or recorded audio. Enhance Audio is a configurable restoration/mastering pipeline, not a single opaque AI button. At minimum it MUST be able to combine appropriate noise/hum reduction, de-click/de-pop, de-reverb where available, clarity/EQ correction, dynamics/level correction and loudness normalisation; speech-focused enhancement MAY use model-backed processing. Denoise MUST provide an automatic one-click path plus an advanced path with strength/amount and preview/bypass. Where the selected backend supports noise-profile learning, Wave MUST allow a selected region to be used as the noise profile.
Enhancement and denoising MUST be previewable, undoable and non-destructive. Long-running model-backed processing MUST expose progress and cancellation. The source asset remains intact; Wave stores the configured processing and/or derived result with provenance. Applying enhancement MUST NOT silently modify unrelated clips, tracks, effects or master routing.
Music Sequencer
Wave MUST include a first-class native music sequencer. Music generation, whether user-authored or AI-assisted, produces editable sequencer content rather than an arbitrary final audio file.
The sequencer supports stable SequenceID/PatternID/NoteEventID/InstrumentID identities, tempo/time-signature maps, piano-roll and step-sequencer editing, note pitch/start/duration/velocity, quantisation, swing/groove, looping patterns, arrangement sections, track/instrument assignment and parameter automation.
Drum sequencing supports drum-grid/pad-oriented patterns, per-step velocity/probability/variation where supported and reusable kits. Melodic sequencing supports chords, scales/key assistance where enabled, note expression and automation.
The arrangement view assembles patterns/regions into song structure such as Intro, Verse, Chorus, Bridge and Outro without flattening them. Users can duplicate/modify a pattern instance or create a linked instance according to explicit identity semantics.
Native instruments and sampling
The sequencer MUST provide a versioned instrument registry. Native instrument families MAY include synthesizers, drums/percussion, sampler instruments and other maintained engines. Each Instrument has structured editable parameters, preset identity/version and automation-capable controls.
Sampler instruments reference canonical audio assets and expose mapped key/range, start/end, loop, pitch/tuning, envelope/filter and other supported parameters without duplicating source bytes unnecessarily.
AI may choose/configure instruments, write notes/patterns, create arrangement structure, automate parameters and mix tracks, but MUST produce the same native Sequencer/Instrument/Effect objects a user can inspect and edit manually.
AI music generation
A request such as 'make a two-minute upbeat electronic track' MUST generate a native music project/section: tempo and meter, sequencer tracks, instrument choices/settings, editable note/pattern data, arrangement, automation and effects/mix state. The canonical AI result is NOT an opaque two-minute waveform.
AI may iterate by editing native structures: 'make the chorus heavier' changes relevant patterns/instruments/automation/effects; 'change the chord progression' rewrites note/chord events while preserving unrelated project structure.
Generated music can subsequently be manually edited in piano roll/step sequencer/mixer. Export renders the structured project into WAV/FLAC/MP3/etc. only when requested.
Sound Effects Builder
Wave MUST include a native Sound Effects Builder for procedural/constructed sound effects. A SoundEffectPatch has stable PatchID and a structured processing/generation graph rather than being merely a rendered audio clip.
The builder SHOULD use the Home Node Graph Framework for editing/visualisation where appropriate, with Wave-specific realtime audio nodes and execution handled by the Wave audio engine.
Core SFX node families include where supported:
Oscillator/wavetable/source generators.
Noise generators.
Sampler/audio-asset sources.
Envelope/ADSR and amplitude shaping.
Pitch/frequency modulation and LFO.
Filters/EQ.
Distortion/waveshaping.
Delay/reverb/modulation effects.
Layer/mix/split/combine.
Randomisation/probability and parameter modulation.
Output/render.
A request such as 'create a futuristic laser blast' causes AI to build/configure an editable native patch graph, envelopes, oscillators/noise, pitch movement and effects. The generated patch can be auditioned and inserted onto the timeline, but the patch remains the canonical editable source.
The UI SHOULD offer simple high-level macro controls for common users while allowing advanced users to open the complete patch graph.
Text to Speech
Wave MUST include native Text-to-Speech components. A SpeechSynthesis object stores stable SpeechID, text/script, selected VoiceID/model/runtime, language/locale, pronunciation/phoneme overrides where supported, speed, pitch, style/emotion/prosody controls, timing/alignment metadata and revision.
Editing the text or voice/prosody regenerates the derived speech render while retaining the same structured SpeechSynthesis source. Speech may be split into utterances/paragraphs/regions and aligned on the timeline without flattening into an anonymous generated waveform.
Where a TTS backend exposes word/phoneme timings, Wave stores them for transcript/alignment editing. Export may render speech to ordinary audio, but the editable Wave project retains the speech component.
Voice cloning/conversion or user-supplied voice references, if supported, require the applicable consent/permission and provenance rules.
Other generated native components
The same native-generation rule applies to generated ambience, transitions and other constructible audio. AI should build Wave-native source/processing structures — for example layered samplers plus filters/envelopes/automation for ambience — instead of defaulting to opaque audio generation.
When a capability fundamentally requires an externally generated waveform that cannot be represented by existing native generators, that waveform MAY enter Wave only as an explicit GeneratedSample source asset with model/provenance metadata. It MUST then be treated like a normal editable sample/clip, and the UI must not pretend it has native sequencer/patch editability. Native structured generation remains the default and required path whenever representable.
Transcription and transcript-based editing
Wave transcription is time-aligned to project/source audio and can include speaker diarisation, word timing, language detection, punctuation and corrections where supported. Clicking/selecting transcript text maps to the corresponding audio range.
Transcript-based edits such as deleting a phrase or removing long pauses translate into ordinary native timeline/clip edits after preview/validation. The transcript is a semantic editing view over canonical audio/timeline state, not a replacement authority for the audio project.
Custom censorship
Wave MUST include Custom Censorship for a selected clip, track, time range or whole-project audio scope. A CensorshipRuleSet can contain exact words, phrases, user-defined terms and one or more semantic themes/categories. Word and phrase rules use time-aligned transcription where available; theme rules MAY use supported model-backed semantic classification. Detection MUST produce reviewable candidate time ranges before application, and the user MUST be able to add, remove or adjust matches to correct false positives and false negatives.
Each rule or rule set can choose a treatment including bleep/tone, mute/silence, attenuation, replacement with a user-selected sound, or timeline removal when explicitly chosen. Controls MUST include pre/post padding and fades, and MAY optionally redact matched text from captions/transcripts. Censorship remains a structured editable operation with stable identity; it can be disabled, reconfigured or undone without altering the original source. Export/render follows the active censorship state.
Audio separation and derived stems
Where configured model/backends support it, Wave can separate mixed audio into structured derived assets/tracks such as vocals, drums, bass, other/music, speakers or foreground/background. Source audio remains preserved and the separated outputs receive stable asset/track identities.
AI separation is a transformation workflow, not an excuse to destroy or replace the source.
Stem splitting MUST be exposed as a first-class Split Stems tool rather than only as an AI command. The UI MUST offer every separation mode supported by the configured backend, including common modes such as Vocals/Instrumental, Vocals/Drums/Bass/Other, speaker separation and Foreground/Background where available. The user can choose which derived stems become tracks, preview/audition the result and re-run separation with a different supported mode without replacing the original mixed source.
Markers, regions and chapters
Wave supports stable MarkerID and RegionID entities for navigation, looping, chapters, editing targets and export metadata. Markers/regions may carry names, colours/categories, notes and references without changing underlying clip data.
Podcast, narration and spoken-word workflows
Podcast/spoken-word workflows reuse normal Wave tracks, transcript, markers, effects and export rather than creating a separate engine. Useful capabilities include multi-speaker editing, chapter markers, silence cleanup, loudness targets, intro/outro, metadata and transcript export.
Present narration and other 9to1 speech assets can open in Wave for detailed editing while retaining canonical timing/asset references.
Motion and Present interoperability
Motion and Wave MUST share compatible audio asset/clip/effect/timeline primitives. A Motion audio track can be opened/edited in Wave and return as the same canonical audio/project reference where supported, avoiding an unnecessary export-edit-import loop.
Present recording/narration can use compatible Wave/shared-media assets and can deep-link to Wave for advanced cleanup/mix/editing without losing timing/reference identity.
Files and storage identity
Files remains authoritative for source/export asset storage identity, create/move/rename/delete/recover/share and provider/cloud hydration. Wave project structures reference stable FileID/asset identities rather than absolute file paths.
Recorded/generated/imported assets receive canonical storage/asset identity. Moving/renaming the underlying File does not detach the Wave reference.
Import and export
Wave import MUST support common maintained codecs/formats through the shared media backend. Source sample rate, channels, timing and metadata are preserved where applicable.
Export can target full project, selected region, track(s), stems, selected clips or selected native generated components. Common outputs include WAV, FLAC, MP3, AAC/M4A and OGG/Opus where supported, plus other maintained codecs.
Export options include sample rate, bit depth where applicable, bitrate/quality, channel layout, loudness/normalisation, metadata and relevant loop/chapter settings. Export never silently mutates the project.
Persistent AI bar
Wave MUST host the global persistent Dulche AI bar. Semantic context includes ProjectID, selected TrackIDs/ClipIDs/GeneratedComponentIDs, selected time/frequency range, playhead, markers/regions, sequencer patterns/notes/instruments, SFX graph selection, speech object/text, effects/automation state, transcript selection, sample rate/timebase and revision.
Write-capable AI changes Wave only through typed Wave/shared-media/NodeGraph actions. It MUST NOT simulate timeline mouse gestures when semantic APIs exist.
Wave API
Wave's first-party API catalogue is exhaustive under the global API-parity rule. Minimum canonical entry points include:

9to1.Wave.Export(projectID, target, format, options);
Sound Effect Builder graph mutation uses 9to1.NodeGraph.* where the shared Node Graph Framework is the canonical graph-editing layer. Shared media operations SHOULD use their owning shared API namespace when that is canonical.
Automation and integration events
Automations, Spaces, Dulche and other authorised clients can use the exhaustive Wave action catalogue. Long recording/render/export/transcription/separation jobs expose progress, cancellation, retry/idempotency where relevant and typed result/error state.
Wave emits meaningful typed events such as project/revision changes, recording completed, export completed, render failed and generated component changed; it MUST NOT flood Automations with raw per-sample or pointer events.
Collaboration and revision conflicts
Project/track/clip/pattern/note/patch/speech mutations are revision-aware. Independent object edits MAY merge when safe; incompatible concurrent edits to the same canonical object surface conflict rather than blind last-write-wins.
A running render/export/recording is pinned to the required source/project revision and MUST NOT silently switch to a newly edited revision mid-job.
Accessibility
Wave MUST be keyboard-operable for transport, clip selection/editing, sequencer editing, mixer controls, transcript editing and generated-component workflows. Waveforms/spectrograms provide semantic time/level/frequency information and non-pointer equivalents for required operations.
Meters, clipping, mute/solo, automation and error states MUST NOT rely on colour alone. Screen-reader users can inspect track/clip/note/patch/speech object identity and values.
Performance and realtime safety
The realtime audio path MUST remain isolated from blocking UI, disk, AI/model, network and export work. Playback/recording cannot glitch merely because waveform thumbnails, transcription, generation or export are running.
Waveforms/spectrograms are incrementally analysed/cached; large recordings are streamed/tiled rather than fully decoded into RAM. Realtime-safe effect/instrument processing obeys bounded allocation/latency constraints.
Generated sequencer/SFX/TTS components render incrementally/cached for preview while preserving the structured source. Background renders are cancellable and caches are bounded/revision-invalidated.
Recovery and failure behaviour
Wave durably stores project structure, current recording chunks/takes, native generated-component state and edit history often enough to maximise crash recovery. Restart can recover incomplete recordings/project mutations without replaying committed destructive actions.
Structured failures include ProjectNotFound, TrackNotFound, ClipNotFound, GeneratedComponentNotFound, InvalidTimeRange, InvalidSequence, InvalidPattern, InstrumentUnavailable, InvalidSoundEffectGraph, VoiceUnavailable, RecordingDeviceUnavailable, RecordingFailed, CodecUnsupported, RenderFailed, ExportFailed, RevisionConflict, PermissionDenied and CapabilityUnavailable, plus shared backend/model errors.
A failed AI/native generation/render/export leaves the prior valid project and source assets intact.
Platform capability behaviour
Wave MUST provide useful Windows, 9to1-OS and web editing/creation experiences over the same canonical project model. Input devices, realtime audio APIs, codecs, plugin/instrument backends, MIDI/controller access and local/cloud model capabilities are explicit/queryable.
Web MUST remain a useful multitrack/sequencer/editor experience rather than a static player. Unsupported platform capabilities are disabled with a clear reason while preserving project state for another capable client.
Acceptance requirements
Wave is implementation-complete only when acceptance coverage verifies at least:
A multitrack project can be recorded, edited, mixed, closed/reopened and exported while preserving stable TrackID/ClipID/revision identity.
Recording supports device selection, metering, track arm and crash-safe recovery of an interrupted take.
Waveform clip editing is non-destructive and split/trim/move/fade/crossfade/undo survive restart.
Mixer/effects/automation are structured and editable, with realtime playback remaining stable during background work.
Waveform/spectrogram editing and native/audio-model repair operate without destroying the original source.
Music Sequencer persists editable note/pattern/instrument/arrangement/automation data and can render/export the result.
An AI music request generates a native sequencer arrangement with editable notes, patterns, instruments and effects instead of an opaque waveform.
Sound Effects Builder persists an editable native patch graph and an AI request such as a laser sound generates/configures that graph rather than only returning rendered audio.
Text-to-Speech persists editable text/voice/prosody state and regenerated speech remains linked to the same native SpeechSynthesis component.
Generated ambience/transitions use native Wave generators/patches/components whenever representable; an unavoidable external GeneratedSample is explicitly identified as a sampled fallback with provenance.
Transcript-based deletion maps to ordinary timeline edits and remains undoable.
Separation produces derived stable tracks/assets while preserving the mixed source.
Enhance Audio and Denoise are available as ordinary manual tools, support preview/bypass or equivalent before commitment, remain undoable/non-destructive and preserve the original source.
Custom Censorship can detect at least an exact word/phrase rule and a semantic-theme rule, exposes detected ranges for review/correction, applies the selected treatment and remains reversible without altering the source.
Split Stems is directly accessible from the Wave UI, creates stable derived track/asset identities for a supported separation mode and preserves the original mixed source.
Motion/Present interoperability uses shared canonical audio primitives rather than export/import duplication.
The persistent AI bar edits tracks/clips/sequences/patches/speech through typed APIs rather than raw UI simulation.
Large projects/recordings remain responsive through streaming, incremental analysis and bounded caches.
Windows, 9to1-OS and web preserve the same project/generated-component model while capability-negotiating audio hardware/backend differences.
When Home is absent at process start, Wave follows the global Install Home/bootstrap contract rather than launching an incompatible private runtime.
Motion
Product role and native project principle
9-1 Motion is the native CUI video editing, compositing, animation and motion-graphics application. It combines professional non-linear editing, layered visual composition, animation, titles/graphics, colour, audio production, AI-assisted editing and generative-video workflows while keeping the default editing experience approachable.
The canonical result of work in Motion is a structured MotionProject, not a rendered video. Normal edits such as trimming, crop, speed changes, transforms, masks, effects, colour changes, captions, keyframes, procedural animation and AI-assisted mutations MUST remain inspectable editable project state. Rendering, proxies, previews, caches and exports are derived outputs and MUST NOT silently replace canonical project state.
Shared engines and dependency boundaries
Motion MUST reuse shared 9to1 engines aggressively wherever the underlying capability belongs to more than one product. Shared capability MUST live in the appropriate shared engine/library rather than requiring another app UI process or duplicating private implementations.
Motion reuses the Wave/shared-media engine for audio clips, tracks, waveform/spectrogram analysis, effects, mixing, generated speech/music/SFX and audio rendering; Picture/shared visual primitives for compatible raster/vector composition, masks, paths, still-image effects and object-level image manipulation; Present/shared animation primitives for compatible easing, interpolation and timing concepts; the Shared Productivity Engine for compatible text, vector shape, drawing/ink and transform primitives; Rnote-derived drawing/path primitives for annotation, matte/mask drawing and rotoscoping assistance; Files for canonical asset identity; Dulche/model infrastructure for analysis and generation; the shared Node Graph Framework for advanced graphs; and CUI for the shell/navigation/interaction system.
Dependency direction MUST remain acyclic and engine-oriented. Motion MUST NOT require the Picture or Wave UI processes merely to crop an image or adjust audio. Picture, Wave and Motion consume compatible shared implementations. If Motion needs a capability that Picture, Wave, Present or another surface also materially needs, the implementation SHOULD be placed in the owning shared engine rather than copied.
Canonical project model
MotionProject has stable ProjectID, Sequences[], AssetReferences[], GeneratedComponents[], GlobalSettings, ColourSettings, ProxyCacheSettings, CreatedAt, ModifiedAt and Revision.
Sequence has stable SequenceID, Width, Height, PixelAspectRatio, FrameRate/timebase, Duration, VideoTracks[], compatible AudioTracks[], Markers[], Guides/safe-area state where used, colour/HDR state and Revision.
VisualTrack has stable TrackID, name, ordered Elements[], visibility, lock state, compositing state where applicable and Revision. Audio tracks use compatible Wave/shared-media track primitives rather than a second incompatible audio model.
MotionElement has stable ElementID, ElementType, SourceAssetID or GeneratedComponentID where applicable, TrackID, TimelineStart, Duration, SourceRange, Transform, Crop, Opacity, BlendMode, Masks[], Effects[], ParameterAnimation[], graph references where applicable and Revision.
Masks, EffectInstances, AnimationTracks, Keyframes, Titles/TextObjects, CaptionTracks, CaptionCues, analysis records and Motion node-graph objects MUST have stable identity and revision-aware state where they are addressable/editable. AI, Automations, collaboration and undo/redo address canonical object IDs and properties rather than screen coordinates.
Main workspace and contextual editing
The default Motion workspace consists of Media/Assets, Viewer/Canvas, contextual Inspector and Timeline. Panels MAY be docked, resized, collapsed, moved or hidden, but the initial workspace MUST avoid exposing an unnecessarily large professional-panel wall to a new user.
The Inspector is selection-sensitive: selecting video exposes video/transform/effect controls; text exposes typography/layout/animation; masks expose mask/path controls; audio exposes Wave-compatible controls; generated objects expose generation/provenance controls; and no selection exposes sequence/project controls.
Direct manipulation in the Viewer/Canvas MUST mutate the same canonical properties and typed actions used by the Inspector, keyboard operations, APIs and AI. The viewer MUST NOT maintain a separate UI-only transform or mask state.
Timeline and non-linear editing
Motion MUST provide a professional multi-track NLE timeline with accurate frame/timecode semantics, in/out ranges, source/sequence viewing, snapping, multi-selection, markers, grouping, linked audio/video, track controls and nested sequences.
Minimum typed editing operations include insert, overwrite, append, blade/split, trim, ripple trim, roll, slip, slide, ripple delete, lift, extract, move, duplicate, group/ungroup, link/unlink audio and video, track lock, video visibility, audio mute/solo where applicable, range selection and nested-sequence creation/use.
Transport MUST support ordinary play/pause, frame stepping and efficient shuttle/scrub control, including keyboard-first operation such as J/K/L-style transport where appropriate. Editing operations MUST be deterministic at the sequence timebase and MUST NOT depend on pixel coordinates in the timeline UI.
Video tracks may contain video, images, Picture assets, titles/text, vector graphics, shapes/ink, generated media, adjustment/effect layers, nested sequences and other registered compatible visual elements. Timeline editing remains non-destructive by default.
Source media, proxies, preview and cache
Motion MUST separate canonical source media from proxy media, decode caches, analysis caches, preview renders and final render output. Editing against a proxy MUST preserve the same canonical source identity, timing, ElementID and project semantics.
Motion MUST support automatic proxy generation, user-requested proxies, configurable proxy resolution/codec where supported, per-asset proxy state, background generation, lower-resolution viewer playback and render/pre-render caching.
Final render/export MUST use canonical source media at requested output quality unless the user explicitly chooses a proxy-derived or otherwise lower-quality source path. Missing or stale proxies/caches are recoverable derived-state problems and MUST NOT make the canonical project invalid.
Viewer, transforms and visual composition
The Viewer doubles as an interactive composition canvas. Users can directly inspect and edit position, scale, rotation, anchor/pivot, crop, opacity, masks, alignment/guides, text bounds and compatible shape/path properties.
Transform and visual-property edits MUST be represented by canonical property mutations. Source pixels/frames remain unchanged unless the user explicitly performs a destructive source-operation workflow outside normal Motion project editing.
Motion MUST support layered compositing with opacity, blend modes, alpha, masks, mattes, track mattes, chroma/luma keying, nesting/precomposition, adjustment layers and explicit compositing order where supported.
Animation and keyframes
Suitable numeric, vector, colour, mask, effect, text and generated-component properties MUST be animatable through a common parameter-animation system rather than each feature inventing incompatible keyframe storage.
Keyframes have stable identity and support create, move, copy, duplicate, delete and value editing. Supported interpolation includes at least hold/step, linear and smooth/eased interpolation, with Bézier/value curves where meaningful. Motion MUST provide easing presets and a graph/curve editor for advanced editing.
Shared Present animation/timing primitives SHOULD be reused when semantics are compatible, while Motion remains authoritative for timeline/frame-based video state.
Advanced node editor
Motion MUST include a full visual node editor for advanced compositing, effects, transitions, motion graphics and procedural animation. It reuses the shared 9to1 Node Graph Framework for GraphID/NodeID/PortID identity, pan/zoom, selection, grouping, comments, typed ports, connection validation, copy/paste/duplicate, undo/redo, graph revisioning, AI graph mutation and execution-state visualisation.
Motion registers a rich Motion-specific node catalogue. Minimum families include media/sequence inputs, transform, crop, masks/mattes, compositing/blending, chroma/luma keying, colour processing, blur/sharpen, distortion/displacement, tracking data, procedural shapes, text/title generation, time offsets, retiming, parameter maths, curves, interpolation/easing, switching/conditions, generators and compatible particle/procedural systems where implemented.
Node graphs are structured project state. Branching graphs MUST NOT require destructive intermediate renders merely because an operation is non-linear. Render/cache intermediates MAY be produced for performance, but graph topology, parameters and inputs remain canonical.
The normal Motion UI MUST remain usable without nodes. Common effects and animation can be edited directly. Where an advanced representation is appropriate, Open in Node Editor/Advanced exposes or creates the structured graph without silently replacing unrelated project state.
Motion graph types and reusable graph assets
Motion defines native reusable graph objects including MotionEffectGraph, MotionTransitionGraph, MotionAnimationGraph and MotionCompositionGraph. Each has stable identity, revision state, typed inputs/outputs, internal NodeGraph identity, exposed user parameters and provenance/origin metadata where applicable.
Graphs may be embedded in one project or saved as reusable presets/components. Shared-definition instances MUST have explicit semantics for edit-this-instance, detach/copy or update-shared-definition; editing one instance MUST NOT unexpectedly rewrite every use.
Registered custom node types MAY be supplied through the broader 9to1 extension system subject to capability, trust and permission rules. First- or third-party node providers MUST participate in typed graph contracts rather than injecting arbitrary UI-only behaviour.
Custom transitions
Transitions MUST support ordinary built-in transitions and reusable MotionTransitionGraph assets. A custom transition graph receives at least outgoing visual input, incoming visual input, normalised transition progress from 0 to 1, frame/time context, sequence dimensions and any declared exposed parameters.
Transition graphs can therefore implement animated masks, zoom/whip transitions, blur, displacement, glitch/RGB treatments, procedural reveals and other advanced effects. The resulting transition remains editable and reusable rather than being permanently rendered into replacement clips.
Transition duration, alignment and exposed parameters remain ordinary structured timeline state and can be animated where compatible.
Procedural animation and property drivers
MotionAnimationGraph can drive compatible properties without baking every frame into ordinary keyframes. Minimum useful node families include constants, vectors, arithmetic, clamp, map/remap range, curves, noise, oscillators, frame/time, velocity, distance, interpolation, easing, deterministic seeded random, tracking data, audio amplitude/frequency analysis and safe formula/expression nodes where supported.
Keyframes, procedural graphs, tracking and linked values MUST interoperate through one canonical parameter-source model. A property can have a base/static value, keyframed value, procedural contribution and/or tracked/linked contribution only where the combination semantics are explicitly defined. The Inspector MUST make it clear what currently drives a property.
Example: a title may follow tracked subject position, retain hand-authored keyframed movement and add a small procedural noise offset without baking thousands of frame values.
Masks, tracking and rotoscoping
Masks are native editable objects supporting compatible path geometry, feather, opacity, expansion and animation. Manual drawing/path editing SHOULD reuse shared Picture/Rnote-derived primitives where semantics match.
Motion SHOULD support point, planar, subject or object tracking according to configured backends. Tracking data is structured and may drive transforms, masks, effects, text or procedural graphs.
Model-assisted subject/object segmentation and rotoscoping MAY initialise or update masks, but users MUST be able to inspect and correct results. Frame-by-frame/manual correction remains possible. Tracking or segmentation MUST NOT silently destroy source media.
Colour pipeline
Motion MUST include first-party colour correction/grading suitable for normal production. Minimum controls include exposure, contrast, highlights/shadows, temperature/tint, saturation and curves, plus channel/colour-wheel or equivalent advanced controls where implemented.
LUT import/use, histograms/scopes and per-clip or adjustment-layer grading SHOULD be supported where the backend permits. Sequence/project colour-space state MUST explicitly represent SDR/HDR and managed-colour configuration where supported rather than relying on hidden backend defaults.
Effects, titles and graphics
Effects are structured EffectInstance objects with stable identity, provider/type identity, ordered placement, parameters, bypass state and animation references. Core families include colour, blur/sharpen, transform, keying, distortion, stylisation and utility effects. Effect stacks remain reorderable, bypassable, editable and removable.
Titles and graphics MUST remain native structured objects rather than pre-rendered video. Text/title state includes text content, font/style, paragraph/layout, fills/strokes, backgrounds, transforms, shapes/images, effects and compatible animation.
Lower thirds, callouts, captions and reusable title compositions can therefore remain editable. Complex title/graphic systems MAY use Motion node graphs while retaining the same canonical object identity.
Captions and transcript-based editing
Motion MUST support time-aligned transcription and first-class CaptionTrack/CaptionCue objects. Capabilities include transcript correction, generated captions, editable cue timing/text, split/merge, styling, multiple caption tracks/languages where supported and import/export of maintained subtitle formats such as SRT/WebVTT.
Export MUST support appropriate sidecar, embedded and burned-in caption output according to chosen container/backend capability.
Transcript-based edits such as deleting a spoken phrase or removing long pauses MUST translate into ordinary native timeline edits after preview/validation. Transcript state is a semantic editing view over the canonical timeline, not a parallel hidden authority.
Audio and Wave interoperability
Motion audio tracks/clips use compatible Wave/shared-media primitives. Motion directly exposes normal video-production audio controls such as gain/volume, pan, fades, waveform display, effects, normalisation, automation and applicable dialogue cleanup.
Where supported, Motion can invoke the shared Enhance Audio, Denoise, Custom Censorship and Split Stems capabilities defined by Wave/shared media without creating incompatible private versions.
Open/Edit in Wave MUST preserve canonical asset/clip/timing references so advanced audio work can return to Motion without a lossy export-edit-import cycle. Wave remains the full audio-production surface; Motion provides the subset appropriate to video workflows.
AI-assisted editing
Dulche operates Motion through typed Motion/shared-engine actions and NodeGraph actions, never by pretending to drag timeline or canvas UI when semantic actions exist.
Examples: 'remove long pauses' performs transcript/time analysis and native ripple edits; 'make this vertical for a short' creates or adapts an appropriate sequence and uses structured reframing/crop/tracking; 'add animated subtitles' creates caption/title objects and animation; 'make this shot warmer' changes colour parameters; 'create a 30-second highlight reel' creates a new sequence referencing selected source ranges.
AI-generated edits MUST remain inspectable, undoable/revisioned project state. AI MUST NOT render an opaque replacement video and declare the structured editing task complete when Motion can represent the requested result natively.
Generative and model-backed video workflows
Subject to installed/configured provider capability, Motion MAY provide video generation, image-to-video, generated B-roll, object/background removal, semantic segmentation, smart reframing, scene/shot detection, motion/subject tracking, video restoration/denoise, enhancement/upscaling, frame interpolation, slow-motion generation, generative fill, temporal inpainting and frame/outpainting/extension.
When a generated result can be represented as editable native Motion structure, that representation remains canonical. When the model inherently returns raster/video frames that cannot reasonably be decomposed into lower-level Motion objects, Motion may create a GeneratedVideoAsset with stable identity, model/provider provenance, generation parameters, source references and revision metadata.
Native-generation rules MUST NOT be misinterpreted as requiring generated video pixels to be decomposed into fake editable vectors. The requirement is to preserve genuine structure where it exists and preserve provenance/editability around sampled/generated media where it does not.
Media analysis and indexing
Motion MAY maintain source/revision-aware analysis metadata for cuts/scenes, transcript/speech, silence, audio peaks, motion, tracked subjects/objects, semantic tags and other useful signals supported by configured analysis backends.
Analysis results are cacheable derived metadata tied to source identity/revision. Unchanged media SHOULD NOT be repeatedly reanalysed merely because a project was reopened. Stale analysis is invalidated or refreshed explicitly when its source assumptions change.
Files, asset identity and offline media
Files remains authoritative for source/export asset storage identity, move/rename/delete/recover/share and cloud/provider hydration. Motion projects reference stable FileID/AssetID identities rather than absolute paths.
Moving or renaming an underlying File MUST NOT detach a Motion reference. Unavailable source enters an explicit offline-media state and retains timeline/project identity. Relink resolves the existing reference rather than silently creating a new unrelated element.
Generated, proxy, cache and rendered assets MUST be distinguishable from canonical source identity and carry appropriate provenance/derivation metadata.
Import, export and render queue
Motion import MUST support maintained video, image and audio formats exposed by the approved shared media backend. GStreamer/GStreamer Editing Services or an explicitly documented equivalent production-capable backend is approved for decode/encode/playback/timeline primitives. Backend-specific IDs MUST NOT leak into the canonical public Motion project contract.
Export MUST support sequence/project render, selected range, frame stills, audio-only output, caption/subtitle output and appropriate individual-clip/component exports. Options include maintained container/codec choices, resolution, frame rate, quality/bitrate, audio codec/rate/channels, hardware encoder selection or automatic acceleration and SDR/HDR/colour-space options where supported.
Motion MUST provide a render queue/background-job model with stable job identity, progress, cancellation, typed failure state and safe retry. Export/render MUST be pinned to the intended project/source revision and MUST NOT silently switch to newly edited state mid-job.
Persistent AI bar
Motion hosts the global persistent Dulche AI bar. Semantic context includes ProjectID, SequenceID, selected TrackIDs/ElementIDs/GraphIDs, selected timeline range, playhead, viewer selection, masks/effects/keyframes, transcript/caption selection, source assets, colour state, analysis state and project revision.
Write-capable AI changes Motion only through typed Motion/shared-engine/NodeGraph actions and respects normal permission, trust, revision and undo/audit contracts.

All node mutation uses the shared 9to1.NodeGraph.* contract where Node Graph Framework is canonical. Shared media, Files, Picture and other shared-domain operations SHOULD use the owning shared API namespace when that is canonical. First-party UI capabilities MUST NOT exist only as inaccessible private UI commands.
Automation and integration events
Automations, Spaces, Dulche and other authorised clients can use the exhaustive Motion action catalogue. Long proxy, analysis, tracking, generation, render and export jobs expose stable progress, cancellation, retry/idempotency where relevant and typed result/error state.
Motion emits meaningful typed events such as project/revision changed, source offline/relinked, analysis completed, proxy ready, tracking completed, render/export completed/failed and graph/generated-component changed. It MUST NOT flood Automations with raw frame, pointer or realtime preview events.
Collaboration and revision conflicts
Project/sequence/track/element/mask/effect/keyframe/graph/caption mutations are revision-aware. Independent object edits MAY merge when safe; incompatible concurrent edits to the same canonical object or property MUST surface conflict rather than blind last-write-wins.
Running proxy, tracking, generation, render and export jobs are pinned to their required source/project revisions. Their results MUST record which revision/input produced them.
Accessibility
Motion MUST be keyboard-operable for transport, timeline selection/editing, track controls, inspector properties, captions, keyframes, render jobs and graph editing. Pointer-only gestures cannot be the sole route for required editing operations.
Screen-reader users can inspect project/sequence/track/element identity, source/offline state, time positions, duration, transform/effect values, keyframes, captions, graph nodes/ports and render/job state. Visual states such as lock, disable, offline, clipping, selection and errors MUST NOT rely on colour alone.
Viewer/canvas operations that normally use direct manipulation MUST expose equivalent numeric/semantic controls.
Performance and realtime preview safety
Motion MUST decode/render frames on demand using bounded caches rather than loading entire long-form or high-resolution sources into memory. Thumbnail, waveform, proxy, analysis, tracking, generation and render work runs outside latency-sensitive interactive paths.
GPU acceleration and hardware decode/encode SHOULD be used where safe and available, with explicit capability fallback. 4K/8K and otherwise heavy media remain workable through proxies, reduced preview quality, caching and tiling according to available hardware rather than an architecture that assumes full-resolution residency.
Interactive editing MUST remain responsive while background jobs run. Preview quality MAY adapt under load, but canonical time/frame calculations and final requested render quality MUST remain deterministic and source-based.
Recovery and failure behaviour
Project saves/autosaves MUST be crash-safe and preserve canonical project integrity. A crash or termination during proxy generation, analysis, tracking, generation, render or export MUST leave the project valid and the derived job recoverable/retryable where feasible.
Partial derived output MUST NOT be reported as complete. Failures expose typed state such as ProjectNotFound, SequenceNotFound, ElementNotFound, AssetOffline, CodecUnsupported, ProxyFailed, AnalysisFailed, TrackingFailed, GraphInvalid, NodeUnavailable, GenerationFailed, RenderFailed, ExportFailed, RevisionConflict, PermissionDenied and CapabilityUnavailable plus shared backend/model errors.
Undo/redo and revision history MUST restore structured project changes without requiring source media to be rewritten.
Platform capability behaviour
Windows, 9to1-OS and web preserve the same canonical Motion project/graph/generated-component model while capability-negotiating codecs, GPU/hardware acceleration, camera/device access, model availability and performance differences.
A platform may disable an unavailable codec, hardware encoder, node provider or model-backed feature with explicit CapabilityUnavailable state, but MUST NOT silently create an incompatible project schema.
When Home is absent at process start, Motion follows the global Install Home/bootstrap contract rather than launching an incompatible private runtime.
Acceptance requirements
Motion is implementation-complete only when acceptance coverage verifies at least:
A multi-track project containing video, image, title and audio elements can be edited, closed/reopened and exported while preserving stable project/sequence/track/element identity.
Insert/overwrite, split, trim, ripple trim, roll, slip, slide, ripple delete, lift/extract, linking and nested-sequence operations produce deterministic structured timeline state and remain undoable.
Normal transforms, crop, masks, effects, colour and speed changes remain non-destructive and survive save/reopen.
Proxy editing retains canonical source identity and final export uses original source quality unless explicitly configured otherwise.
Keyframed animation persists stable property/keyframe state and the graph/curve editor reproduces the same rendered motion after reopen.
A MotionCompositionGraph can branch/composite multiple visual inputs without flattening the canonical graph; graph edits remain inspectable after restart.
A custom MotionTransitionGraph receives outgoing/incoming inputs and normalised progress, renders between clips and remains reusable/editable.
A MotionAnimationGraph can procedurally drive a property and can coexist with explicitly defined keyframe/tracking contributions without baking per-frame values.
Registered graph nodes enforce typed-port validation; an invalid connection is rejected without corrupting the graph.
Masking, chroma/luma keying, tracking and manual correction create inspectable editable state rather than rewriting source frames.
Titles/text remain editable native objects after animation/effects and do not require pre-rendering for ordinary editing.
Transcript/caption workflows create first-class timed caption state; transcript-based deletion maps to ordinary timeline edits; maintained subtitle import/export round-trips representative content.
Motion and Wave share compatible audio identity so advanced Wave editing returns to the same Motion audio reference without an unnecessary export/import duplicate.
Shared Enhance Audio, Denoise, Custom Censorship and Split Stems can be invoked from Motion where capability is available without creating an incompatible private audio model.
AI editing examples such as pause removal, vertical reframing, animated subtitles and highlight-sequence creation execute through typed Motion actions and leave inspectable native state.
Generated video that cannot be represented structurally is stored as a provenance-bearing GeneratedVideoAsset rather than misrepresented as a fully editable native composition.
Offline source media preserves timeline/project identity and relink restores the existing reference.
Render queue jobs expose progress/cancellation/failure and remain pinned to the intended project revision; interrupted derived jobs do not corrupt the project.
Large/high-resolution projects remain responsive through proxies, bounded caches, background analysis and adaptive preview rather than full-media RAM loading.
Keyboard and assistive-technology paths can perform required timeline, property, caption, graph and render-queue operations without pointer-only dependency.
Windows, 9to1-OS and web preserve the same canonical project model while capability-negotiating backend/hardware/model differences.
When Home is absent at process start, Motion follows the global Install Home/bootstrap contract.
Data Apps
Data
Product role and data paradigms
9-1 Data is the native CUI spreadsheet, structured-data, relational-database, SQL-query and analytical workspace. It combines conventional spreadsheet work, rich structured cells, relational modelling, multidimensional analytical data, charts/pivots, data transformation, database exploration and AI-assisted analysis in one coherent product.
Data MUST support four native data paradigms without forcing one paradigm onto every project: spreadsheet/grid data, relational database data, hierarchical/rich structured data and multidimensional analytical data. These paradigms may interoperate through explicit projections, relationships and transformations, but their semantics MUST NOT be silently conflated.
The ordinary spreadsheet remains the approachable default. Advanced relational, nested, multidimensional and query capabilities appear when the data or user workflow requires them. Native .9to1d projects MAY represent richer structures than XLSX/ODS; compatibility formats MUST NOT constrain the native model.
Shared engines, donor source and implementation authority
LibreOffice Calc is the spreadsheet-compatibility/donor engine for established spreadsheet behaviour, formula compatibility and XLSX/ODS interoperability. DuckDB is the local analytical SQL engine for local tables, files, queries and relational projections. Configured providers MAY add PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, SQLite, SQL Server and other supported external database systems through typed connection adapters.
The 9to1 source tree MUST contain or fetch the appropriate maintained LibreOffice Calc donor source required by the architecture, subject to the global donor-source and licensing contract. The implementation agent MUST NOT treat a missing LibreOffice installation or missing checked-out donor source as permission to build a miniature replacement spreadsheet engine. If the required donor source is absent during an autonomous development pass, the agent MUST obtain/fork the latest appropriate compatible source and record the exact upstream/version used before continuing dependent implementation.
Data MUST integrate donor capability into the 9to1 product model, CUI and typed APIs. Merely shelling out to soffice as an opaque external black box while leaving the canonical Data experience or API surface incomplete does not satisfy the implementation requirement.
Shared charting, Node Graph, Files, identity/permissions, credential storage, AI/model, action/audit and other cross-product infrastructure MUST be reused where canonical rather than privately reimplemented.
Canonical Data project model
DataProject has stable ProjectID, Workbooks[], DataSources[], Connections[], SavedQueries[], DataModels[], TransformPipelines[], DataCubes[], Visualisations[], Charts[], PivotModels[], project settings, CreatedAt, ModifiedAt and Revision.
A project MAY contain only a workbook, only database/query resources, only a multidimensional model, or any compatible combination. A user MUST NOT need to create unrelated projects merely because one analysis starts in a spreadsheet and later uses SQL or a transformation pipeline.
Data resources reference stable identities rather than UI coordinates wherever the resource has independent semantic identity. Ordinary A1/R1C1-style references remain available for spreadsheet compatibility, but tables, records, queries, charts, pivots, connections, relationships, visualisations and pipelines have stable IDs.
Workbook and spreadsheet model
Workbook has stable WorkbookID, Sheets[], workbook names/named ranges, calculation settings, external/link metadata, compatibility metadata and Revision.
Sheet has stable SheetID, ordered rows/columns/cells, tables, drawings/charts where applicable, filters, freeze state, view state and Revision. Reordering or renaming a sheet MUST NOT invalidate stable references that use SheetID.
Cells support ordinary scalar values, formulas, formatting, validation, comments/notes, hyperlinks/references and compatible Calc spreadsheet features. Grid coordinates identify a location in a sheet; they are not the sole identity mechanism for richer Data objects.
Normal spreadsheet workflows include direct cell/formula-bar editing, fill/copy, pattern autofill, insert/delete rows and columns, row/column resize/hide/freeze, multi-range selection, find/replace, sort/filter, named ranges, tables, validation/dropdowns, conditional formatting, comments/notes, sheet management, protection where compatible and undo/redo.
Rich native cells and multiple values
A native .9to1d cell MAY contain a typed value object rather than only one scalar. Supported native value families include scalar number/text/boolean/date/time/duration, formula, list/array, set/tags, record/key-value object, nested table, canonical 9to1 object reference, query-backed value, calculated structured value and other explicitly registered structured types.
Multiple values in one cell are first-class typed members, not comma-separated text. A list/set/record cell can expose member ordering, labels/keys, type validation, per-member editing, filtering/query semantics and explicit expansion into rows/columns when required.
The grid MAY display a concise collapsed summary such as '3 values' or '5 related records'; selecting or expanding the cell exposes the complete structured value without altering the underlying schema.
Formula, filter, Visualise and SQL-projection semantics for structured cells MUST be defined explicitly. Unsupported operations produce typed errors or require an explicit projection/flattening step rather than silently stringifying complex values.
Nested cells, nested tables and hierarchical data
A cell MAY own a nested table/record structure with stable nested identity and schema. Nested data is not represented as an untyped blob. Data supports drill-down, expand/collapse and focused child-table editing so hierarchical information can be represented without forcing every child structure onto a separate top-level sheet.
Data MUST distinguish nested owned data from references to separate related records. A nested child table is part of the parent value/object lifecycle; a relation/reference points to independently canonical records and MUST NOT duplicate them merely for display.
Hierarchical structures MAY nest beyond one level when the schema requires it, subject to performance and usability limits. The UI MUST avoid expanding an entire deep hierarchy by default.
Multidimensional and 3D analytical data
Data MUST support native multidimensional datasets beyond a two-dimensional row-by-column grid. A DataCube has stable CubeID, Dimensions[], Measures[], DimensionMembers/hierarchies, fact/cell storage or query definition, calculated measures, source/provenance and Revision.
A common three-dimensional example is Product × Region × Month, but the model MUST support additional dimensions such as Scenario, Currency or Channel. The UI presents manageable two-dimensional slices, pivots, comparisons and Visualise views rather than attempting to render arbitrary high-dimensional data literally.
Users can switch or compare dimension members, for example Month=January versus Month=February, without duplicating twelve nearly identical sheets. Multidimensional state remains canonical and may be queried through explicit relational projections/views.
DataCube projections to spreadsheet, SQL, pivot or Visualise views MUST preserve source identity and declare the projection rules.
Multiple views over one canonical dataset
The same canonical dataset MAY be viewed as an ordinary spreadsheet grid, structured/nested table, relational table, pivot, hierarchy/tree, multidimensional slice, SQL relation, transformation graph or Visualise view. These are views/projections of the same data where possible, not independent copied datasets.
Creating a new view MUST NOT silently duplicate source data unless the user explicitly requests a snapshot/materialised copy. Edits through a writable view update the same canonical object subject to that view's mapping and permissions.
Formula engine and calculation
Data MUST preserve Calc-compatible formula semantics wherever spreadsheet compatibility is claimed. Supported families include arithmetic, logical, text, date/time, lookup/reference, statistical, financial, array/dynamic-array behaviour where supported and error-handling functions.
Formula dependencies MUST be tracked so recalculation can be dependency-aware. Data MUST NOT blindly recalculate an entire large workbook after every unrelated edit when a narrower dependency recomputation is possible.
Formula errors remain typed and inspectable, including divide-by-zero, invalid/missing references, type mismatch, circular dependency and backend/function availability errors. Data MUST NOT collapse distinct formula failures into a generic error string.
Structured/native cell values may expose additional functions for contains/count/map/filter/member access and projection where explicitly supported; compatibility exports must detect when such formulas cannot be represented faithfully.
Tables, records and stable row identity
Structured DataTable objects are first-class rather than merely formatted ranges. A DataTable has stable TableID, schema/header metadata, Records[], filters/sorts, source/query relationship, constraints and Revision.
Database-mode rows are Records with stable RecordID. Sorting, filtering or moving a visible row MUST NOT change the record's identity. Relationships and AI/Automation references target stable record/key identity rather than 'whatever is currently on row 37'.
A SQL result may materialise into or back a query-linked DataTable. Conversely, eligible DataTables can be exposed to DuckDB as relations without exporting them first.
Relational schema and field design
Any eligible DataTable may be promoted/configured as a relational table with explicit field/schema metadata. Fields support name, data type, nullability/required state, default, validation/check rules, uniqueness, generated/computed definition, key role, references and backend-specific metadata where applicable.
Native field types include integer, decimal, currency, text, boolean, date/time, duration, enum/category, UUID/ID, reference, list/set, record/object, nested table and calculated/computed types. External database tables restrict available types and constraints to the connected backend's declared capability.
Data MUST provide a Table Design/Schema view where field definitions, keys, required state, defaults, references and constraints can be inspected and edited directly without relying on scattered context menus.
Primary keys, candidate keys and indexes
Relational tables support single-column and composite primary keys, candidate/unique keys, generated IDs and UUID-style stable keys. Primary-key changes MUST validate duplicates, missing values and dependent references before commitment.
Indexes are explicit schema metadata where the backend supports them, including primary/unique, ordinary and compound indexes. Data SHOULD explain index capability and likely purpose without automatically creating indexes everywhere.
Project-local structured tables MAY use stable RecordID independently of a user-visible relational primary key; external relational projection semantics MUST define which key is authoritative for joins and persistence.
Foreign keys and sheet/table relationships
Data supports explicit relationships between tables/sheets through foreign-key/reference objects rather than requiring VLOOKUP/XLOOKUP-style formulas to express every data relationship.
Relationship types include one-to-one, one-to-many and many-to-many through a junction/association table. A relationship has stable RelationshipID, source table/fields, target table/key, cardinality, optionality, referential action rules and Revision.
Example: Students.TutorID → Tutors.TutorID. The UI may display a friendly related value such as tutor name while storing the stable referenced key/record. Selecting such a reference can offer Open related record without duplicating the target record.
Relationship designer and ER diagrams
Data MUST provide a visual Relationship Designer showing tables/entities, key fields and typed relationship edges with cardinality/optionality. Users can create, inspect, edit and delete relationships and can generate a junction table for a many-to-many relationship.
The Relationship Designer SHOULD reuse the shared Node Graph Framework for pan/zoom/selection/grouping/connection mechanics while preserving Data-specific relationship semantics and constraints.
Data can generate an entity-relationship diagram showing entities/tables, fields, primary keys, foreign keys, cardinality, optionality and junction tables. The ER diagram is a Visualise/data-model representation, not a second independent schema.
Referential integrity and cascade behaviour
Relationships may enforce referenced-key existence, restrict deletion/update, cascade delete/update or set-null according to backend/native capability. Consequential cascade operations MUST be previewable with affected-object/record impact where knowable.
If a relationship prevents deletion, Data MUST expose which dependency blocks the operation. It MUST NOT silently disable referential integrity or orphan dependent records.
A large cascade such as deleting one parent that affects thousands of dependent records requires an explicit impact surface before execution in manual protected workflows and always in AI-originated mutation workflows.
Normalisation and denormalisation
Data MUST include a Normalise tool that analyses selected relational/tabular structures for common design problems such as repeating groups, duplicated entities, non-atomic values where a relational design is desired, partial dependencies, transitive dependencies, duplicated lookup data and missing candidate keys.
Normalisation assistance may propose transformations toward 1NF, 2NF, 3NF and, where appropriate for advanced users, BCNF. The proposal MUST show new tables, keys, relationships and record-migration effects before mutation. Data MUST explain assumptions rather than blindly applying a theoretical normal form to data that is intentionally hierarchical or multidimensional.
Data also supports explicit Flatten/Denormalise transformations for analytics/export. Normalisation and denormalisation are controlled structured transformations, not destructive reinterpretations.
Lookups and related-record navigation
A foreign-key/reference field may display a user-friendly target field while retaining the stable referenced key/record internally. Lookup display configuration MUST NOT replace the actual stored relationship.
One-to-many relationships can expose related-record counts or expandable related-record views. Such displays reference canonical records; they MUST NOT copy the children into a nested owned structure unless the user explicitly converts the relationship.
Data sources and connections
Data distinguishes static/imported data, linked files, project-local queryable data and external/live connections. Static/imported sources include declared CSV/TSV/JSON where supported and spreadsheet formats. Local query sources include DuckDB-accessible tables/files such as CSV/Parquet where supported. External/live connections use typed provider adapters.
DataSource and Connection objects have stable identity, provider/dialect, scope, capability metadata, source schema/version information where available and refresh state. Credentials/secrets MUST use the 9to1 credential/trust infrastructure and MUST NOT be embedded in .9to1d project content, query history or ordinary logs.
Connection capability negotiation defines supported transactions, snapshots/checkpoints, schema introspection, DDL/DML features, explain plans, cancellation and backup/recovery options.
SQL workspace
Data MUST provide native SQL authoring/execution with syntax highlighting, dialect-aware parsing/validation, schema/object browser, table/column/function completion, relationship-aware join suggestions, query formatting, parameters where supported, saved queries, query history, execution timing/statistics, cancellation, paged/virtualised result sets, EXPLAIN/plan access where supported and result export/materialisation.
DuckDB SHOULD make local analytical querying nearly frictionless: eligible project tables and supported local files can be queried directly without requiring users to provision an external database.
SQL results can be inspected, opened in Visualise, saved as a query, materialised to a sheet/table, exported or used as downstream transformation input.
Persistent AI / SQL bar switcher
In Data, the persistent floating input bar contains an explicit mode switcher between AI and SQL. AI mode routes natural-language requests through Dulche and typed Data actions. SQL mode treats the input as SQL and executes it natively against the explicitly selected SQL target; SQL text MUST NOT be sent to AI merely to emulate execution.
SQL mode MUST always display the active execution target, for example DuckDB · This Project or PostgreSQL · Production. The selected connection/database/schema scope MUST be visible enough that users cannot reasonably confuse a local analytical target with a live external target.
Changing the SQL execution target is explicit. Data MUST NOT silently retarget a query because another sheet, panel or connection became focused.
Native SQL execution records and results
Every execution creates a canonical SqlExecution record with stable ExecutionID, ConnectionID/target, dialect, statements, classification, ReadOnly state, initiator, start/completion state, result sets, affected objects/rows where known, recovery strategy/reference where applicable, transaction/savepoint metadata, outcome/error and audit reference.
SQL result sets preserve typed columns and support virtualised/paged browsing. Successful prior result state MUST remain available when a later execution fails unless the user explicitly replaces/discards it.
Query history records target, dialect, classification, result metadata and outcome without storing secrets. SavedQuery objects are persistent editable query resources with stable identity.
Read-only and mutating SQL classification
Data MUST parse/classify SQL before execution. Provably read-only statements such as ordinary SELECT/CTE SELECT, EXPLAIN and supported metadata introspection MAY execute directly subject to connection permissions.
Potentially mutating or schema-changing SQL includes INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE, CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE and provider-specific mutation commands. Classification MUST be conservative when the dialect/parser cannot prove a statement is read-only.
Multi-statement input is treated as one explicit execution plan with per-statement classification and declared atomicity/partial-execution risk.
Protected live-database SQL execution
Consequential SQL against an external/live database enters the protected execution path. Before execution Data MUST identify the target, classify statements, inspect likely affected objects, use a transaction/savepoint where supported, determine preview/impact information where technically possible, establish an appropriate recoverable backup/checkpoint strategy when required, show the effect/recovery state and obtain the applicable confirmation.
Recovery strategy is backend-aware and may use transaction rollback, savepoint, affected-row before-image capture, table snapshot/copy, database-native snapshot, backup file/provider recovery point, schema export plus affected data or another verified recoverable mechanism. Data MUST record the strategy actually established.
If the safety contract for the requested live mutation requires rollback/backup protection and Data cannot establish it, execution MUST stop. Data MUST NOT state or imply that a backup, transaction or rollback exists when it does not.
After execution Data verifies the actual outcome where feasible, records audit/recovery information and truthfully reports partial success/failure. It MUST NOT blindly retry consequential SQL without operation identity/idempotency or renewed confirmation where required.
DDL and dependency impact
