Terminal, Dev, Files, credentials and Home permissions remain canonical in their owning namespaces.
Automation and typed events
Mini Computer emits typed events such as VMCreated/Updated/Deleted, VMStateChanged, SnapshotCreated/Restored/Deleted, ProviderConnected/Unavailable, MediaAcquisitionStarted/Completed/Failed, MediaVerificationChanged, DeviceAttached/Detached, NetworkChanged, MetricsUpdated and provider/guest integration events.
Events use stable IDs and avoid embedding secret credentials or unbounded VM console output. Consumers request additional permitted data explicitly.
Extension system
Mini Computer participates in the shared 9to1 extension platform. Extensions may contribute VirtualisationProvider implementations, ISO catalogue/acquisition providers, guest templates/integration providers, device/network/storage adapters, inspectors and diagnostics.
Provider extensions declare host/platform compatibility, required privileges and permissions. Installing a provider UI extension does not automatically grant kernel driver, raw-disk, device or network privileges.
Provider failure is isolated where feasible and does not corrupt unrelated VM canonical metadata.
Accessibility
VM list, create wizard, settings, snapshots, networks, ISO Browser, provider status and power controls are keyboard-operable with screen-reader semantics.
VM lifecycle/provider/security state MUST NOT rely solely on colour or icons. Dangerous Power Off/Delete/Restore/Raw device actions have explicit accessible labels and consequences.
The embedded viewer provides accessible host controls around the guest even when guest OS accessibility itself is outside Mini Computer's control.
Performance and scalability
VM lists, snapshots, ISO/media libraries and monitoring views are virtualised/paged where needed. UI rendering MUST NOT require loading every virtual disk/snapshot into memory.
Provider operations such as import/export, clone, disk conversion, large download, snapshot consolidation and migration run as cancellable/resumable jobs where the provider supports it, with stable JobID/progress/error state.
Mini Computer remains responsive while one or more VMs generate heavy I/O or console output.
Recovery and failure behaviour
Mini Computer distinguishes viewer disconnect, provider service failure, VM crash, host-resource exhaustion, disk/media missing, storage corruption and configuration incompatibility rather than collapsing them into VM failed.
Reopening after UI crash/restart re-discovers provider-managed running/saved VMs by stable mapping and reattaches without duplication where the provider can prove identity.
Structured failures include VMNotFound, ProviderUnavailable, ProviderCapabilityUnavailable, HardwareVirtualisationUnavailable, AccelerationUnavailable, InvalidVMState, DiskNotFound, DiskDependencyBlocked, MediaNotFound, MediaIntegrityFailed, MediaAcquisitionNotPermitted, SnapshotDependencyBlocked, SnapshotRestoreConflict, NetworkConflict, DeviceUnavailable, HostResourceRisk, CredentialUnavailable, ImportUnsupported, ExportFailed, ViewerDisconnected, GuestIntegrationUnavailable, RevisionConflict, PermissionDenied and CapabilityUnavailable plus provider-specific diagnostic codes.
Partial provider/storage operations return succeeded/failed/remaining resources and recovery steps; Mini Computer MUST NOT report rollback/cleanup success unless verified.
Platform capability behaviour
Windows, 9to1-OS and other supported desktop hosts preserve the same canonical VM/provider/media model while capability-negotiating the built-in VirtualBox fork, hardware acceleration, host networking, device passthrough and filesystem/storage behaviour.
Web surfaces may manage/view remote Mini Computer providers/VMs when an authorised remote execution provider exists but MUST NOT pretend the browser itself can provide unrestricted local hardware virtualisation.
Unsupported architecture/provider combinations are explicit release/platform exceptions rather than silent missing UI.
When Home is absent at process start, Mini Computer follows the global Install Home/bootstrap contract.
Acceptance requirements
Mini Computer is implementation-complete only when acceptance coverage verifies at least:
The maintained 9to1 VirtualBox fork is available as the built-in/default provider and a new supported VM can be created without connecting another hypervisor.
The VirtualBox donor-parity audit records preserved/expanded/replaced/not-applicable mature VM capabilities and separately licensed proprietary components are not silently bundled.
A user can connect at least one alternative provider implementation through the VirtualisationProvider contract and provider capability differences are surfaced accurately.
A VM retains stable VMID across rename/reopen and provider-internal identity is mapped rather than becoming the only identity.
A supported guest can be created, install media attached, started, installed, shut down, reopened and run again without configuration loss.
Start, Pause, Resume, Save State, graceful Shutdown and Power Off have distinct verified lifecycle semantics.
Closing/disconnecting the viewer leaves a headless-running VM running according to policy and reopening Mini Computer reconnects rather than creating a duplicate.
Snapshot creation/restoration preserves the provider-declared disk/memory state and clearly excludes state the provider cannot capture.
Deleting/consolidating snapshots cannot silently break a dependent linked clone.
Full clone and provider-supported linked clone create distinct VM identities and preserve base dependencies correctly.
Representative virtual-disk create/attach/resize/convert/delete operations preserve dependencies and require appropriate verification for destructive changes.
BIOS/UEFI and supported Secure Boot/TPM configurations are represented accurately for a representative modern guest.
NAT, bridged/host-only/private and representative port-forward configuration work on a capable provider and network dependencies block unsafe deletion.
Clipboard, drag/drop and shared folders enforce configured direction/read-write policy rather than enabling broad host access automatically.
Physical device passthrough exposes the host-impact warning/permission and does not silently detach devices from the host.
Provider/host Virtualisation Status distinguishes disabled hardware acceleration, provider unavailable and feature unsupported states with actionable diagnostics.
The ISO Browser lists only registered/curated publisher providers rather than arbitrary unverified Internet downloads.
An OfficialDirect ISO acquisition downloads from the publisher-authorised source without CAKE rehosting it and records acquisition provenance.
A MirrorPermitted catalogue entry can be mirrored only when its configured redistribution policy explicitly permits the exact image; otherwise mirroring is blocked.
A downloaded ISO with authoritative checksum/signature metadata is verified before being labelled Verified and a mismatch blocks normal trusted acquisition flow.
UserSupplied and ProviderFlow catalogue policies work without falsely claiming CAKE supplies the operating system image.
The same immutable ISO can be referenced by multiple VMs without unnecessary duplicate canonical copies and removal identifies active mounts/dependencies.
Unattended installation keeps passwords/product keys out of ordinary logs, project source and AI context.
OVF/OVA or representative mature donor import/export previews hardware/network differences and preserves the declared source/revision scope.
Mini Computer Files resources remain addressable while large mutable block data can use an appropriate provider without being misrepresented as ordinary sync documents.
Terminal opens a VM-specific EnvironmentID/serial or guest shell and clearly distinguishes VM from host command execution.
Dev OS Run uses Mini Computer's canonical engine to build/package → attach boot artifact → boot VM → expose viewer/serial/debug state rather than launching a separate hidden hypervisor.
An ephemeral Dev VM can be discarded/preserved according to run policy without mutating the base template.
AI VM actions route through typed Mini Computer/provider APIs and dangerous disk/snapshot/device/network operations receive the applicable impact verification.
Import/export/download/clone/snapshot consolidation jobs report real progress/cancellation/recovery state without fabricating completion.
Keyboard/screen-reader workflows cover VM creation, ISO Browser, VM state controls, settings, snapshots and provider status.
Windows, 9to1-OS and supported remote/web management preserve the same canonical Mini Computer model while capability-negotiating local execution.
When Home is absent at process start, Mini Computer follows the global Install Home/bootstrap contract.
Utilities
Browse
9to1 Browse is a full Firefox-derived browser product with native CUI chrome and native CUI internal surfaces. Firefox/Gecko is the primary donor, default web engine and behavioural baseline. Chromium/Blink is a first-class secondary browser/rendering backend available per tab. Browse MUST remain one coherent browser with one canonical 9to1-owned tab/session model; Chromium support MUST NOT be implemented as a second browser bolted onto Firefox or as a separate user profile universe.
Donor authority and parity
Firefox donor parity is the minimum supported capability set, not the finished feature ceiling. Unless a feature is explicitly replaced, excluded or made incompatible by an approved 9to1 architecture decision, Browse MUST retain mature Firefox functionality and quality-of-life behaviour.
Tabs and windows, including restore/reopen behaviour, pinned tabs and normal navigation history.
Profiles, bookmarks, history, downloads, browsing-data controls, site permissions, privacy/security controls and appropriate password/passkey integration.
Firefox developer tooling, reader/media functionality, picture-in-picture where donor-supported, accessibility, keyboard navigation, crash/session recovery and mature settings/configuration.
WebExtension compatibility to the maximum extent supported by the retained Firefox APIs, with unsupported or engine-specific APIs surfaced explicitly rather than silently ignored.
All Firefox proprietary or embedded AI surfaces are non-authoritative and MUST be removed or replaced by Dulche-backed 9to1 surfaces. The agent MUST NOT preserve a Firefox AI sidebar, chatbot, assistant or proprietary AI integration merely for donor parity.
Web engine architecture
Each web BrowserTab selects a WebEngine value of Firefox/Gecko or Chromium/Blink. The normal user-facing choice SHOULD be labelled Firefox and Chromium; implementation and diagnostics MAY additionally expose the underlying Gecko and Blink engine names. Gecko is the default unless the user or a persisted site rule selects Chromium.
Changing a tab between Firefox and Chromium changes the renderer/backend used for the page, not the canonical identity of the tab, workspace or Browse session. Switching engines reloads/reconstructs the document through the selected backend. Engine-private runtime state such as DOM objects, JavaScript heaps and renderer-process memory is not required to transfer.
Browse MUST own canonical higher-level browser entities instead of allowing Gecko and Chromium to directly share raw profile databases. At minimum the architecture must model BrowserProfile, BrowserTab, NavigationEntry, Bookmark, HistoryEntry, Download, SitePermission, Workspace, TabGroup, SplitView, SearchProvider, SiteEnhancer and EnginePreference as typed 9to1-owned entities or equivalent strongly typed contracts.
Gecko and Chromium MUST be isolated internally. They MUST NOT be pointed at the same physical cookie/profile/session database. Engine adapters translate the relevant canonical Browse state into each backend and propagate supported changes back to Browse.
Users MUST be able to use Firefox for this tab, Chromium for this tab, always Firefox for a site/domain, always Chromium for a site/domain, and reset a persisted site engine preference. A broken page SHOULD be switchable to the other engine with one obvious action without opening a separate browser product.
Automatic upstream maintenance
The Firefox/Gecko and Chromium/Blink frameworks MUST be maintained continuously against the latest appropriate upstream release and MUST automatically detect and ingest newer upstream versions when available. A long-lived stale engine is a maintenance defect.
Automatic update does not mean blindly shipping an unvalidated upstream binary. The update pipeline MUST fetch/rebase or reapply maintained 9to1 changes, build the affected engine integration, run Browse compatibility and regression suites, verify CUI integration, engine switching, extension baselines, session/profile isolation, Site Enhancer behaviour, DevTools integration and Dulche browser capabilities, and promote the new engine only after the applicable acceptance gates pass. Security-sensitive upstream releases receive expedited priority. The previous known-good engine build MUST remain rollback-capable until promotion is proven stable.
CUI and URI namespace contract
Browse has four distinct first-class content namespaces. They MUST remain architecturally and security-distinct even when multiple namespaces ultimately render through CUI.
cui:// — generic CUI-rendered surfaces and extension-defined/custom CUI pages. This is the general CUI namespace and is not synonymous with Browse internals.
browse:// — Browse-owned internal pages such as browse://newtab, browse://settings, browse://downloads, browse://history, browse://extensions and other Browse-owned management surfaces.
9to1:// — native 9to1 application surfaces hosted inside a Browse tab, for example 9to1://Spaces, 9to1://Write or a typed deep link such as 9to1://Write/<resource>. These are the actual application surfaces, not web versions or reduced browser copies.
https:// and http:// — ordinary web content. User-facing normal web navigation uses these web schemes; Browse-owned, CUI and native-app content MUST NOT masquerade as an HTTP(S) origin.
Internal compatibility plumbing inherited from donors MAY exist only where technically unavoidable, but it MUST NOT be exposed as a competing public routing model. The 9to1 routing contract above is authoritative.
Native 9to1 app surfaces in tabs
Opening 9to1://<App> MUST instantiate the real CUI application surface and the real application services inside the Browse tab. It MUST NOT load a separately implemented web edition, feature-reduced embedded edition or imitation of the app. Responsive layout adaptation is allowed and expected; capability divergence merely because the app is hosted in Browse is not.
9to1:// routes MUST be registered centrally by the application/router registry and support typed deep links to canonical resources where the owning app supports them. A tab title and icon should reflect the actual resource/app instead of exposing an opaque route string as its primary label.
The same canonical app data/state MUST be addressed regardless of whether the app is opened in its normal standalone surface or through 9to1:// in Browse. Opening the same Write document, Board, Space or Data workbook in multiple valid surfaces MUST NOT silently create disconnected copies.
9to1 native app tabs participate in normal Browse capabilities including tab groups, pinning, workspaces, restore/reopen and Split View. A user can therefore place 9to1://Write with a research document beside an https:// research page, or combine two different native 9to1 apps, without requiring a separate web version of either app.
Profiles and workspaces
Browser profiles are tab-scoped, not window-scoped. Every BrowserTab carries a ProfileID or equivalent profile context, allowing one window, one workspace and one Split View to contain tabs from different profiles simultaneously.
A BrowserProfile is an identity/storage/privacy boundary. Depending on supported configuration, it owns or scopes cookies, login sessions, site storage, site permissions, browsing-data attribution, extensions and extension state, search preferences, Site Enhancers, credentials/passkeys and other profile-specific browser configuration.
A Workspace is an organisational/session construct rather than an identity boundary. A workspace may contain tabs from multiple profiles and owns organisational state such as open tabs, groups, split arrangements, workspace pins and layout. Switching workspace MUST NOT inherently sign the user into or out of websites.
Profile identity MUST be visually discoverable on tabs and in relevant browser UI so the user can tell which account/session context will be used. Consequential actions and Dulche-controlled actions SHOULD make the active profile context clear where confusion could cause the action to occur under the wrong identity.
Changing a tab to another profile MUST reopen/recreate its web session under the destination profile rather than copying authentication material across profile boundaries. Safe navigation/organisation metadata such as URL, group, workspace and split position may be preserved where applicable.
Tabs, groups and placement
Browse MUST provide modern tab management in addition to Firefox donor parity. Tab groups are first-class canonical entities with stable identity, naming, optional colour/icon metadata, collapse/expand state, persistence, restore, drag/drop and movement between windows/workspaces. Dulche and other typed APIs can address a group directly.
Tab-strip placement MUST be a first-class configurable preference with full feature parity in all four orientations:
Horizontal tabs at the top.
Horizontal tabs at the bottom.
Vertical tabs on the left.
Vertical tabs on the right.
The interface MUST adapt properly to each orientation rather than mechanically moving a top strip. Groups, pinned tabs, profile indicators, drag/reorder, tab search, previews, context menus, engine state where surfaced, close/reopen, Dulche mentions and split operations MUST remain functional in every orientation. Compact/collapsed and appropriate auto-expand behaviours may be provided as configurable presentation options.
Split View
Split View displays two independent BrowserTab entities side-by-side in one browser content area with a resizable divider. The split container owns presentation only; each pane remains a real tab with its own URL/route, navigation history, profile, renderer/backend where applicable and canonical tab identity.
A split may mix any compatible tab surface classes, including web + web, 9to1 app + web, 9to1 app + 9to1 app, Browse internal + web and tabs from different BrowserProfiles. Either pane can be swapped, unsplit or moved without destroying the underlying tab.
The two-pane experience is the required baseline. The architecture SHOULD avoid assumptions that make future multi-pane layouts impossible, but more than two panes is not required unless separately specified.
New Tab canvas
browse://newtab is a fully customisable CUI-native canvas rather than a fixed shortcut grid. Users can add, remove, move, resize and configure components. Layout persists according to the active profile and may support workspace-specific overrides where configured.
The canvas can host deterministic widgets, browser widgets, 9to1 app widgets, extension-provided CUI widgets, static content and Generative Areas. It SHOULD reuse shared 9to1 canvas/layout infrastructure where practical instead of creating an incompatible bespoke layout system.
A Generative Area is a persistent container defined by a natural-language instruction, for example 'put some YouTube videos here for me to watch' or 'show my upcoming deadlines'. It stores the instruction/configuration, not merely one frozen model answer. It may refresh manually, on New Tab open or on an allowed schedule and may expose source restrictions, maximum item count, presentation style and network/Dulche permissions.
Generative Areas MUST resolve real canonical entities when the requested content refers to tabs, Files, events, 9to1 objects or other structured data. They MUST NOT fabricate canonical objects merely to fill a container. Generated/recommended content SHOULD remain distinguishable from deterministic widget output.
Search and AI entry
The primary New Tab/address search entry MUST expose two explicit modes: Search and AI. Search is the default. The active mode is clearly visible and switchable quickly, including by keyboard.
Search mode performs normal navigation/search behaviour and MUST NOT invoke an LLM merely to execute an ordinary URL or provider query. AI mode sends the request to Dulche and can use permissioned Browse capabilities and referenced browser/app context.
Browse MUST support a typed SearchProvider contract and allow the user to configure a default provider plus an optional secondary provider. Providers may supply query construction, suggestions and declared privacy/capability metadata. Extension-defined providers may participate through the same contract.
Browse MUST support searching two providers at once. Dual-provider search creates one real tab per provider for the same query and places those tabs into the standard Split View, one provider per pane. This MUST reuse normal BrowserTab and SplitView infrastructure rather than a bespoke dual-search renderer. Single-provider search remains the normal default unless the user configures otherwise.
Dulche browser experience
Dulche is the only authoritative AI system in Browse. Firefox-provided proprietary AI surfaces MUST be removed/replaced. Browse SHOULD provide both a persistent Dulche sidebar for larger tasks and a lightweight floating/command bar for contextual requests, using the shared Dulche runtime rather than launching a browser-specific model server.
The Dulche UI MUST support @-mentioning canonical browser context. At minimum users can mention tabs and SHOULD be able to mention tab groups, workspaces, split panes and other supported Browse entities. Mention autocomplete resolves to stable canonical IDs rather than copying only titles/URLs into the prompt.
Examples include comparing @Durham with @York, summarising all tabs in @Coursework, or asking Dulche to use a referenced 9to1://Write document together with an https:// research tab. Where the referenced surface is a native 9to1 app, Dulche MUST use that app's semantic APIs rather than screen-scraping its CUI.
Permissioned autonomous browsing
With explicit user permission, Dulche can autonomously operate Browse for a task. A request such as 'scroll through YouTube and pick out some good videos' may inspect visible/accessible results, scroll, open candidates, compare them and return recommendations without requiring confirmation for every benign intermediate interaction.
Permission scope MUST be explicit and composable. The implementation must support equivalents of read this page, control this tab, control these selected tabs and control Browse for this task. Granting one scope MUST NOT silently grant permanent global browser control.
Browser automation SHOULD use structured semantic capabilities such as Navigate, OpenTab, CloseTab, ActivateTab, ReadPage, ReadElement, Find, Scroll, Click, FillField, SelectOption, GoBack, GoForward and Reload when structured control exists. Blind coordinate input is a fallback, not the primary architecture.
Consequential external actions remain governed by the shared 9to1 permission/confirmation policy. Purchases, publishing/sending, destructive account changes, security changes, credential disclosure/entry and comparable external side effects MUST NOT become implicitly authorised merely because Dulche was permitted to browse.
Extensions and CUI extension surfaces
Firefox/WebExtension compatibility MUST be retained to the maximum practical extent. Because a tab may use Firefox/Gecko or Chromium/Blink, extension capability MUST be explicit. An extension may be Gecko-compatible, Chromium-compatible through supported adapters, compatible with both, Browse/CUI-only, partially compatible or unsupported in the active engine.
Switching one tab to Chromium MUST NOT silently uninstall an extension, disable it globally or make it disappear. Engine-specific limitations MUST be surfaced predictably.
Extensions can register supported CUI surfaces using cui:// routing and the extension CUI API, including settings pages, dashboards, sidebars, tool panels, New Tab components or other permitted custom pages. CUI rendering permission does not imply unrestricted Browse or 9to1 internal access; capabilities remain sandboxed and permission-scoped.
Site Enhancer
Browse MUST provide a first-class Site Enhancer feature inspired by mature site-customisation systems such as Arc Boosts while remaining a 9to1-native capability. A SiteEnhancer is a versioned, enable/disable-able canonical object associated with one or more domain/site match patterns.
Site Enhancers can define supported visual customisation such as colours, typography, spacing/layout adjustments, element visibility, backgrounds and custom CSS, plus controlled client-side behaviour/scripts where explicitly supported. They must declare permissions/capabilities and execute within a defined safety boundary.
Dulche can help create or modify a Site Enhancer from natural language, for example 'make YouTube less cluttered and hide Shorts'. Dulche MUST present the proposed effect/permissions at the appropriate confirmation boundary rather than silently installing arbitrary persistent scripts. Extensions may provide Site Enhancers through the same permissioned model.
Files, drag/drop and cross-app integration
Browse retains a mature Download entity/lifecycle while completed files integrate with the shared Files system so reveal/open/share/drag workflows use canonical 9to1 file semantics. Interrupted downloads, retries and completion state remain visible and recoverable.
Split panes and tabs SHOULD support semantic drag/drop. Where both surfaces understand a canonical 9to1 entity, transfer the typed entity/link instead of degrading it to copied text. Examples include dragging a Maps place into Planner or a Board item into Write. Web upload targets may receive files through normal browser security/permission rules.
Sites can open project previews in Browse and Browse development context can offer Open project in Sites/Open source in Dev when the page is linked to a local project. Dev can launch localhost/development targets directly into Browse. Mature Firefox developer tools MUST be retained/adapted rather than replaced by a feature-poor custom inspector.
Security and origin isolation
cui://, browse:// and 9to1:// are privileged/non-web namespaces with separate routing and origin/capability rules. Ordinary HTTP(S) pages MUST NOT be able to inspect native app state, call privileged CUI/Browse APIs, forge trusted 9to1:// content or inherit internal permissions simply by navigating to or linking an internal route.
A web page may request navigation to an allowed registered internal route only through the normal navigation/policy boundary. Navigating to 9to1:// does not grant the originating site the destination app's authority. Profile cookies/credentials and engine-private state MUST remain isolated according to their owning profile/backend.
Recovery and degraded states
Browse MUST handle Firefox renderer crashes, Chromium renderer crashes, whole-browser crashes, failed engine startup, unavailable selected engines, extension incompatibility, interrupted downloads, invalid/corrupt engine-private state and failed engine switches without corrupting the other engine or canonical Browse profile state.
Session recovery SHOULD restore tabs, groups, workspaces, split arrangements, ProfileID and per-tab engine preference wherever safe. If a preferred engine is unavailable, Browse MUST surface the degraded state and offer a safe fallback rather than silently losing the tab or rewriting profile data.
Browse acceptance requirements
Firefox donor parity remains present except for explicit 9to1 replacements/exclusions; proprietary Firefox AI surfaces are replaced by Dulche.
Gecko-default and Chromium alternative rendering work within one canonical Browse tab/session model, with engine/profile isolation and per-site engine rules.
Both upstream engine frameworks can update automatically through validated build/test/promotion and rollback pipelines.
cui://, browse://, 9to1:// and HTTP(S) routes resolve to the correct security/content surface, including real native 9to1 app rendering inside tabs.
Profiles can be mixed per tab, per workspace and inside Split View without cross-profile cookie/session leakage.
Tab groups, split tabs and top/bottom/left/right tab-strip placement retain equivalent core functionality.
browse://newtab provides the customisable widget/generative canvas, Search/AI switch and dual-provider split search.
Dulche @ mentions resolve to canonical browser/app entities and permissioned autonomous browsing uses semantic browser capabilities with consequential-action safeguards.
Extension compatibility states, extension CUI surfaces and Site Enhancer permissions behave explicitly and recoverably.
Crash/session recovery preserves canonical Browse state and a failure in one renderer does not corrupt the other renderer/profile state.
Maps
9to1 Maps is the canonical geospatial, place, landmark, routing and navigation service for the 9to1 ecosystem as well as a full user-facing CUI application. Other apps MUST consume Maps entities, APIs and embeddable CUI surfaces rather than independently inventing incompatible place, route or location models.
Primary donor and default provider stack
The primary mature donor is the latest appropriate CoMaps source. The maintained 9to1 Maps fork/adaptation MUST preserve applicable CoMaps mapping, offline-map, POI, favourites, tracks, navigation and route-planning functionality and mature quality-of-life behaviour unless this specification explicitly replaces it. CUI replaces/adapts the donor user interface without reducing the mature capability baseline.
9to1 Maps MUST separate the donor application from provider services behind typed interfaces. The default open stack is:
OpenStreetMap data as the principal open geographic dataset.
MapLibre Native as the default provider-facing/vector-map rendering framework where appropriate.
The retained CoMaps-derived offline map/rendering/search/routing pipeline for mature downloadable/offline operation where it provides capability not equivalently supplied by the online stack.
Pelias as the default self-hostable online geocoding, reverse-geocoding and place-search service.
Valhalla as the default self-hostable routing/navigation service for supported travel modes.
GTFS/GTFS-Realtime-compatible transit data through a typed transit provider; an OpenTripPlanner-compatible implementation may be used where appropriate.
Traffic, satellite, terrain, street-level imagery and specialist datasets as optional provider capabilities rather than hard-coded assumptions.
The implementation MUST NOT make public OpenStreetMap community tile or public Nominatim endpoints an unlimited production dependency. Provider-specific usage, caching, attribution, redistribution and offline-storage rules MUST be enforced. 9to1-hosted/self-hosted services and user-connected providers can be substituted through the same typed provider contracts.
One provider does not need to supply every capability. Rendering, map data, geocoding, search, routing, transit, traffic, imagery and offline datasets MUST be independently replaceable where technically possible. Provider identity, provenance, freshness and required attribution MUST remain available to Maps.
Canonical geospatial entities
Maps MUST define stable canonical entities rather than allowing each app to store copied address strings. At minimum, the typed model must cover Place, Address, Coordinate, Route, RouteLeg, RouteStep, SavedPlace, PersonalLandmark, CommunityPOI, MapView, SearchResult, SearchProvider, MapProviderReference and SavedRoute/CustomJourney or equivalent strongly typed contracts.
A Place may reference one or more provider records, OpenStreetMap objects, community objects or user-authored data without making any single provider identifier the canonical 9to1 identity. Provider records are provenance references, not the primary identity of a saved 9to1 entity.
Planner, Events, Spaces, Boards, Write, Present, Forms, Automations and other apps MUST reference canonical Place/Route/Landmark IDs through typed APIs where a persistent location relationship is required.
Search / AI interaction
Maps MUST use the same explicit Search / AI interaction pattern established elsewhere in 9to1. Search is the default mode. The selected mode is always visible and can be switched immediately without losing the selected place, route or current map context.
Search mode performs deterministic geographic discovery and manual route construction. It must search, as applicable, addresses, postcodes, coordinates, named places, businesses/POIs, categories, saved places, PersonalLandmarks, CommunityPOIs and supported 9to1 entities with attached locations. Provider result confidence and ambiguity MUST remain visible; Maps MUST NOT fabricate an exact address or place identity from weak geocoding.
Selecting a result opens a canonical place/details surface with provenance and relevant actions such as View, Navigate, Add to route, Set as start, Set as destination, Add stop, Save, Share and other capability-appropriate actions.
AI mode is a Dulche-backed natural-language Maps interface operating the same canonical Maps state and APIs. Requests such as 'take me to the nearest Starbucks', 'find somewhere quiet to study within a 15-minute walk', 'find a bench along this route' or 'add a coffee stop halfway home' MUST be resolved through real search/location/routing capabilities rather than invented model knowledge.
A request such as 'take me to the nearest Starbucks' should resolve the permitted current location, search real place providers, rank valid candidates according to the user's request and actual route/travel distance where available, resolve the chosen candidate to a canonical Place, calculate a route and start/present navigation according to the explicit user intent. If multiple interpretations materially affect the result, Maps must present candidates or request the minimum necessary disambiguation rather than guessing.
Search and AI are interoperable. A place found manually can become AI context, and an AI-generated route/place remains a normal canonical Maps object that the user can inspect, edit, reorder, save or share manually.
Saved places and personal landmarks
Users can save ordinary provider/OpenStreetMap places and create PersonalLandmarks anywhere on the map. A PersonalLandmark does not require an existing mapped place, recognised address, road, POI or provider object; a coordinate and user-defined identity are sufficient.
Users MUST be able to drop a pin at any coordinate, name it, optionally categorise it, add notes/metadata, save it privately, share it explicitly and navigate to it. Examples include a meeting point, favourite viewpoint, shortcut entrance, personal picnic spot or a specific bench.
Common saved places such as Home, College, Church or Work are canonical SavedPlace references. Other apps resolve these references through Maps rather than retaining independent copies of the underlying address.
Personal/private landmarks are private by default. Creating a private landmark MUST NOT implicitly publish its coordinates, name, notes or category to the community database or an external provider.
Community POIs and landmark presets
Maps MUST provide a first-class community POI system so users can contribute useful hyperlocal geographic data over time. Users can choose a structured preset when dropping a pin, including extensible categories such as Bench, Bin, Recycling point, Picnic table, Picnic area, Public toilet, Drinking-water point, Bicycle parking, Bicycle repair/pump, EV charger, Bus stop, Crossing, Defibrillator, Viewpoint, Playground, Entrance, Accessible entrance, Steps, Lift, Ramp and Shelter.
Presets represent typed POI categories, not merely icons. A category can expose optional structured attributes appropriate to that object. For example, a Bench may record backrest, armrests, cover, capacity, material, accessibility or condition; a Bin may record waste/recycling type and condition. The common contribution path MUST remain fast: a user can submit a useful POI with minimal required fields and enrich it later.
Users choose explicitly between keeping a landmark private and submitting it publicly. Public submission creates or proposes a CommunityPOI in the 9to1 community geographic database; it is not the same action as contributing to OpenStreetMap.
CommunityPOI records must retain stable identity, coordinate, category, structured attributes, source/provenance, creation/update metadata, verification state, edit history, confidence/quality information and reports/flags as applicable.
The community system MUST support a quality lifecycle such as Submitted/Unverified, Community-confirmed and Verified, together with corrections such as Removed, Wrong location, Wrong category, Duplicate and Details changed. A user can confirm that an existing object is still present without recreating it.
Before creating a public POI, Maps SHOULD perform deterministic nearby duplicate detection using distance, category compatibility and known identifiers. If a likely duplicate exists, the user can confirm/update the existing object or explicitly state that the new object is distinct.
Community POIs are first-class searchable/routable destinations. Users can search for categories such as benches, bins or picnic tables, enable category layers and ask Dulche structured queries such as 'find a walking route with benches along the way'.
Where a community contribution maps cleanly to OpenStreetMap semantics, Maps MAY separately offer an explicit 'Contribute to OpenStreetMap' flow subject to OSM account, licensing, validation and editing rules. Public submission to the 9to1 community database MUST NOT silently publish to OpenStreetMap or another third party.
Routing and route planning
Maps MUST support route planning for driving, walking, cycling and public transport where the active providers/data support those modes, with typed extension points for additional modes. Routes contain structured legs/steps, provider provenance, travel-mode information, timing/freshness where applicable and sufficient geometry for rendering/navigation.
A route can be referenced, embedded, shared and manipulated by other 9to1 apps. A route is not reduced to copied text directions. Alternative routes and provider uncertainty/freshness remain available where supported.
Normal route building in Search mode MUST allow selecting an origin/destination, adding intermediate places, reordering/removing stops and editing route preferences without invoking AI.
Saved custom routes / Custom Journeys
Users MUST be able to build, name, save, edit, duplicate, share and later start reusable custom routes/journeys. A custom route can describe both where the user travels and what the user intends to do along the way; it is richer than a simple list of waypoints.
A SavedRoute/CustomJourney must support ordered typed steps such as TravelStep, StopStep, WaitStep, ActivityStep and ManualInstructionStep or equivalent. Examples include walk to a coordinate, sit on a named bench, wait ten minutes, grab coffee from a selected place, use a shortcut, take a particular entrance, then continue to college.
Each step may include a canonical Place/Landmark/Coordinate reference, transport mode, optional timing or stop duration, notes, routing preferences and required/preferred/optional semantics. These semantics allow dynamic rerouting to adapt ordinary travel segments without silently removing user-authored intent.
Users may create user-defined path segments that are not present in provider routing graphs, for example a campus cut-through, alley, informal footpath or other personally known shortcut. Such segments MUST be visibly marked as user-defined/unverified by provider routing data and MUST NOT be presented as provider-validated infrastructure.
AI mode can create and edit SavedRoutes from natural language, for example: 'Create my Walk to College route: walk to the bench by the river, sit there for ten minutes, grab coffee from Z, take the shortcut behind the library, then turn right to college.' Dulche resolves real referenced entities where possible and must present ambiguity rather than hallucinating a landmark.
During active navigation, non-travel steps such as 'sit on Riverside Bench for 5 minutes' or 'grab coffee' are valid current journey steps. The route can continue after the user marks/completes/skips the step according to the journey model.
Saved custom routes can be shared with other users where permissions allow, preserving route geometry, user-defined instructions, typed stops and shared/community landmark references. Private landmark details must not be leaked merely because a route is shared; sharing semantics must explicitly handle private dependencies.
Navigation to arbitrary/custom destinations
Any canonical Place, PersonalLandmark, CommunityPOI or raw permitted coordinate can be a navigation destination even when no street address exists. Routing SHOULD bring the user to the closest supported route-graph point and then represent the actual final coordinate honestly rather than inventing a road/entrance.
Custom/community destinations must participate in navigation, route sharing, Planner/Event references and Dulche requests just like provider-defined places, while retaining provenance and verification status.
Live information and dynamic routing
Where providers support it, Maps can expose live traffic, incidents, road closures, transit departures/delays and dynamic journey times. Live-looking information MUST retain provider provenance and freshness timestamps/state. Stale data MUST NOT be represented as current.
Saved/custom journeys may be dynamically rerouted around disruptions while preserving required user-authored stops/instructions where feasible. If a required custom/user-defined segment cannot be validated or becomes impractical, Maps must surface the conflict rather than silently deleting that instruction.
Location permissions and privacy
Location data is sensitive. Maps/Home permissions MUST distinguish at least resolving a known PlaceID, searching places, approximate current location, precise current location and background location. Location history, if implemented, requires a separately explicit capability/retention model.
An app does not automatically receive the user's live location merely because it can call Maps APIs. Dulche natural-language requests are subject to the same location permissions; 'near me' and routing requests cannot bypass precise-location controls.
Search history, route history, precise locations, Home/Work-style places, saved routes and private landmarks require user-visible retention/clear controls. Sensitive location history MUST NOT automatically become globally indexed Go content or extension-readable data.
Offline operation
Maps MUST retain mature CoMaps-derived offline capability and support downloadable regions where data/provider licences permit. Offline mode should support map rendering and, where the retained/local datasets allow it, place search/geocoding and routing without requiring a live cloud service.
Downloaded region management must show storage usage, version/freshness and update state. Licence/provider rules govern whether particular imagery/tiles/datasets may be cached or redistributed; unsupported offline caching MUST fail explicitly rather than silently violating provider terms.
CUI embeds and cross-app composition
Maps is both a full app and a CUI surface provider. It MUST expose reusable typed CUI components such as PlaceCard, MapView/MiniMap, LocationPicker, RouteCard and Journey/Navigation surfaces so other 9to1 apps can embed real Maps functionality without cloning it.
Planner/Events can attach canonical Places/Routes; Boards and Spaces can embed interactive Place/Map cards; Write/Present can insert linked map/place/route objects; Forms can use the canonical LocationPicker; Automations can reference place/location conditions subject to permissions.
Maps MUST be available as the real native surface through 9to1://Maps and support typed deep links to canonical place/route/journey objects. It therefore participates naturally in Browse tabs and Split View, for example Maps beside Planner or Write beside a route.
Dulche integration
Dulche accesses Maps through typed semantic capabilities, not map-pixel scraping. Capabilities can include SearchPlaces, ResolvePlace, GetCurrentLocation, BuildRoute, ModifyRoute, SearchCommunityPOIs, CreateLandmark, CreateSavedRoute, AddRouteStep and StartNavigation subject to the appropriate permission/action policy.
Natural-language context such as 'near me', 'near college', 'between here and home', 'along this route', 'around that place' or 'the restaurant I just looked at' must resolve against real permitted Maps state: current location, SavedPlaces, selected Places, active route/journey and recent canonical Maps entities.
Automations and extensions
Maps may expose automation triggers such as arrive at place, leave place, enter/exit radius, material route-duration change or transit disruption where platform/background capabilities and permissions support them. Persistent/background location requires explicit OS/Home permission and MUST NOT be inferred from ordinary foreground Maps access.
Extensions may add providers, overlays, POI categories, route modes, map layers or specialist geospatial tools through typed capability contracts. Providing a layer/provider does not automatically grant precise location, private landmark access or route history.
Safety, provenance and disclaimer
Maps MUST present map and calculated route data as guidance rather than guaranteed ground truth. A displayed road, path, crossing, entrance, restriction, building, POI or route MUST NOT be represented as guaranteed to exist, be accessible, be legal to use or be safe merely because it appears in provider/community data.
The following compact user-facing disclaimer is required in Maps and MUST be available during route/navigation use: 'Map data is sourced by third party providers and community volunteers. Check important routes.'
A fuller safety/data notice may additionally explain that provider/community data can be incomplete, inaccurate or outdated and that users should follow real-world signs, restrictions and conditions. The compact notice does not replace the product's separately reviewed legal terms.
Community/unverified objects must expose verification/provenance state where relevant and MUST NOT be styled in a way that falsely implies the same confidence as independently established/provider-verified data.
Maps acceptance requirements
The latest appropriate CoMaps donor baseline is retained/adapted with CUI without losing mature offline/navigation behaviour except where explicitly replaced.
Open provider interfaces support the agreed default OSM/MapLibre/Pelias/Valhalla stack and allow independent replacement of rendering, search/geocoding, routing, transit, traffic and imagery capabilities.
Place, Route, SavedPlace, PersonalLandmark, CommunityPOI and SavedRoute/CustomJourney have stable canonical identities usable across 9to1 apps.
Search mode supports deterministic place discovery/manual route building; AI mode uses Dulche against the same canonical Maps state and typed capabilities.
Users can drop a pin anywhere, create a private custom landmark, navigate to it, choose structured POI presets and explicitly submit community POIs.
Community POI duplicate detection, provenance, verification/update lifecycle, reports and routable/searchable behaviour are implemented without silently publishing to OpenStreetMap.
Saved custom routes support typed travel/stop/wait/activity/manual steps, required/preferred/optional intent, user-defined shortcut/path segments, AI creation/editing and safe sharing.
Location permissions distinguish approximate/precise/background access and prevent unrelated apps/extensions from inheriting sensitive location data.
Offline maps remain usable where licences/data permit and do not rely on prohibited bulk use of public community endpoints.
9to1://Maps and reusable Maps CUI surfaces integrate with Planner, Events, Boards, Spaces, Write/Present, Forms, Automations, Browse and Dulche.
The required route/data disclaimer and provenance/freshness states are present; Maps never represents provider/community route data as guaranteed real-world truth.
Launcher
9to1 Launcher is the Android/9to1-OS home launcher. It is a maintained fork/adaptation of the latest appropriate Lawnchair source and is a distinct product from Shelf. Launcher MUST NOT be implemented as the cross-platform 9to1 package installer/updater or as the Shelf quick-access library.
Lawnchair donor authority
Lawnchair is the primary donor and mature behavioural baseline for Launcher. Applicable donor functionality and quality-of-life behaviour MUST be retained unless this specification explicitly replaces it. The goal is not merely donor parity: 9to1 Launcher is intended to be substantially more customisable than conventional Android launchers, including mature highly-customisable launchers such as Nova Launcher, while remaining coherent, performant and accessible.
Core launcher surfaces
Launcher owns the Android-style home screen, home pages, app drawer, dock, folders, widgets, app shortcuts, gestures, app discovery and visual organisation of installed applications. It consumes the authoritative installed-application/package registry owned by Home/platform package infrastructure; it does not maintain a competing package database.
Multiple configurable home pages with drag/reorder and persistent layout.
App drawer with configurable organisation, sorting, categories, visibility rules and search.
Configurable dock, including size, rows/columns where supported, presentation and behaviour.
Folders with configurable appearance, layout, ordering and appropriate actions.
Pinned/favourite apps, hidden apps and application shortcuts/actions.
Compatible Android widgets plus 9to1-native CUI widgets through a shared widget abstraction.
Backup/restore of launcher layout and settings, with account/device sync where enabled and compatible.
Full accessibility, keyboard/navigation support and appropriate touch/controller interaction.
Extreme customisation
Launcher MUST expose unusually deep customisation while preserving usable defaults. The architecture must avoid hard-coding one visual layout so additional options can be added without rewriting core launcher state.
Grid dimensions, independent horizontal/vertical spacing, margins, page padding and icon placement behaviour.
Icon size, icon shape/masking, per-app icon overrides, icon packs, labels, label typography and label visibility.
Dock geometry, drawer geometry, folder geometry and home-page-specific layout configuration where supported.
Backgrounds, transparency, blur, theme/accent integration and supported animation/transition behaviour.
Gesture mapping including swipe, double-tap, pinch and other supported gestures, with actions resolved through typed commands rather than hard-coded donor-only behaviour.
Per-page, per-folder and per-component presentation options where doing so remains understandable and performant.
Import/export of launcher configuration and recoverable handling of unsupported/missing configuration after platform or donor updates.
Launcher should offer strong defaults and discoverable presets so extreme customisation does not require every user to configure dozens of controls before the launcher is usable.
Applications and stable identity
Launcher placement MUST reference stable InstalledApplication/Application IDs from the authoritative platform registry rather than raw executable/package paths. Updating an app must not destroy its home-screen placement, folder membership or configured icon unless the application's canonical identity actually changes.
Launcher can represent Android apps, 9to1-native apps and other platform-recognised application targets exposed through the OS compatibility/application registry. Package install, uninstall, update, repair, rollback and channel management remain Home/platform responsibilities. Launcher may surface status/actions such as 'update available' but delegates execution to the authoritative package service.
Widgets
9to1-native apps and extensions can register typed CUI launcher widgets with declared supported sizes, configuration surfaces, update behaviour, data permissions and actions. Compatible Android App Widgets remain supported where the Android platform layer permits them. Launcher MUST present both through a coherent placement/resizing model without pretending they share identical runtime/security semantics.
Dulche integration
Dulche is a first-class Launcher capability rather than an add-on. With user permission it can inspect and modify semantic launcher layout/configuration through typed APIs instead of simulating touch gestures.
Example requests include 'make a page for college', 'put all my games into folders', 'move Maps into the dock', 'make this page denser', 'add my upcoming events widget' or 'make a Development page with Dev, Stack and Terminal'. Dulche MUST operate on canonical launcher entities and honour the same profile, permission and package boundaries as manual actions.
Search and Go integration
Launcher can expose search/application discovery, but universal retrieval/navigation/action logic belongs to Go, which is specified under OS. Launcher search SHOULD consume Go providers/results where appropriate and render them in Launcher context rather than implementing an incompatible second system-wide index.
Profiles and OS boundaries
Launcher MUST respect Android/OS user, work-profile and application-profile boundaries. Profile-specific apps/widgets/shortcuts must retain their owning profile identity and should be visually distinguishable where confusion could cause the user to act under the wrong account or authority.
Launcher acceptance requirements
The latest appropriate Lawnchair donor is forked/adapted and mature donor launcher behaviour is retained unless explicitly replaced.
Launcher is the Android/9to1-OS home launcher only; Shelf remains a separate quick-access product and Home/platform services own package management.
Home pages, app drawer, dock, folders, widgets, gestures, shortcuts, hidden apps, backup/restore and accessibility are production-capable.
Customisation materially exceeds the donor/default Android baseline and supports deep grid, icon, folder, dock, page, theme, animation and gesture configuration without destabilising canonical launcher state.
Dulche can safely manipulate launcher layout through typed semantic APIs.
Application placement survives normal app updates because layout references canonical application identity rather than copied package/executable metadata.
Shelf
Shelf is the cross-platform quick-access library for things the user wants to launch or open frequently. It is a separate product from the Android Launcher. Shelf can organise applications, games, 9to1 surfaces, projects, files, folders, websites and other supported shortcuts into reusable user-defined collections.
Core model
Shelf MUST model launch targets as stable typed LaunchItem entities rather than a grid of copied shortcuts. A LaunchItem can represent, where supported and permitted:
Installed desktop/native applications.
9to1 applications and 9to1:// routes/deep links.
Games detected from supported game/application sources or added manually.
Android applications where the hosting platform supports them.
Executable/application targets with supported arguments and working-directory configuration.
Files and folders.
Web URLs and registered URI schemes.
Dev/Stack projects or other 9to1 canonical resources with a launch/open action.
Explicit user-created shortcuts and other extension-defined launch targets.
Each LaunchItem can retain a stable ID, name, icon/artwork, target type, canonical target/reference, optional launch parameters, tags, collection membership, launch behaviour and supported contextual actions. Shelf MUST preserve the underlying target identity instead of duplicating the actual app/game/file.
Collections and organisation
Collections are first-class many-to-many organisational entities, not filesystem-style one-parent folders. The same LaunchItem may appear in multiple collections without duplication. Examples include Offline Games, FNAF Games, 9to1 Apps, Development, Blender & Unreal, Coursework or any user-created grouping.
Shelf MUST support manual collections, favourites/pins, ordering, tags and smart/dynamic collections where reliable typed criteria exist. Dynamic collections may automatically surface targets such as detected Unreal projects or installed games matching declared offline-capability metadata without converting those results into duplicate LaunchItems.
Collections should support configurable presentation such as list/grid/card density, artwork/icon treatment and ordering while keeping the same canonical contents underneath.
Discovery and target import
Shelf can discover supported locally installed applications, platform-recognised games, 9to1 applications and registered projects through typed providers. Discovery MUST be permission-aware and reversible; detected items do not have to be added to the user's curated Shelf unless the user chooses or a configured smart collection references them.
Users can always add a supported target manually when automatic discovery is unavailable. Missing/uninstalled targets SHOULD remain recoverable as unavailable entries when preserving them is useful, rather than silently deleting the user's organisation.
Search / AI
Shelf uses the shared Search / AI interaction pattern. Search mode performs deterministic lookup across LaunchItems, collections, tags and supported metadata. AI mode uses Dulche to interpret natural-language library requests and operate Shelf's typed APIs.
Examples include 'add all my FNAF games to a FNAF collection', 'find all Unreal projects and put them in Development', 'show games I can play offline', 'where is that game I installed last month?', or 'open everything I use for Refuelled'. Dulche MUST resolve real discovered/canonical targets and MUST NOT invent installed applications or projects.
Launching and actions
Opening an item delegates to the owning platform/application service using the target's canonical semantics. 9to1-native targets use their registered 9to1:// identity/deep-link contracts where applicable. Files/folders use Files/platform open semantics; web targets use Browse/default-browser semantics; applications/games use the appropriate registered launcher/provider.
Shelf may expose typed contextual actions such as Open, Open with, Reveal in Files, Open project, Launch with arguments, Pin, Add/remove collection, Edit metadata or provider-specific actions where the underlying target supports them. Consequential or command-like launch actions remain subject to normal 9to1 permission/risk policy.
Cross-device and missing-target behaviour
Shelf organisation is user state and should be serialisable/synchronisable where enabled. A synced collection may contain a target unavailable on another device. That device MUST represent the item as unavailable/not installed or resolve an appropriate equivalent only through explicit canonical mapping; it must not silently substitute an unrelated app.
Extensions
Extensions may register LaunchItem providers, target types, discovery providers, metadata enrichers, actions and smart-collection predicates subject to permissions. Providing Shelf integration does not grant unrestricted filesystem enumeration, package inventory or private project access.
Shelf acceptance requirements
Shelf remains a distinct cross-platform quick-access product and is never conflated with the Lawnchair-derived Android Launcher.
Apps, games, 9to1 routes, projects, files, folders, URLs and supported shortcuts can be represented as typed stable LaunchItems.
Collections support many-to-many membership so an item can belong to multiple groups without duplication.
Manual and supported smart collections, search, favourites, tags, custom ordering and unavailable-target recovery work consistently.
Dulche can organise, discover and launch real Shelf targets through typed APIs without hallucinating installed content.
Launching delegates to the target's authoritative owner/platform service and respects normal permission/security boundaries.
Frameworks
Dulche
Framework role
Dulche is 9-1’s shared llama.cpp-derived local model framework/runtime. One Home-managed Dulche instance serves every 9-1 app through a broker API; apps must never launch their own competing local model servers. It owns model loading, inference lifecycle, resource limits, cancellation and local capability discovery while preserving upstream provenance.
Voice
Voice is a Dulche capability. Dulche owns the audio-session runtime, speech/model lifecycle, streaming, interruption and integration with requests, tools, permissions and logs. The user-facing controls live in Vision & Voice rather than Home.
Voice API
Dulche.Voice();
Entry point to the Dulche Voice subsystem for the caller’s current context.
Dulche.Voice.StartSession(sessionID?);
Dulche.Voice.StopSession(sessionID);
Dulche.Voice.PauseSession(sessionID);
Dulche.Voice.ResumeSession(sessionID);
Dulche.Voice.Interrupt(sessionID);
Dulche.Voice.SetInputDevice(deviceID, sessionID);
Dulche.Voice.SetOutputDevice(deviceID, sessionID);
Dulche.Voice.SetVoice(voice, sessionID);
Dulche.Voice.SetModel(model, sessionID);
Dulche.Voice.SendAudio(audio, sessionID);
Dulche.Voice.GetState(sessionID);
The documented Voice APIs are authoritative but not exhaustive. Additional APIs required for complete voice functionality may be added following Dulche’s existing API conventions and the global API-parity rule.
Translate
Translate is a first-class Dulche framework capability for multilingual translation, localisation and cross-language interpretation. It is not owned by a standalone Translate app. The primary user-facing product is the built-in Translate Space, while Write, Mail, Boards, Browse, Vision & Voice, AI Overlay, Sites and other authorised surfaces may invoke Dulche Translate directly for contextual translation.
Dulche Translate owns language/locale resolution, translation execution, multi-target Translation Sets, variant identity, glossary/protected-term application, segment alignment, structured-artifact translation contracts, translation job lifecycle, provenance and translation-specific recovery. It MUST use the shared model/provider layer and normal Home/Dulche permission and audit contracts.
Translation Sets and variants
A translation request MAY target one or many languages/locales in a single operation. The canonical result is a TranslationSet with stable TranslationSetID, source reference/revision where applicable, source language/locale, request/instruction metadata, glossary references, model policy, created/modified timestamps and one or more TranslationVariants.
Every TranslationVariant MUST have stable TranslationVariantID, TranslationSetID, target language/locale, status, translated content or canonical output reference, revision, provenance, errors/warnings and segment map where available. Retrying, regenerating, manually editing, applying or publishing one language MUST NOT discard successful sibling variants.
Language identity MUST use canonical language/locale identifiers. When a user supplies an ambiguous or unsupported language label, Dulche Translate MUST request/return a structured resolution requirement rather than silently guessing another language.
Conversational Translate Space rendering
The built-in Translate Space renders translation work as normal conversation rather than a two-box translator. The selected target-language chips sit immediately above the standard Space chatbar; all source/context selection uses the normal Spaces context architecture.
When one conversational request returns multiple TranslationVariants, each language variant MUST appear as its own assistant speech bubble. The language/locale name is displayed directly above that bubble. The bubbles are linked as siblings by the same TranslationSetID/request but remain independently addressable for retry, regenerate, edit, apply, export or agentic follow-up.
A prompt may temporarily target a subset/additional language without necessarily changing the Space's persistent language chips. Explicit requests to add/remove/change the default language set update the Translate Space configuration.
Conversational refinement and agentic actions
Translate MUST support natural follow-up refinement such as 'make the German version less formal', 'keep Action Graph untranslated everywhere', 'add Japanese', 'only redo French', or 'update these because the source changed'. Refinements target the canonical TranslationSet/variant rather than creating unrelated copies unless the user requests a separate result.
Translate Space MAY perform multi-step agentic localisation workflows using normal Space Plugins, Skills, persistent Dulche Agents, Automations and typed app actions. For example, 'translate this page into French, Spanish, German and Italian, then push them to the live site' may resolve the current page semantically, create/update four TranslationVariants, validate each owning artifact/site route and invoke the authorised Sites/WordPress/publishing APIs.
Dulche Translate MUST NOT implement generic hidden publishing or file mutation that bypasses owning apps. Applying translations to Write/Present/Data/Boards/Sites/WordPress/GitHub or other systems uses those systems' canonical typed actions, revision checks, permissions, approvals, audit and idempotency contracts. Partial downstream failure MUST preserve already-successful translations/actions and expose targeted retry.
Structured artifacts and semantic preservation
Dulche Translate MUST translate human-language content while preserving supported non-linguistic structure and identity. For 9to1-native artifacts it should operate through the owning app/shared Productivity Engine using stable object identities rather than flattening the artifact into plain text.
Write translation preserves document structure/styles/tables/images/links/comments and other supported metadata while translating intended text. Present translation preserves slides/layout/theme/text boxes/speaker notes/animations/transitions and detects translated-text overflow instead of silently clipping. Data translation distinguishes human labels/descriptions/comments from formulas, numbers, cell references and identifiers. Boards translation preserves page/block identity and supported embedded artifact references.
Code, commands, URLs, formulas, JSON keys, identifiers, markup/code fences and other structured technical content MUST follow explicit structure-aware rules and MUST NOT be casually translated as prose. The user may explicitly request translation of translatable string literals/comments where the owning format supports safe editing.
Whole-artifact translation SHOULD create a translated derivative/locale variant by default rather than destructively overwrite the source. Explicit in-place commands such as Replace selection with translation use the owning app's normal undo/revision semantics.
Segments, provenance and incremental updates
Where the source supports stable segmentation, Dulche Translate SHOULD preserve segment identity/alignment between source and each target variant. Segment maps enable side-by-side review, targeted retry, terminology correction and incremental updates.
Translated derivatives MUST retain provenance sufficient to identify source artifact/file/entity, source revision, source/target language, TranslationSetID/VariantID, glossary IDs, model policy and translation time. When the source changes, Translate MUST be able to report that a translation is stale.
Where safe segment identity exists, updating a stale translation SHOULD retranslate only changed/affected source segments while preserving unaffected translated content and user edits. Conflicts between manual target edits and changed source content MUST be surfaced rather than silently overwritten.
Glossaries and protected terminology
Dulche Translate MUST support reusable and request-scoped glossaries. Glossary entries MAY define source term, required/preferred target translation by locale, Do Not Translate, notes/context and applicability scope.
Protected terminology MUST support names, trademarks, product names, case names, technical identifiers, commands and other content that should remain unchanged. Glossary/protected-term application MUST be recorded in translation provenance so unexpected terminology can be diagnosed.
Text, image, document and media translation
Dulche Translate MUST support direct text and semantic selection translation. Image/screenshot translation MAY return extracted translated text and, where the selected model/tooling supports it, a translated visual derivative with mapped text regions. Semantic text from a 9to1 surface is preferred over OCR/pixels when available.
PDF handling MUST distinguish text, scanned and mixed PDFs where detectable. Structured text PDFs should preserve layout/structure as far as supported; scanned/mixed PDFs may require vision/OCR-style extraction. Any layout fidelity loss or uncertain extraction MUST be surfaced before export/apply.
Audio translation may produce translated text and, where supported, translated speech. Video translation MAY produce translated transcript/subtitles and advanced dubbed output where supported. Live realtime interpretation is exposed through Vision & Voice → Live Translate while reusing Dulche Translate language/context/glossary functionality.
Model routing and privacy
Dulche Translate uses the shared Universal Model Picker/model-routing system. Ordinary translation requests SHOULD resolve the highest-quality compatible configured route for the requested languages, modality, context size, latency, privacy/locality, entitlement/cost and tool requirements without forcing the user to manually choose a model.
An explicit local-only/private policy MUST NOT silently fall back to cloud translation. Unknown language-pair/provider capability is represented as unavailable/unknown rather than fabricated support.
Translation jobs and recovery
Long or multi-artifact translation MUST use durable TranslationJob state with stable TranslationJobID and statuses such as Preparing, Translating, ReviewAvailable, Applying/Exporting, Completed, Paused, Failed and Cancelled as applicable. Progress MUST derive from real segments/pages/slides/files/variants rather than invented percentages.
Partial failure MUST preserve successful completed segments/variants. A failed page/language/action can be retried independently. Pause/resume/retry MUST not repeat already-completed consequential downstream actions without idempotency/operation identity.
Canonical Dulche Translate API
Dulche.Translate.DetectLanguage(input, options?);
Dulche.Translate.Text(input, targetLanguages, options?);
Dulche.Translate.CreateSet(source, targetLanguages, options?);

Dulche.Translate.AddLanguages(translationSetID, targetLanguages);
Dulche.Translate.RemoveLanguage(translationSetID, targetLanguage);
Dulche.Translate.RefineVariant(translationVariantID, instruction);
Dulche.Translate.RegenerateVariant(translationVariantID, options?);
Dulche.Translate.TranslateArtifact(sourceRef, targetLanguages, options?);
Dulche.Translate.TranslateImage(source, targetLanguages, options?);
Dulche.Translate.TranslateAudio(source, targetLanguages, options?);
Dulche.Translate.CreateJob(config);
Dulche.Translate.GetJob(translationJobID);
Dulche.Translate.PauseJob(translationJobID);
