An ordinary natural-language request, an @App mention or failure of a typed app API MUST NOT silently activate Computer Use.
The Computer Use capability may control eligible graphical applications through supported pointer, keyboard, accessibility/automation and visual-interaction primitives. It SHOULD use the fastest reliable state channel available, including accessibility/automation metadata where appropriate, avoid unnecessary human-speed delays, batch safe independent interactions where supported and verify state transitions instead of relying on fixed sleeps. Speed MUST NOT weaken verification or permission gates.
By default, the first attempted interaction with each target application in a Computer Use run requires user approval for that AppID/process identity, and changes to application or operating-system settings require approval before mutation. Home settings MUST allow the user to change this policy to automatic approval for eligible apps and to an Approve All eligible-apps policy. Persisted approval policy remains scoped by user/profile, app identity and the normal Home trust/permission model.
Auto-approve and Approve All MUST NOT bypass hard exclusions, administrator policy, OS security boundaries or other non-overridable safeguards. Computer Use receives no more filesystem, network, credential, settings or app authority than the invoking user/request already possesses.
Generic Computer Use MUST NOT attach to, send input to, automate or manipulate game executables or anti-cheat-protected game surfaces, including games launched or managed through platforms such as Steam or Epic Games Launcher. When classification is uncertain and anti-cheat/game automation risk is plausible, the target is ineligible by default. This exclusion exists independently of user trust level because generic automation can create account/anti-cheat risk.
The game exclusion does not prohibit Dulche Agents from participating in games deliberately configured through the 9to1 Play framework. Play interaction MUST occur through Play's typed GameDefinition/Match/contestant actions and capability isolation, not by using generic Computer Use to drive an external game client.
Every Computer Use run MUST produce an inspectable action stream with target app/window identity, action type, timestamps, relevant pre/post state evidence, approvals, failures and side effects. Sensitive screen regions, credentials and typed secrets MUST follow the normal redaction and permission rules; logs MUST NOT become a second plaintext credential store.
Dulche Autoreview MUST inspect proposed and recent Computer Use actions continuously. It MUST flag patterns including repeated identical or near-identical actions without progress, repeated failing commands, oscillation between states, privilege escalation, bulk/destructive deletion, destructive shell commands such as rm -rf or platform equivalents, security-setting changes, suspicious executable/download flows and other high-risk sequences. High-confidence imminent destructive risk MUST be able to pause the next action for review rather than merely add a passive warning.
Autoreview findings are structured ProblemEvents and MUST feed the shared Problem handling contract. A Computer Use recovery intervention MUST preserve the current request, state and logs and SHOULD redirect to a safer or more direct interaction strategy. It MUST NOT hide that a risky action was proposed or attempted.
Thinking logs, work state and ETA
Thinking-log presentation is a first-class Dulche feature backed by Runtime events. Home MUST expose one global user preference with the modes Precise, Concise, Detailed and Ramble; compatible apps inherit it unless an explicitly supported per-surface override exists. If no preference has been set, Precise is the default.
Precise shows only thinking/work events that materially advance the task, such as a resolved decision, discovered blocker, completed verification step or changed plan. It MUST suppress repetitive self-talk and events that do not change task state.
Concise renders short activity summaries suitable for rapid scanning, for example 'Moving a square', 'Opening Browse', 'Checking the build' or 'Waiting for approval'. These summaries MAY be generated from richer telemetry but MUST remain faithful to the underlying action/state.
Detailed exposes substantially more model/provider-permitted reasoning trace and task rationale, including intermediate decisions and why a strategy changed when that information is actually available and permitted. It MUST still distinguish observed facts, tool results, summaries and model reasoning.
Ramble exposes the maximum provider/model-permitted thinking/work trace available to Dulche, including abandoned approaches, self-corrections and changes of mind when the provider actually supplies those events. Ramble MUST NOT reconstruct, infer or falsely label undisclosed private chain-of-thought as if it had been exposed by the model/provider.
Thinking mode changes presentation only. It MUST NOT change the model's configured reasoning effort, tool permissions, stored audit truth, Action Graph or provider privacy rules. Provider-unavailable thinking remains Na/Unavailable under the existing Result contract.
While active, permitted thinking/work events render inline in chronological position with the conversation rather than in a separate hidden console. The visual treatment MUST be lower-emphasis/ghost-like relative to user/model message text while still meeting accessibility contrast requirements and MUST use non-colour cues so users can distinguish message content from thinking/work content.
When the active thinking/work phase ends, the inline region collapses under a disclosure labelled 'Thought for <duration>' when no tool/action execution occurred, or 'Worked for <duration>' when one or more tools/actions were executed. Duration uses the Runtime's active execution span for that phase rather than queue time. Expanding the disclosure restores the permitted events according to the selected display mode.
After 60 seconds of continuous active execution in one foreground 9to1 turn, Dulche MUST request an ETA from the active orchestrating model through a canonical ETA request. The model returns an estimated completion timestamp plus optional confidence/reason. The UI displays the timestamp in the user's locale/time zone and clearly marks it as an estimate, not a guarantee. Paused/AwaitingUser time does not count as continuous active execution.
Dulche MUST expose an operation equivalent to Dulche.RequestETA(requestID). An ETA response includes RequestID, AttemptID, EstimatedCompletionAt, GeneratedAt and optional Confidence/Reason. If the active model cannot provide a meaningful estimate, the result is explicitly unavailable; Dulche MUST NOT invent a timestamp. Material replanning MAY request an updated ETA and MUST replace rather than stack stale estimates in the primary UI.
Problem detection, autoreview and recovery
Problem handling is a first-class Dulche Runtime capability for detecting, surfacing and recovering from common model/agent failure modes without forcing every app to implement its own ad-hoc watchdog.
The canonical ProblemType set MUST support at least Looping, NoProgress/Stuck, Repetition, HallucinationOrFabrication, OverAgreement/Sycophancy, InstructionDrift, ContradictionWithGroundedState, RepeatedToolFailure, UnsafeActionPattern and Other/UserReported. Additional typed categories MAY be added versionably without collapsing distinct existing meanings.
Loop detection MUST consider semantic and action-level repetition, not only identical text. Examples include repeatedly issuing the same failing command, alternately undoing/reapplying the same mutation, reopening the same surface without new evidence, recreating completed work or repeatedly restating the same answer while the task remains unfinished.
Hallucination/fabrication detection SHOULD use available grounded evidence such as tool results, canonical app state, source provenance, stable object IDs and completion evidence. Dulche MUST flag fabricated claims of completed actions, nonexistent files/entities/tool results or unsupported factual assertions when confidence is sufficient; it MUST NOT treat disagreement with an unverified model statement as proof that the user is wrong.
OverAgreement/Sycophancy detection SHOULD flag responses that materially adopt or endorse a user's factual premise, conclusion or requested assessment without adequate evidence when the task calls for grounded evaluation. Recovery prompts the model to re-evaluate the evidence and user request; it MUST NOT mechanically disagree with the user merely to appear independent.
When automatic detection reaches its configured intervention threshold, Dulche creates a ProblemEvent and injects a clearly identified Runtime recovery directive at the next safe boundary. The directive tells the model what failure pattern was detected, relevant evidence and the required correction, such as stop repeating the command, reassess grounded state, use a different strategy or verify the claimed result. Runtime recovery directives MUST NOT be forged as user-authored messages.
If the detected problem is associated with a proposed consequential or dangerous tool/Computer Use action, Dulche MAY pause dispatch before the action and require re-planning or applicable approval. Lower-risk reasoning-quality problems SHOULD normally correct the active request without cancelling the turn or discarding valid completed work.
Every conversational 9to1 AI surface MUST expose a small Problem pill above/adjacent to the compose bar. The user can invoke it even when automatic detection did not fire, select a ProblemType and optionally add a note. Manual reports enter the same ProblemEvent/recovery pipeline and are delivered to the active request at a safe boundary without implicitly stopping the request.
ProblemEvents MUST record stable ProblemEventID, RequestID/AttemptID, category, detector source (automatic, autoreview or user), timestamp, safe evidence references, confidence when machine-detected, intervention taken, affected action/node and resolution outcome. They MUST appear in FullLog/Action Graph with sensitive content redacted as required.
Problem detection MUST itself be bounded and loop-safe. A false-positive recovery that does not improve state MUST NOT trigger an endless reviewer/model ping-pong. Repeated unresolved problems should escalate to a visible blocker, alternate model/strategy where permitted, or user decision while preserving completed work.
Dulche Den
Purpose
Dulche Den is Dulche's persistent, cross-harness storage standard. It allows Dulche state to remain available across compatible apps and harnesses rather than being tied to one running endpoint or one application session.
Model catalogue
A user's Den can maintain their model catalogue using stable model IDs alongside user-facing names. IDs provide unambiguous model references; names are intended for human-facing use and may be duplicated, which is why name lookup returns a list rather than assuming a single match.
Cross-app state
Den is also intended to provide persistent storage for cross-app context, agents and related Dulche state so compatible 9to1 surfaces can share the same underlying information instead of maintaining isolated copies.
Storage structure and portability
Den is a directory-based persistent store with a versioned den.json manifest, structured records, a transaction journal and separately stored or referenced large objects. Portable records use UTF-8 JSON; local databases and indexes may accelerate access but must not be the only readable copy or create an incompatible private format. Exports contain authorised records and explicitly selected attachments. Reference model weights and external Files documents by identity/content hash rather than copying them by default. No special bundle extension is mandated.
The manifest identifies DenID, FormatVersion, SchemaVersion, minimum reader/writer versions, namespaces, storage locations and required capabilities. Validate manifests, paths, sizes and hashes before import. Importing never executes code or automatically enables agents, tools, connections or permissions.
Identity, namespaces and model records
Every model, agent, conversation, context object, workflow and request has a stable ID independent of name/path. Separate personal, team, organisation and app namespaces; device paths and hardware settings stay device-local. Shared namespaces are opt-in.
Model records contain logical ID, display name, aliases, provider/source, immutable revision/artifact hash, family, format, quantisation, modalities/capabilities, context/output limits, ordered reasoning levels, configuration overrides, installation references, timestamps, provenance and replacement history. Parameters, active MoE parameters, storage and hardware metrics use Runtime's availability rules. Local paths are not portable identities.
ID lookup is unambiguous in its namespace. Name/property lookup returns all matches, never silently chooses a duplicate. Aliases are explicit namespace-scoped references. Model replacement may retain logical ID/name but records changed artifact/provider identity, retained/reset settings and rollback history.
Sessions, context and checkpoints
Den persists messages/revisions, authorised context, agent definitions, requests/results, tool records, approvals and checkpoints as distinct record types. Runtime executes work; Den stores information needed to inspect or resume it.
Portability covers supported messages, context, configuration, definitions and history, not arbitrary backend caches, GPU state or undisclosed internal model state. Checkpoints declare backend/model compatibility. Distinguish a continuation attempt from exact resumption and never automatically repeat completed external actions.
Context records identify source, owning app, timestamps, author/inference provenance, access scope and retention. Distinguish user-authored, imported and inferred context. Sharing a conversation does not automatically share its referenced sources, secrets, attachments or private inferences.
Persistent Memory
Persistent Memory is a core Dulche Den subsystem for durable cross-session information about the user, recurring entities, preferences, decisions, projects and other scoped context that Dulche should be able to retrieve in future conversations or authorised surfaces. It is separate from Background Learning.
Memory is not one opaque prompt file. A persistent MemoryEntry should carry stable identity, content or structured value, subject/entity, memory type/category, scope, source/provenance, confidence where applicable, created/updated state, supersession/correction relationships, retention state and user-edited/locked state where supported.
Scopes
Memory can be scoped so unrelated Agents/apps do not receive unnecessary context. Supported scopes should include global/user memory plus narrower project, Agent, app/surface or other explicit contexts where appropriate. Retrieval MUST respect both scope and permission.
Creation and retrieval
Dulche may create or update memories from eligible conversations/context according to the user's Memory Frequency and memory policy. Retrieval is relevance-based: only memories useful to the active request/context should be injected, rather than the complete memory store.
Explicit user corrections supersede contradictory earlier memories. Den MUST retain enough provenance/revision information to distinguish an explicit user statement from an inference and to avoid repeatedly resurfacing a memory that has been corrected, superseded or deleted.
Memory Frequency
Settings MUST expose a Memory Frequency preference with exactly four user-facing levels: Never, Sometimes, Often and Always. The selected level controls how readily Dulche autonomously creates, reinforces or updates Persistent Memory from eligible non-temporary interactions.
Never: Dulche MUST NOT autonomously create, reinforce or update Persistent Memory from ordinary interactions. Direct user-invoked memory-management actions are separate explicit operations.
Sometimes: use a conservative threshold and retain only clearly durable, repeatedly useful or high-value information.
Often: use a lower threshold and remember useful preferences, decisions, entities and ongoing context more readily when they are likely to help future responses.
Always: evaluate every eligible interaction for durable memory and normally retain information that satisfies the memory policy, while still deduplicating noise, respecting scope/retention rules and avoiding ineligible information.
Changing Memory Frequency affects future autonomous memory behaviour; it MUST NOT silently delete existing memories. The setting is independent of Background Learning.
Temporary chats in Spaces
Spaces can provide Temporary Chats. Persistent Memory creation is disabled inside a Temporary Chat regardless of the user's Memory Frequency. While a chat is temporary, Dulche MUST NOT autonomously create, update, reinforce, merge or promote Persistent Memory from that conversation.
Any explicit action that would save new Persistent Memory from a Temporary Chat must be unavailable or clearly report that memory creation is disabled for temporary chats. Temporary-chat memory-write suppression MUST NOT be bypassed by an Agent, plugin, Skill, tool or Background Learning pipeline.
This rule governs memory creation/writes. Whether existing authorised memories are retrieved into a temporary chat is a separate context/privacy policy and MUST NOT be inferred from the memory-write prohibition.
Management and lifecycle
Users must be able to inspect, search, edit/correct, supersede and delete persistent memories through the appropriate settings/Den surfaces. Deletion and retention use Den's normal lifecycle, sync and purge contracts. Memory export/import must preserve scopes, provenance and deletion/supersession semantics rather than flattening entries into plain prose.
Persistent Memory acceptance requirements
Persistent Memory exists as a distinct Den record system and is not substituted by Background Learning, session context or Agent-only memory.
Memory retrieval is relevance-, scope- and permission-aware.
Never/Sometimes/Often/Always control autonomous memory creation/reinforcement with the semantics above.
Temporary Chats in Spaces cannot create, update or reinforce Persistent Memory regardless of frequency or calling surface.
Corrections/supersession are durable and user-manageable, and explicit user statements remain distinguishable from inference.
Permissions and secrets
Authorise access per principal, namespace and object/action. Reading context, modifying an agent, executing tools and administering Den are separate permissions enforced below the UI. Revocation applies to future reads/searches/executions; it does not erase copies already disclosed.
Store credential references, not plaintext API keys, passwords, private keys or tokens in records, exports or logs. Resolve references through secure credential storage on the relevant device/service. Protect sensitive storage and transport, document key ownership/recovery and redact sensitive log payloads without falsifying whether an action occurred.
Concurrent writes and recovery
Use atomic transactions or crash-safe journalled updates. Mutable objects have revisions; updates supply expected revisions and return Conflict instead of overwriting newer data. Support concurrent readers and coordinated writes with bounded locking. Operation IDs make safely retryable writes idempotent.
Validate before commit, preserve the previous valid record until commit and recover/quarantine incomplete writes after crashes. Export consistent snapshots. Caches and indexes are rebuildable, not the sole authority.
Synchronisation and conflicts
Cross-device/team sync is optional and namespace-scoped. Track IDs, revisions, origin device and deletion tombstones. Offline changes wait for an authorised sync target. Merge compatible disjoint edits; preserve conflicting versions for review. Wall-clock timestamps alone never choose the winner.
Concurrent conversation edits create explicit revisions or alternate continuations. Sync does not execute stored requests or replay tools. Device-local paths, secrets and hardware settings are not portable values. Recheck permissions on reconnection and record deletion/restoration/revocation explicitly.
Lifecycle and storage policy
Support create/open, inspect/search/update, export/import, backup/restore, soft-delete and explicit permanent purge. Retention is configurable and visible by namespace/category; do not assume indefinite retention or silently discard work under storage pressure. Soft-delete preserves recoverable revisions until expiry. Purge covers managed replicas/indexes/derived records under policy, with explicit limits for offline copies and external backups.
Large files use content-addressed blobs or authorised external references. Reference counting prevents deletion while another owner needs an artifact. Distinguish quotas for metadata, logs, caches, attachments and model weights. Den metadata does not make a temporary Pull permanent: Install or an explicit pin creates persistent ownership.
Compatibility and migration
Publish versioned schemas, examples and conformance tests. Compatible writers preserve unknown optional fields; unknown security-critical fields or required capabilities block unsafe writes. Validate, back up and transactionally migrate schemas. Unsupported newer versions may open read-only when safe, never discard fields to force a downgrade.
Round-trip null for empty metrics and Na for provider-unavailable metrics, serialised as "Na"; measured zero stays 0. Permission-filter search/index results and include revision/provenance.
Supporting APIs and acceptance
Preserve Dulche.Den.GetModelByID(id) and Dulche.Den.ListModelsByName(name). Add compatible create/open, scoped search, revision-checked update, export/import, sync, restore and purge APIs with documented signatures and failures.
Acceptance covers cross-harness round-tripping, duplicate names, concurrent edits, offline conflicts, crash recovery, revocation, safe import, secret-free export, model replacement/rollback, retention/restore and migrations without data loss.
Generative UI
Generative UI is a Dulche capability that allows a model or Agent to return arbitrary structured user interfaces when an interface is more useful than prose. Generated interfaces may be visual, interactive and stateful, but MUST be expressed through a validated declarative Generative UI schema and MUST NOT execute arbitrary model-generated application code.
Rendering and trust boundary
CUI is the rendering layer for Generative UI. Generated surfaces render inside a CUI <GenerativeContainer> or equivalent trusted host component using approved CUI primitives, design tokens, theming, layout, accessibility and interaction behaviour. Any authorised 9to1 app may host a GenerativeContainer without implementing its own incompatible renderer.
Dulche may choose the structure and composition of the interface, including novel layouts, but the model output is data/schema rather than executable JavaScript, Python, shell commands, native binaries or arbitrary application code. The Generative UI runtime validates schema version, component types, properties, state bindings, declared actions and capability references before rendering.
Templates
Generative UI provides reusable high-level templates for common interaction patterns. Templates are starting structures, not hard limits; Dulche can instantiate, extend, combine or restyle them through supported schema properties.
Flashcard set / study deck.
Table, sortable/filterable data table and comparison grid.
Quiz, practice exercise and answer/reveal workflow.
Timeline and step-by-step guide.
Checklist and progress tracker.
Card grid / gallery / result browser.
Form, questionnaire and multi-step wizard.
Kanban/task-board style layout where appropriate.
Glossary / FAQ / concept-reference layout.
Diagram, relationship map and structured visual explainer.
Other shared templates added by the Generative UI framework or authorised extensions.
Primitive composition
When no template fully fits the task, Dulche can compose a custom surface from approved lower-level primitives. The supported primitive set should include, where appropriate, text/heading blocks, icons or generated illustrations, cards, badges/tags, buttons, inputs, dropdowns, toggles, sliders, chips, lists, tables, grids, tabs, accordions, progress indicators, layout containers, drag containers, drop zones, connectors/relationships, semantic-object views and other safe CUI primitives.
The primitive library is extensible through versioned framework/extension contracts. Unsupported component types MUST be rejected or downgraded safely; a model cannot create a new privileged executable component merely by naming it in the schema.
State and interaction
Generated surfaces may maintain bounded typed state. Supported interactions can include selecting options, sorting/filtering, expanding/collapsing content, progressing through steps, editing fields, revealing hints/answers, checking responses, reordering items, dragging supported objects between declared drop zones, switching views and updating selected data.
State mutations are handled by the Generative UI runtime or by declared typed actions. Interaction support does not grant the model arbitrary code execution or unrestricted access to the host application's process.
Progressive conversational evolution
A generated surface is a first-class conversation artifact and may evolve across turns. Dulche should be able to patch or transform an existing surface instead of rebuilding unrelated output from scratch. Examples include turning a static explanation into an interactive exercise, adding another column to a table, converting notes into flashcards, adding filters, changing a card grid into a comparison view or preserving quiz progress while adding new questions.
Updates must address stable SurfaceID/component/state identities or equivalent schema identities so user interaction state is retained wherever the requested transformation allows it. Partial regeneration is preferred when only part of a surface changes.
Typed actions and side effects
Generated controls bind to declared typed actions rather than arbitrary executable handlers. An action definition includes stable identity, expected input schema, allowed state mutation or API binding, required capability/permission and result/error contract.
Pure presentation and local interaction may execute inside the Generative UI runtime without external side effects. Actions that invoke 9to1 APIs, tools or external services remain subject to the same permission, confirmation, auditing and consequence rules as the underlying capability. Generative UI MUST NOT be a path around security prompts or tool permissions.
Data binding and semantic objects
Generative UI can bind to authorised structured data and canonical 9to1 entities instead of flattening everything into prompt text. Examples include Data ranges, Planner tasks, Maps Places/Routes, Board items, Write selections/documents, search results, translation sets, code diffs or Dulche Action Graph state.
Bindings retain source identity and permissions. A rendered card or table row that represents a canonical object should reference that object rather than silently creating a disconnected copy unless the user explicitly asks for a snapshot.
Ephemeral and saved artifacts
A generated surface may remain ephemeral to the current response/session or be promoted through an explicit supported conversion/save path. Examples include saving generated flashcards as a study resource, converting a generated task board into a Board, inserting a generated table into Write/Data or saving a generated route through Maps. Promotion uses the destination app's canonical API and permissions.
Third-party visual examples and assets
Generative UI may reproduce the functional idea or spatial structure needed to explain a third-party product/game without copying proprietary artwork merely to imitate the source. Where licensed/authorised assets are not available, it should use generic, stylised, text-labelled or newly generated representations sufficient to communicate the concept.
Example: if the user asks how an item is crafted in Minecraft, Dulche may create a visual 3x3 crafting-grid representation using generic/stylised ingredient tokens and an output slot rather than copied official item textures or proprietary interface artwork. In later turns the same surface may be made interactive using approved drag/drop primitives so the user can move ingredient tokens, receive validation, request hints or turn the recipe into a quiz.
Accessibility and visual consistency
Generated UI MUST inherit the host CUI theme/design system and remain accessible. The runtime should enforce semantic roles, labels, focusability/order, keyboard operation, screen-reader information, non-colour-only meaning and accessible alternatives for interactions such as drag/drop wherever the component library supports them.
Failure and fallback
Invalid, unsupported or unsafe generated schemas MUST fail closed without executing arbitrary content. Dulche may repair/regenerate the affected surface or fall back to a non-interactive/native representation while preserving the user-visible answer where possible.
Result contract and acceptance
Result.GeneratedUI contains the generated UI payload when present and returns null when no generated interface is produced. The payload must identify schema version, surface identity, component tree, declared state/bindings and declared actions/capabilities required to reproduce the surface safely.
Dulche can create arbitrary useful UI structures without arbitrary code execution.
Built-in templates and lower-level CUI primitives can be combined and extended within the declarative schema.
Generated surfaces support safe stateful interaction and can evolve across conversation turns without unnecessarily discarding user state.
All external side effects route through typed permission-aware actions.
Structured 9to1 data can be bound by canonical identity, and generated artifacts can be promoted through destination-app APIs.
Generated UI follows CUI theming/accessibility and safely handles invalid schemas or unavailable components.
Background Learning
Background Learning is an explicitly opt-in Dulche personalisation subsystem. It is separate from Persistent Memory. Enabling Background Learning allows Dulche to learn useful patterns, interests and reusable knowledge from eligible 9to1 activity over time; it does not itself enable or disable Persistent Memory and it does not imply continuous fine-tuning of the underlying base model.
Eligible learning classes
Background Learning can maintain three broad classes of learned information:
9to1 usage and project context: which authorised surfaces the user uses most, recurring workflows, recently or frequently active projects, apps commonly used together, important project terminology/entities and other usage patterns that improve contextual relevance.
Interests and topic Knowledge Banks: recurring subjects the user appears to care about, together with reusable factual/reference material that can improve later answers and remain available offline. For example, repeated questions about cars may lead to an Interest record for cars and a local Cars Knowledge Bank containing useful terminology, concepts and sourced reference material.
Other relevant personalisation information: additional permitted information that materially improves responses, such as preferred terminology, recurring goals, explanation preferences, established project conventions, frequently used tools, entity relationships and corrections that should influence future response behaviour.
Usage and project learning
The usage-learning layer SHOULD retain useful semantic state rather than an indiscriminate permanent clickstream. For example, it may learn that Dev and Stack are frequently used for a particular project or that a project is currently active. Raw activity used to derive these signals should be retained only to the extent required by the configured retention/privacy model.
Learned project context can help Dulche resolve ambiguous references, rank context candidates, suggest likely relevant surfaces and prepare authorised Agents with useful project context. It MUST remain scope-aware: project-specific learning does not automatically become unrelated global context.
Interest Knowledge Banks
Background Learning can create and maintain topic-specific KnowledgeBank entities. A KnowledgeBank can contain a stable ID, topic/title, entries, source/provenance metadata, confidence, freshness, creation/update state, storage/sync policy and enabled/disabled state. Knowledge Banks may be created automatically from recurring interests or explicitly managed by the user.
Knowledge Bank entries may include reusable summaries, terminology, relationships, reference facts and other material previously obtained from authorised local sources, user interactions or trusted retrieval. Factual entries MUST retain enough provenance/freshness information for Dulche to distinguish durable knowledge from information that may need refreshing.
Knowledge Banks are not the same as Persistent Memory. For example, 'the user is interested in cars' is personalisation/user context; a structured offline bank explaining engines, EV charging and vehicle terminology is subject knowledge. Dulche may use both when relevant, but they remain separately inspectable and manageable.
Structured learned state
Background Learning MUST store structured learned records rather than relying on one opaque free-form profile. Records should carry stable identity, category/type, subject/entity, learned value, provenance, confidence, creation/update state, last reinforcement/use where useful, freshness/expiry semantics and user-edited/locked state where applicable.
Explicit user corrections outrank contradictory inferred learning. If a user corrects an inferred preference, project status or interest, the system MUST revise/supersede the stale inference instead of allowing both to compete indefinitely as equally valid facts.
Selective retrieval
The complete learning store MUST NOT be injected into every request. Dulche must retrieve only learning context relevant to the active request, Agent, app and permission scope. Retrieval should use current entities/topics/project context to select the smallest useful set of records and Knowledge Bank material.
Privacy and cloud boundaries
Background Learning data is private by default and exists to personalise the user's 9to1 AI experience. It MUST NOT be sold, used to build advertising profiles or indiscriminately uploaded to third parties. Enabling Background Learning does not itself grant permission to transmit learned information to a cloud model/provider.
If a Dulche request uses a remote/cloud provider, disclosure of any learned context remains subject to the normal provider, privacy, permission and data-minimisation rules for that request. The implementation MUST distinguish permission to learn/store information from permission to disclose that information externally.
Any optional cross-device synchronisation of Background Learning state must be user-controlled and protected by the applicable authenticated/encrypted 9to1 sync/storage architecture. The feature MUST remain useful locally and must not require insecure cloud upload merely to personalise responses.
User controls
Users must be able to enable/disable Background Learning, pause new learning, inspect learned information, inspect and manage topic Knowledge Banks, correct inaccurate learning, delete individual learned records or a complete topic bank, clear learned categories and configure which apps/projects/categories may contribute where supported. Disabling learning stops creation/reinforcement of new learned state but MUST NOT silently delete existing Persistent Memory or unrelated user data.
Relationship to Persistent Memory
Persistent Memory and Background Learning are independent. Persistent Memory stores durable cross-session memories under the Memory policy; Background Learning is the opt-in process that derives usage patterns, interests, Knowledge Banks and other personalisation state. Neither feature may silently enable, disable, clear or substitute for the other.
Background Learning may identify information that would be useful as a durable memory, but any conversion into Persistent Memory must use the Memory subsystem and preserve that the source was an inference rather than an explicit user statement. Explicit Memory corrections remain authoritative over contradictory Background Learning inferences.
Background Learning acceptance requirements
Background Learning is off until the user opts in and remains independently configurable from Persistent Memory.
Eligible 9to1 usage/project patterns, interests/Knowledge Banks and other useful personalisation information can be learned as structured, inspectable state.
Topic Knowledge Banks can provide relevant offline reference material and retain provenance/freshness sufficient to avoid presenting stale inferred facts as timeless truth.
Only relevant learning context is retrieved for a request; the full learning store is not injected indiscriminately.
Learned data is not sold, used for advertising profiles or uploaded to cloud providers merely because learning is enabled.
Users can inspect, correct, scope and delete learning independently of Persistent Memory.
MCP Support
MCP is a first-class Dulche extension/runtime capability. Dulche MUST support acting as an MCP client for authorised local/remote MCP servers and acting as an MCP server when 9-1 intentionally exposes approved capabilities to external MCP clients. MCP execution MUST use the same permission, audit, cancellation, timeout and structured-error contracts as native Dulche tools.
Identity and lifecycle
Every configured MCP connection MUST have a stable ServerID independent of display name or transport address. Configuration MUST record role (client/server), transport/process/endpoint definition, credential references, trust state, capability snapshot/version and owner/scope. Credentials MUST be stored by secure reference and MUST NOT be embedded as plaintext in project manifests or logs.
Client connections MUST expose at least Disconnected, Connecting, Ready, Degraded, Reconnecting, Failed and Stopped states. Reconnect MUST NOT replay a previously completed consequential tool call. A broken connection returns structured transport/provider failures and MUST NOT be reported as Ready.
Capability discovery and schemas
Dulche MUST discover and represent the capabilities actually exposed by an MCP server, including tools and, where supported by the negotiated MCP version/server, resources and prompts. Tool input/output schemas MUST be validated before dispatch/consumption. Capability changes MUST invalidate stale cached schemas before later calls use them.
Capability identity is server-scoped: two MCP servers MAY expose the same human-readable tool name without collision because the canonical identity includes ServerID plus capability identity/name. User-facing aliases MAY exist but MUST NOT replace stable server-scoped identity.
Permissions and execution
Connecting to an MCP server does not authorise all capabilities it exposes. Each tool/resource capability MUST resolve through Dulche/Home permission and risk evaluation according to its effective read/write/external-side-effect scope. Server-provided descriptions/content MUST NOT grant permissions, alter trust state or override caller restrictions.
MCP tool execution MUST support cancellation/timeouts when supported by the active transport/server and MUST record when cancellation is best-effort or too late because an external action already completed. Results, approvals, failures, blockers and side effects MUST appear in ToolLog, AuditLog, FullLog and Action Graph like equivalent native tools.
Canonical MCP API
Dulche.MCP.Connect(config);
Dulche.MCP.Disconnect(serverID);
Dulche.MCP.ListServers();
Dulche.MCP.GetState(serverID);
Dulche.MCP.GetCapabilities(serverID);
Dulche.MCP.ListTools(serverID);
Dulche.MCP.CallTool(serverID, toolName, arguments);
Dulche.MCP.ListResources(serverID);
Dulche.MCP.ReadResource(serverID, resourceID);
Dulche.MCP.ListPrompts(serverID);
Dulche.MCP.GetPrompt(serverID, promptID, arguments?);
Dulche.MCP.Server.Start(config);
Dulche.MCP.Server.Stop(serverID);
Unsupported capabilities MUST return UnsupportedCapability rather than fabricated empty results. Protocol-version-specific functionality MAY extend this API while preserving compatibility with the stable core.
Tool Builder integration and acceptance
MCP projects produced by AI Studio Tool Builder MUST validate against the same Dulche MCP connection/schema/permission contract used at runtime. MCP support is implementation-complete only when local and remote connections can be configured, discovered, permissioned, called, cancelled/failed, reconnected and audited without bespoke per-app wiring, and when approved 9-1 capabilities can be exposed through server mode without bypassing their original permission model.
Plugins and web integrations — WebMCP and site-hosted MCP servers
Support MUST be added for WebMCP-enabled web pages and for remote MCP servers hosted by websites. These are distinct integration surfaces: browser-side WebMCP support alone does not satisfy remote MCP-server support, and connecting to a remote MCP endpoint alone does not satisfy WebMCP support.
The existing Plugin/MCP integration system MUST expose discovery/inspection, connection or permission setup, tool invocation, cancellation where supported, and disconnect/revocation for the appropriate surface. WebMCP integration MUST use the supported browser capability with explicit capability detection and origin boundaries. Site-hosted MCP connections MUST support the applicable remote HTTP transport and protocol-version/authentication contracts rather than assuming that a page URL is itself a valid MCP endpoint. The implementation MUST record supported browser/protocol versions and visibly report unsupported capabilities instead of claiming a successful integration.
Both routes MUST retain Home-brokered permissions, declared scopes, caller/site identity, secret protection and consequential-action approval. Tool descriptions, page content and tool results MUST NOT be treated as authority to expand permissions. These requirements include interoperability with websites exposing MCP servers; they do not silently select or purchase a new hosting service for the Sites application.
Web integration API and acceptance
Extend the existing canonical MCP/Plugin APIs for capability inspection, discovery, connection/authentication setup, invocation, supported cancellation and revocation. Browser-side WebMCP bindings MUST preserve browser origin/document identity; remote MCP bindings MUST preserve ServerID, endpoint identity and negotiated protocol/transport metadata. Test an authorised WebMCP-enabled page and a website-hosted remote MCP endpoint separately, then test unsupported browser/protocol, denied scopes, disconnected transport, cancellation limits and revocation. Neither route may claim success from a placeholder, silently use a page URL as an MCP endpoint or expose secrets in logs.
Skills + Plugins
Skills and Plugins are separate first-class Dulche extension types. A Skill packages reusable instructions, workflows, context rules and resources for model/Agent/Harness execution. A Plugin packages executable or integrated capabilities and MAY expose typed tools/actions, CUI surfaces or external-service functionality. Neither type is interchangeable with MCP, although a Skill or Plugin MAY declare an MCP dependency.
Common package contract
Every Skill and Plugin MUST have a versioned manifest containing stable PackageID, package type, version, minimum/compatible Dulche versions, provenance/origin, declared capabilities, required/requested permissions, dependencies, entry points/resources, update metadata and integrity/signature information when the distribution channel supports signing. Display name MUST NOT be used as package identity.
Manifest parsing and dependency resolution MUST be deterministic. Unknown required manifest fields/capabilities block installation or enablement with a structured compatibility failure; unknown optional fields MAY be preserved for forward compatibility. Packages MUST NOT execute code merely because their manifest was inspected or imported.
Lifecycle, trust and permissions
Installation, enablement, permissions and trust are separate states. Installing a package registers its files/manifest but MUST NOT automatically enable it for every caller, grant requested permissions, connect external accounts or grant Accept and Always Trust. Enablement only makes the package available within the selected scope; individual actions still use the normal Dulche/Home permission and risk model.
Package lifecycle MUST expose at least Installed, Disabled, Enabled, Updating, Failed and Quarantined states. A package that fails integrity/signature/compatibility validation MUST NOT become Enabled. Quarantine preserves evidence/metadata needed for diagnosis while preventing execution.
Updates MUST be version-aware and transactional. Dulche MUST validate/stage the new version and dependency graph before switching the active version. Failure during update MUST leave the previous known-good version available when rollback is technically possible. Package updates MUST NOT silently expand effective permissions; newly requested scopes require a new permission decision.
Uninstall MUST define what happens to package-owned persistent data. Shared/user-authored data MUST NOT be silently deleted merely because a package is removed. Orphaned package state MAY be retained for recovery/reinstall according to explicit retention policy.
Skill model
A Skill is primarily declarative. It MAY contain instructions, workflow definitions, templates/prompts, context-selection rules, examples, resources/files and references to permitted tools/Plugins/MCP capabilities. A Skill MUST NOT gain arbitrary code execution solely by being a Skill; executable behaviour requires an explicitly declared/authorised executable extension capability such as a Plugin/tool dependency.
Skill activation MUST be explicit and observable in request/run metadata. Dulche MUST record which Skill IDs/versions contributed to a request so Result provenance, logs and Action Graph can identify the active Skill set. Conflicting or incompatible Skills MUST resolve through a deterministic precedence/compatibility rule or return Conflict; Dulche MUST NOT silently merge contradictory required policies.
Built-in Persistent skill
Dulche MUST ship a first-party built-in Skill with the canonical display name Persistent and a stable reserved SkillID. Activating Persistent on a request sets that root request's PersistencePolicy to Persistent. The Skill is declarative: it changes Runtime orchestration semantics and does not gain permissions, tools, external access, budget or trust merely by being active.
Persistent activation MUST be explicit and visible in request metadata, the compose invocation state, FullLog and Action Graph. It MAY be invoked through the shared @ resource picker as @Persistent. The active version MUST be recorded like every other Skill so later inspection can prove which persistence contract governed the run.
The Persistent Skill MUST use the canonical Dulche persistent-request contract. In particular, an ordinary checkpoint, context compaction boundary, provider lease expiry, model restart, recoverable tool timeout or similar continuation boundary MUST NOT be treated as successful completion of the turn. The Runtime preserves/reconstructs execution state and continues under the same RootRequestID until the task's completion criteria are actually satisfied, the user explicitly stops it, or all remaining work is non-terminally AwaitingUser because of an unresolved blocker.
While a Persistent turn is running, an ordinary follow-up message sent by the user MUST join the same root turn as a SteeringMessage and MUST NOT implicitly cancel, replace or interrupt the active work. Dulche consumes the message at the next safe planning boundary, updates the plan and continues. Explicit Stop, explicit replace/edit semantics and any separately exposed interrupt/stack action retain their distinct meanings.
A blocker that cannot be resolved within the request's effective permission and capability bounds MUST be surfaced to the user as a structured blocker immediately. The blocker MUST isolate only the dependent work. Dulche MUST continue any independent runnable work in the same persistent turn; if no independent work remains, the turn enters AwaitingUser without being misreported as complete or timed out. When the blocker is resolved, the same durable turn resumes from current state rather than silently restarting completed work.
Persistent MUST remain compatible with automatic context compaction, Context Summarisation, Subagents, checkpoints, crash recovery and provider/model fallback. None of those mechanisms may erase completed side-effect evidence, duplicate consequential actions or weaken permission/approval requirements.
Plugin model
A Plugin MAY expose typed tools/actions, external-service connectors and optional CUI surfaces. Every exposed callable capability MUST declare input/output schemas, permission scopes, risk/side-effect classification and cancellation/timeout semantics where applicable. Plugin tool calls MUST enter the same ToolLog, AuditLog, FullLog and Action Graph pipeline as native tools and MCP calls.
Plugin CUI surfaces MUST render through approved CUI contracts and MUST NOT inject arbitrary trusted application code/markup outside the declared host surface. A Plugin surface does not inherit permission to invoke its Plugin’s actions without the applicable caller/user permission grants.
External-service Plugins MUST use secure credential references and explicit connection/account scopes. Provider tokens/secrets MUST NOT be stored in plaintext package files, logs or project definitions.
Dependencies and persistence
Package dependencies MUST be expressed by stable PackageID plus version/range and dependency type. Dulche MUST detect missing, cyclic and incompatible dependencies before enablement. Optional dependencies MUST be distinguishable from required dependencies so absence does not masquerade as a broken install.
Dulche Den MUST persist the installed package registry, active versions, enablement scopes, package provenance, dependency graph and relevant package state. Device-specific executable paths/caches remain device-local; shared Den state MUST NOT imply that executable packages are installed on another device unless that device independently satisfies installation/integrity requirements.
Canonical Skill API
Dulche.Skill.Install(package);
Dulche.Skill.List();
Dulche.Skill.Get(skillID);
Dulche.Skill.Enable(skillID, scope?);
Dulche.Skill.Disable(skillID, scope?);
Dulche.Skill.Update(skillID, version?);
Dulche.Skill.Uninstall(skillID);
Dulche.Skill.ResolveFor(request);
Canonical Plugin API
Dulche.Plugin.Install(package);
Dulche.Plugin.List();
Dulche.Plugin.Get(pluginID);
Dulche.Plugin.Enable(pluginID, scope?);
Dulche.Plugin.Disable(pluginID, scope?);
Dulche.Plugin.Update(pluginID, version?);
Dulche.Plugin.Uninstall(pluginID);
Dulche.Plugin.GetCapabilities(pluginID);
Dulche.Plugin.Invoke(pluginID, capability, arguments);
These are minimum canonical entry points. Tool Builder and other first-party clients MUST use the same package/runtime contracts rather than manipulating private package files or registries directly.
Tool Builder integration and acceptance
Skills and Plugins produced by AI Studio Tool Builder MUST validate against the exact manifest/schema/dependency/permission contracts used by Dulche after installation. First-class support is implementation-complete only when packages can be created, validated, installed, enabled/disabled, permissioned, updated/rolled back where supported, used in real Dulche requests, audited, persisted/recovered and uninstalled without bespoke per-app wiring or silent permission escalation.
External App Integrations
External App Integrations is the shared 9to1 framework for connecting, authenticating and operating third-party accounts/services. Authentication, provider scopes, transport, sync, webhooks, rate limits, provider-specific errors and remote-entity identity MUST be encapsulated by this shared layer rather than reimplemented independently inside each consuming app.
Core connection model
The framework MUST define stable typed entities for IntegrationProvider, Connection, ExternalAccount, IntegrationCapability, CredentialReference, RemoteEntityReference, SyncCursor, WebhookSubscription and ConnectionHealth or equivalent contracts. A Connection represents one authenticated provider/account relationship and has stable identity independent of whichever 9to1 app first created it.
Multiple accounts/connections for the same provider MUST be supported. For example, a user may connect separate personal and work Google accounts or multiple GitHub identities without those accounts being merged or ambiguously selected.
Connect once, reuse through authorised capabilities
A provider account should be connected once through the integration framework and then reused by authorised 9to1 surfaces. Consuming apps MUST request capabilities from the existing Connection rather than maintaining private duplicate credentials or running their own hidden authentication flows.
Examples include a Google connection supplying Drive capabilities to Files, Gmail capabilities to Mail, Calendar capabilities to Planner/Calendar and Contacts capabilities to relevant people pickers; a GitHub connection may supply repository/issue/pull-request capabilities to Stack, Dev or authorised Dulche Agents. The exact provider capabilities available remain determined by granted provider scopes and the integration adapter.
Provider scope versus 9to1 permission
Provider authorisation and 9to1 authorisation are separate gates. A Connection may possess provider scopes that a particular app, Agent, Skill, Plugin or extension is not authorised to use. Both the remote provider scope and the applicable 9to1 permission/capability policy MUST allow an operation before it is executed.
Connecting an account MUST NOT implicitly grant every 9to1 surface unrestricted access to that account. Permission decisions should be made at an appropriate capability/resource scope and remain inspectable/revocable.
Typed capability contracts
Consuming apps SHOULD depend on provider-neutral typed capabilities where equivalent semantics exist instead of embedding provider-specific endpoint logic. Examples include Files.List/Read/Upload, Mail.Search/Read/Send, Calendar.ListEvents/CreateEvent, Contacts.Search, Git.ListRepositories/CreateIssue and Chat.ListMessages or equivalent canonical contracts.
Provider adapters map those typed capabilities onto the provider's API. Provider-specific features that cannot be represented faithfully through a common contract may be exposed through explicit provider-namespaced capabilities; the common abstraction MUST NOT silently discard important provider semantics merely to force false parity.
Capability schemas MUST declare input/output shape, supported operations, required provider scopes, relevant 9to1 permissions, pagination/streaming behaviour, provider limitations and error states.
Authentication and credential storage
The integration framework centrally owns supported authentication flows such as OAuth/OIDC, PKCE, device-code flows, API-key authentication or provider-specific enterprise methods where appropriate. Apps MUST NOT request or persist reusable provider credentials directly when the integration framework can broker them.
Credential material such as access tokens, refresh tokens, API keys, passwords and private keys MUST live in approved secure credential storage. Integration records, Den records, logs, exports and app settings store credential references/connection identities rather than plaintext reusable secrets.
Token refresh, expiry, revocation and provider reauthentication are lifecycle concerns of the integration framework. A consumer receives a capability result or typed authentication-required failure, not raw credentials it can reuse arbitrarily.
Scope escalation
If a Connection exists but lacks a provider scope required by a new capability, the consuming surface requests scope escalation through the shared integration framework. The user must be shown which additional provider access is being requested and why. The framework extends/replaces the existing authorisation where the provider supports it rather than creating a hidden duplicate connection.
Remote identity and canonical 9to1 entities
External objects MUST retain their remote identity and provenance. A RemoteEntityReference should identify the provider, Connection, remote object ID, remote revision/version where available, remote URL/reference and any mapped canonical 9to1 entity.
Opening or referencing a remote object does not automatically create a separate canonical copy. The UI and APIs MUST distinguish operations such as Open remote, Import/copy into 9to1, Link/reference and Keep synchronised.
Where an external object is mapped to a canonical 9to1 entity, the relationship must remain explicit so the system does not create multiple disconnected local copies of the same remote item or accidentally treat provider IDs as globally unique without Connection/provider context.
Live, cached, imported and synchronised state
The integration layer MUST distinguish live remote data, cached metadata, cached content, imported local copies and synchronised mirrors. Consuming apps must be able to determine whether displayed information is current, cached, stale or locally diverged.
Caching policies must respect provider terms, account permissions, data sensitivity and user settings. A cached object must not be presented as live merely because a prior request succeeded.
Sync, webhooks and change feeds
Where a provider supports webhooks, push notifications or incremental change feeds, the integration framework SHOULD use them rather than each app independently polling the same account. It owns webhook registration/renewal/validation, change cursors, deduplication, retry/backoff and background refresh.
Polling remains available where required by the provider or capability, but should be centralised enough to avoid redundant traffic and quota consumption. Sync state must include sufficient cursor/revision information to continue incrementally after restart or temporary offline periods.
Offline and queued-operation behaviour
Consumers may continue to display authorised cached state while a provider is unavailable, but the stale/offline state and last successful sync/freshness information MUST remain visible when material. The framework MUST NOT silently claim remote mutations succeeded when they have only been queued locally.
If queued remote writes are supported, each operation needs stable identity, retry/idempotency semantics, dependency ordering where applicable, visible pending/failed state and explicit conflict handling. Reconnection must not blindly replay an action that is no longer valid or that already completed remotely.
Conflicts and versioning
For synchronised/mirrored objects, use provider revision identifiers, ETags/version tokens or equivalent change metadata where available. Wall-clock timestamps alone MUST NOT be the only conflict authority.
Compatible disjoint edits may be merged where the owning capability can prove a safe merge. Otherwise preserve both versions or surface a conflict to the owning app/user. Provider-side deletion, permission loss and remote moves/renames require explicit typed states rather than being treated as generic missing-file errors.
Connection health and failure states
Connections expose typed health/lifecycle states such as Connected, AuthenticationRequired, ScopeRequired, RateLimited, ProviderUnavailable, Degraded, SyncError, Revoked and Disabled or equivalent. Apps consume these states and present appropriate user-facing recovery rather than leaking raw HTTP/provider exceptions.
Health information should include the failing capability/provider account where relevant, last successful contact/sync, retryability and the action required from the user when one exists.
Rate limits and reliability
The shared layer MUST centrally support pagination, retry-after handling, provider quotas, transient network retries, exponential backoff/jitter, idempotency, request cancellation, partial response handling and provider-specific service limits. Consuming apps MUST NOT each invent incompatible retry/quota behaviour.
Connection management UI
9to1 MUST provide a central integrations management surface, hosted under the appropriate Home/Settings area, showing provider, connected account identity, connection status, provider-granted scopes/capabilities, authorised 9to1 consumers where exposed, recent/last successful activity, errors, reconnect/re-authorise, permission management and disconnect/revoke actions.
Individual apps may deep-link into this management flow or expose capability-specific connection prompts, but connection state remains owned by the shared framework.
Dulche and Agent access
Dulche, Agents and AI surfaces use External App Integrations through the same typed capabilities and permissions as first-party apps. Dulche does not own a parallel account-authentication layer.
For example, a request to find an email uses an authorised Mail capability for an existing connection; a request to create a GitHub issue uses the relevant Git capability. Normal Dulche tool/action permissions and consequential-action confirmation requirements still apply. Merely connecting an account does not grant every Agent permission to mutate it.
Relationship to Plugins and MCP
External App Integrations, Plugins and MCP are distinct abstractions. External App Integrations represent durable authenticated third-party account/service relationships and their capabilities. Plugins are installable packages that may add executable/integrated functionality. MCP is a protocol by which Dulche can discover/use tools/resources.
They may interoperate: a Plugin may register a provider adapter; an integration capability may be surfaced to Dulche through an approved tool/MCP bridge. Such composition MUST preserve the underlying Connection identity, provider scopes and 9to1 permission checks rather than laundering authority through another abstraction.
Provider SDK and extension
9to1 SHOULD expose a versioned Integration Provider SDK/manifest contract so additional providers can be implemented without changing every consuming app. A provider definition can declare provider identity/branding metadata, authentication method, capability schemas, provider scopes, remote entity types, webhook/change-feed support, rate-limit semantics, health checks and provider-specific settings.
Third-party provider adapters remain sandboxed/permissioned according to their implementation model. Registering a provider does not grant unrestricted access to other Connections, credential stores or unrelated local data.
Disconnect and revocation
Disconnect semantics MUST be explicit and predictable. Disconnecting a Connection should stop sync/background activity, invalidate or remove local credential references as appropriate, disable provider capabilities and clear/expire caches according to policy. Where supported and requested, provider-side token revocation should also be attempted.
Disconnecting an account MUST NOT automatically delete unrelated local 9to1 artifacts previously imported from it. For linked/synchronised objects, the UI must explain what local data remains, what becomes unavailable and whether any pending remote operations are abandoned.
Security invariants
Possessing a provider credential does not grant any app, Agent, Skill, Plugin or extension unrestricted access to the associated account.
Every external operation must pass both provider scope/capability validation and the relevant 9to1 permission boundary.
Consuming apps receive capability access/results, not raw reusable credentials.
Connection/account identity, remote-object identity, provenance and provider limitations must remain explicit across app boundaries.
Logs, exports and Den records must not contain plaintext reusable provider secrets.
External App Integrations acceptance requirements
One authenticated Connection can be reused safely by multiple authorised 9to1 apps without duplicated credentials or hidden per-app OAuth implementations.
Multiple accounts per provider are unambiguous and stable.
Typed provider-neutral capabilities work where semantics align, with provider-specific extensions exposed explicitly rather than silently discarded.
Provider scopes and 9to1 consumer permissions are enforced as independent gates.
Live/cached/imported/synchronised states, remote identity and conflict/version state remain explicit and recoverable.
Webhooks/change feeds, polling, retries, rate limits, queued operations and connection health are handled centrally with deterministic failure semantics.
Dulche/Agents use the same connection/capability layer and cannot bypass account permissions.
Disconnect/revocation, secure credential storage and provider SDK integration are implemented without deleting unrelated local artifacts or exposing reusable secrets.
9to1-OS
Platform foundation and donor authority
9to1-OS is derived from the latest appropriate maintained Ubuntu/GNOME stack. The project forks/adapts the complete relevant desktop/system stack rather than treating Ubuntu merely as a kernel image, then rebuilds the 9to1 user-facing desktop environment and first-party system interfaces in CUI.NET while preserving mature non-replaced functionality underneath.
The governing donor rule is preserve unless replaced: applicable Ubuntu/GNOME behaviour, hardware support, accessibility, session management, networking, Bluetooth, audio, displays, power, notifications, multi-monitor support, virtual desktops, filesystem/system integration and other mature platform behaviour MUST remain available unless this specification explicitly replaces or supersedes it.
Where 9to1 requires a CUI.NET replacement for functionality already supplied by Ubuntu/GNOME and that 9to1 product does not already have a different authoritative donor, the latest appropriate corresponding Ubuntu/GNOME application becomes its donor. The replacement preserves applicable donor functionality and rebuilds/extends its GUI in CUI.NET. Existing explicitly assigned donors take precedence; Files, for example, retains its existing donor rather than switching to the Ubuntu file manager.
Once an authoritative 9to1 app fully replaces a donor graphical application, the duplicate donor user-facing app SHOULD be removed from the default OS image. Required lower-level libraries/services remain installed where technically necessary. The objective is functional preservation without parallel competing GUIs.
Desktop shell and Windows-style interaction model
The default 9to1-OS shell uses a familiar Windows-like desktop interaction model while retaining Linux/Ubuntu capabilities. Conventional minimise, maximise/restore and close controls, taskbar representation, window switching, context menus, system tray/status, desktop workspaces and predictable mouse/keyboard behaviour are first-class rather than hidden or intentionally omitted.
Window management and quality-of-life
Drag windows to edges/corners to preview and snap them into supported layouts.
Support built-in and user-defined snap layouts, including half, thirds, quarters and custom rectangular regions with configurable gaps/margins.
Provide smooth configurable window movement, open/close, minimise/restore, maximise, snapping and desktop-transition animations, with reduced-motion/disabled options.
Support conventional app/window switching, previews, multiple windows per app, virtual-desktop awareness, task-view/overview and keyboard-first operation.
Support user-configurable per-app/window rules such as initial monitor, desktop, size, snap region, maximised/fullscreen and always-on-top where compatible.
Linux/GTK/Qt and other compatible desktop applications remain runnable even when they are not CUI-native. They participate in the taskbar, window switching, snapping, desktops and supported system integration to the extent the underlying platform permits.
Taskbar framework
The taskbar is a first-class highly customisable shell framework, not a fixed strip of running applications. The default layout places Go at the left/start position and system/status controls toward the end, but supported regions/items can be rearranged.
Users can configure edge/position, floating versus edge-attached presentation, width, thickness, margins, corner radius, padding, item spacing, alignment, opacity, blur/material, borders, shadows, icon size, labels, grouping/combining, auto-hide/intelligent hide, animations, per-monitor behaviour, clock/tray content and compatible multi-row or multiple-taskbar arrangements.
Taskbar Layers
A taskbar instance supports between one and five independently configurable Taskbar Layers. Scrolling or a configured vertical gesture while the pointer/focus is over the taskbar moves discretely between adjacent layers and snaps to a complete layer; layers are not an infinitely scrollable strip.
Every layer has stable identity, name/order, item layout, presentation and visibility settings. Layers may differ in item size, alignment, grouping, height and visual presentation where supported. A visible accessible layer-position indicator shows the current position and number of available layers; its presentation can be configured but must not rely on colour alone.
A layer can contain typed items such as pinned/running apps, individual windows, Go, system controls, quick actions, settings, files/folders, Shelf items/collections, 9to1 routes, Dulche Agents, Agent runs, Automations actions, widgets, status indicators, media controls, spacers and authorised extension-provided modules.
Examples are illustrative rather than hard-coded: one user may create Running Apps, Quick Actions, AI Agents, Development and Personal layers. No layer type is reserved to a specific category.
Desktop Spaces, Virtual Desktops and Desktop Pages
Naming and conceptual separation
The OS-level mode system is named Desktop Spaces. The existing conversational/AI product is named LLM Spaces. Documentation, APIs and UI MUST use these distinct names to avoid ambiguity.
Virtual Desktops organise sets of windows within the current shell experience. Desktop Spaces redefine the surrounding shell/interaction experience. Desktop Pages are multiple pages of desktop icons/widgets within a desktop surface. These are separate orthogonal concepts.
Desktop Spaces
A Desktop Space is a versioned shell/behaviour profile that may change taskbars, taskbar layers, Go layout, quick settings, notification presentation, window rules, widgets/overlays, input model, theme, animations, performance/resource profile, default actions and Dulche behaviour without requiring applications to restart where avoidable.
First-party examples include a Gaming Desktop Space that can replace the standard taskbar with a lightweight floating gaming pill showing configurable telemetry such as FPS/frame time, CPU/GPU/RAM/VRAM, temperature, battery/power and latency, with an expandable quick menu; and a Touch Desktop Space that increases targets/spacing and adapts window controls, Go, quick settings, gestures, keyboard integration and snapping for tablet use.
Users can create, duplicate, rename, reorder, import/export, sync and delete custom Desktop Spaces. Optional triggers may suggest or activate a Desktop Space based on convertible posture, controller connection, application launch, display configuration, schedule or other supported state; automatic activation behaviour is user-controlled.
Virtual Desktops
Virtual Desktops support create/delete, names, ordering, keyboard/touchpad switching, window movement between desktops, configurable transition, task-view overview, optional per-desktop wallpaper and configurable taskbar visibility across current/all desktops.
Desktop Pages and Widgets
Each desktop surface can contain multiple ordered Desktop Pages that users may add/remove, rename, reorder and navigate by configured gesture/scroll. Pages may contain icons, files/folders, Shelf collections, shortcuts and native CUI widgets and may be global or Desktop-Space-specific according to configuration.
Desktop widgets are first-class CUI entities with resizing, grid/free placement where enabled, ordering, transparency/background material, interaction, update policy and per-page/per-Desktop-Space presence. First-party apps can expose widgets such as Planner, Maps, Files folders, Shelf collections, media, system resources, battery, clock/calendar, quick actions, Dulche Agents and Agent-run state.
Customisation Framework
Customisation is an architectural property of 9to1-OS. The requirement is not satisfied by wallpaper, accent colour and taskbar-position options. Stable shell behaviour and presentation that can reasonably be represented as configuration SHOULD be configurable unless doing so would materially compromise security, accessibility, compatibility or system integrity.
The OS MUST expose substantially deeper supported first-party customisation than stock Windows or stock GNOME without requiring registry hacks, shell patches, unsupported extensions or third-party Start/taskbar replacements. Configuration uses versioned typed schemas and transactions so Settings, Dulche, Automations and authorised extensions operate on the same underlying state.
Configuration scopes and precedence
Applicable settings can be scoped globally, per device, display, Desktop Space, Virtual Desktop, application/window class or input mode. The implementation MUST define deterministic precedence so a Desktop-Space/display/app override cannot unpredictably conflict with global defaults. Device/display-specific state must not be blindly synced to incompatible hardware.
Visual and behavioural scope
Mouse pointer/cursor theme, colour, size, outline/high-visibility behaviour and supported custom pointer packs.
Window button order/side, visible controls, button size/spacing/shape, title alignment, titlebar height, icon/title visibility and compatible extra window actions.
Window corner roundness, borders, shadows, glow, transparency, active/inactive treatment and user-selectable numerical/preset radius where supported.
Theme profiles covering light/dark/automatic mode, colours, gradients, accents, glow, blur, transparency, shadows, borders, roundness, spacing/density, typography, icons, control shapes and animation character.
Built-in visual personalities such as clean/minimal, glow, playful, glass/classic or other first-party presets act as editable starting profiles rather than locked themes; users can create custom profiles.
Icon packs, per-app icon overrides, icon scale/shape/treatment and notification-badge presentation.
Global and per-category animation enablement, speed, reduced-motion and presets/custom timing.
Rebindable keyboard shortcuts, supported mouse/touchpad/touch/controller gestures and conflict detection.
System tray/status ordering, visibility policy, overflow, icon size/spacing, clock/date/seconds/time-zone presentation, battery percentage/remaining-time presentation and network/audio/Bluetooth/VPN indicators.
Safe application and recovery
Large shell changes SHOULD support preview/keep/revert flows. Configuration mutations are transactional where practical and the shell maintains last-known-good recovery paths including reset current element, reset taskbar, reset Desktop Space, reset appearance, restore previous configuration and safe/default shell mode.
Configuration schemas are versioned and migrations MUST preserve supported user state across OS updates rather than silently discarding a highly customised desktop.
Quick Settings and system flyouts
Quick Settings combines Windows-style desktop system controls with Android-style customisation. Users can add/remove/reorder tiles, choose supported sizes, resize tiles, use multiple pages, configure layout/density/panel placement and install authorised custom tiles.
First-party tiles should cover relevant controls such as Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, airplane mode, brightness, volume/audio output, microphone, battery saver/performance mode, night light, accessibility, hotspot, VPN, display/casting, input, focus/do-not-disturb, location, screenshot/recording and Dulche/AI state.
Tiles are typed CUI modules that may expose live state, icon, primary/secondary labels, toggle/action, slider and expanded view. Apps/Plugins may register tiles through a permissioned contract with declared supported sizes/actions; arbitrary shell code injection is not a tile API.
Related flyouts such as audio, network, Bluetooth, calendar, battery and notification centre must provide friendly direct controls and the expected Windows-class QoL, including optional battery percentage, output-device switching, tray overflow, date/calendar, power/session controls and useful status detail.
Dulche and AI-native OS integration
Dulche is an always-available OS assistant, not merely another application. 'Always available' does not require a large model to remain permanently resident: users control model residency/background behaviour while the lightweight service remains integrated with Go AI mode, shortcuts, voice where enabled, context menus, selections, taskbar layers/widgets, notifications, Settings and first-party apps.
AI settings
Settings contains first-class AI areas for Models/Universal Model Picker, Dulche service/background behaviour, Always-active AI, Persistent Memory and Memory Frequency, Background Learning, Agents, MCP servers, Skills/Plugins, privacy and resource policy. Built-in MCP management includes add/remove, transport/endpoint configuration, authentication, capability inspection, enable/disable, Agent/app permission assignment, health and logs/errors.
Always-active AI is a configurable service mode and MUST NOT grant blanket access to microphone, files, external services or other sensitive capabilities. Those remain separately permissioned.
AI-aware RAM optimisation
The default OS must be aggressively memory-efficient without sacrificing specified functionality or quality so local models can use more of the machine. 9to1-OS should lazy-load non-critical services/surfaces, suspend or trim eligible inactive apps, reclaim caches, use appropriate compression/zram and memory mapping, avoid duplicated runtime state and unload inactive models/compatibility environments when policy permits.
Users can configure a managed System Memory Budget/profile such as Minimum, Balanced, Performance, AI/Maximum model capacity or Custom. This is a target for reclaimable/non-critical OS consumption rather than an unsafe hard cap on kernel/critical services.
