An optional Prioritise AI memory policy may reclaim eligible caches/background apps/models more aggressively to make room for a requested local model. Dulche/runtime should report what can be reclaimed and coordinate with the OS resource manager rather than simply failing at the first memory-pressure condition.
GUI-first administration
Common useful system-administration operations that Ubuntu frequently exposes primarily through Terminal SHOULD have first-party CUI.NET workflows wherever they can be represented safely and coherently. Terminal remains fully available for advanced/unrestricted workflows, but ordinary maintenance must not require memorising shell commands.
Software/package install, removal, update and repository/source management.
System updates, recovery, backups/snapshots and repair.
Drivers, devices, displays, audio, networking, DNS, VPN, firewall and hotspot.
Disk/partition/filesystem management, mounts, storage cleanup and health information.
Users/groups, permissions/ownership, startup/background services, scheduled jobs and environment/PATH management where appropriate.
Logs/journal/crash diagnostics, process/resource management and compatibility/runtime management.
Friendly GUIs should call stable typed system services/APIs rather than merely concatenate opaque shell strings. Where a shell tool is the only practical backend, arguments must be structured, privilege requirements declared and output/errors/progress handled safely.
Terminal safety and privileged destructive operations
9to1 Terminal Command Mode includes a Dangerous Command Guard that parses known commands/arguments/targets and classifies risk rather than relying only on substring matching. Potentially major irreversible operations such as destructive recursive deletion, filesystem formatting, partition-table mutation, mass permission changes or dangerous system/boot-path modification require OS-mediated protection.
For a Dangerous operation the mandatory sequence is consequence-specific warning -> trusted user authentication -> second consequence-specific confirmation -> execution. Authentication is never treated as final consent. The warning should identify resolved targets and expected consequence where feasible.
Terminal AI Mode, Dulche, Agents, Plugins and Automations cannot type the password, approve their own warning or bypass the final confirmation. Script/program execution cannot be perfectly predicted; recognised dangerous privileged operations should still pass through the system safety broker where technically possible, without claiming semantic proof over arbitrary executable code.
Multiple users and administrator policy
9to1-OS supports multiple isolated user accounts/profiles with standard and administrator roles, secure per-user data/settings/secrets, fast switching/sign-out and clearly scoped system-wide versus user-specific configuration.
Administrators can create managed policy profiles for family, school, organisation or kiosk-style deployments. Policies can control application allow/deny lists, package/app installation, external providers, Plugins/MCP, Terminal/admin access, removable storage, networking/VPN, Desktop Space/customisation options, web/content controls where supported, update policy and other security-sensitive capabilities.
A School profile can, for example, block launching unapproved applications and prevent the restricted user from disabling that policy without administrator authentication. Enforcement MUST occur below the normal app UI so renaming a binary, launching through Go/Terminal/Shelf or invoking an Agent does not trivially bypass policy.
Managed restrictions must be visible and attributable ('Managed by administrator/school policy') rather than presented as broken UI. Administrators require auditability of policy changes and clear recovery controls; administration must not silently expose another user's private content unless an explicit policy/capability legitimately grants that access.
First-party apps and deep OS integration
All release-scope first-party 9to1 applications are installed by default as part of the complete 9to1-OS experience, while application updates are independently deliverable from full OS updates. A central update/package service handles discovery, automatic/manual updates, integrity checks, history, repair and supported rollback instead of every app shipping a private updater.
First-party apps MUST behave as native OS components and register applicable typed integration with Go, Automations, Dulche, notifications, taskbar/layers, Desktop Spaces, widgets, system search/indexing, Files/open-with/default apps, share/clipboard/drag-drop, URI routes, permissions, External App Integrations, background tasks, crash/System Log, updates, backup/recovery, theming/accessibility and resource management.
Automations is a particularly strong integration requirement: apps should expose supported typed triggers/actions/events through the shared Automation framework rather than implementing incompatible private automation engines.
First-party apps should expose lifecycle information allowing safe trim/suspend/resume under memory pressure without losing unsaved work. Desktop Spaces own shell layout/presentation; apps contribute declared widgets/actions/status rather than taking arbitrary control of the shell.
Setup and first-run experience
9to1-OS MUST provide a friendly graphical CUI.NET installer and first-run/OOBE experience. A normal installation MUST NOT require interacting with the traditional Linux text/terminal installer or memorising shell commands. Advanced/technical options may be exposed through expandable UI without making them mandatory for ordinary users.
The setup flow should cover applicable language/region, keyboard, accessibility from the first screen, networking, installation target/disk choices, encryption, timezone, user creation and administrator role, optional managed school/organisation setup, privacy/telemetry choices, update preferences, restore from an existing 9to1 backup/profile, initial appearance/Desktop-Space choices and optional Dulche/model/provider onboarding.
Installation progress is staged and truthful. Failures expose actionable explanation, retry/back navigation where safe, logs/technical details and recovery rather than dropping users into an unexplained terminal. Critical-stage failure MUST NOT be presented as successful installation.
Recovery environments
9to1-OS provides a custom CUI recovery environment designed for ordinary users. It should expose Continue/boot normally, automatic startup repair, restore a previous healthy snapshot, undo the latest system update, safe mode, package/system repair, filesystem/disk checks, disable problematic drivers or shell extensions, recover/reset shell configuration, inspect System Log, backup/restore, advanced Terminal and supported repair/reinstall-with-data-preservation flows.
The custom 9to1 Recovery environment supplements rather than replaces the underlying Ubuntu/Linux recovery environment. The stock/default recovery path MUST remain available as an emergency fallback if the custom CUI recovery environment is damaged or cannot launch.
The custom and stock recovery paths must obey the existing boot-safety contract: ordinary snapshot restore, repair and rollback do not rewrite firmware or bootloader code. Any bootloader/firmware update is a separate tightly guarded operation.
Setup/recovery acceptance requirements
A normal user can install, create an account, configure basic hardware/privacy choices and reach the desktop without Terminal.
Accessibility and technical details are available during setup rather than only after installation.
9to1 Recovery provides friendly repair/rollback tools, while the lower-level Ubuntu/Linux recovery environment remains independently reachable.
Installer/recovery failures preserve diagnostic information and do not falsely report success or silently perform bootloader/firmware rewrites.
System updates, recovery and backups
System maintenance has a first-party CUI Settings workflow for checking, downloading, scheduling and installing OS updates, viewing changelogs/details, restart requirements, progress, failure/retry and update history. Terminal/package-manager commands remain optional advanced interfaces, never the required normal update path.
Consequential system updates use verified recoverable system snapshots/rollback state where technically feasible. The system should confirm successful boot/health before retiring rollback state and provide a friendly recovery environment with restore previous snapshot, repair OS/package database, safe mode, diagnostic logs and extension/driver disablement.
Ordinary backup/snapshot restoration and update rollback MUST NOT overwrite or restore firmware or bootloader code as part of the rollback transaction. Bootloader/firmware updates, if ever necessary, are separate tightly guarded operations with their own compatibility/recovery process so a normal failed OS update is not turned into a bricked device.
Software and package management
9to1-OS includes a friendly CUI graphical package manager with search, categories, source/publisher, version, architecture, size, installed/update state, screenshots/metadata where available, dependency/permission information and install/update/uninstall/repair workflows.
The package manager uses typed PackageProvider adapters for applicable Linux package ecosystems such as Ubuntu/Debian packages, Flatpak, Snap if retained and coherent AppImage handling, plus Winget for supported Windows/Wine scenarios and 9to1 package sources. It may show multiple sources for the same product and explain meaningful differences instead of silently choosing an arbitrary provider.
PackageProvider contracts define search, metadata, versions, install/update/uninstall, dependencies, progress, source trust, errors and capability limitations so additional providers can integrate without rewriting the package-manager UI.
System diagnostics and storage management
System Log and crash diagnostics
9to1-OS includes a CUI System Log surface that translates underlying journal/service/app events into useful searchable/filterable diagnostics while retaining advanced technical detail. Events can expose timestamp, component/process, severity, subsystem, version/build, crash ID, stack/debug data where available and related logs/actions.
Crash records should group repeated failures, support export/diagnostic bundles and permit user-authorised Dulche analysis such as explaining why a component repeatedly crashed. Diagnostic information MUST NOT be silently uploaded.
Disk Management
Settings includes CUI Disk Management covering physical disks, partitions, filesystems, mounts, labels, free/used space, removable storage, format/partition operations, encryption state, filesystem checks and SMART/health data where supported. Destructive operations require clear device identification and appropriate confirmation/authentication.
Task Manager and other donor-backed utilities
Task Manager is rebuilt in CUI.NET using the appropriate Ubuntu/GNOME system-monitor tooling as donor baseline unless another donor is explicitly assigned. It preserves mature process/resource functionality and extends it with Windows-style usability plus 9to1-specific visibility for models, Agents, containers/compatibility environments and relevant GPU/RAM usage.
The same donor fallback rule applies to Settings and other required CUI system utilities when an appropriate Ubuntu/GNOME app exists and no different donor has already been assigned.
9to1-OS acceptance requirements
Ubuntu/GNOME mature non-replaced functionality is preserved while the authoritative user-facing shell/system GUIs are CUI.NET and duplicate replaced donor apps are removed from the default image.
The taskbar is deeply customisable and supports one to five discrete snapping layers with a visible accessible layer indicator.
Desktop Spaces, Virtual Desktops, Desktop Pages and LLM Spaces remain explicitly separate concepts.
The shell supports deep first-party customisation of taskbar, Go, Quick Settings, pointer, window chrome/roundness, themes, widgets, desktops, gestures, tray/status, animations and scoped per-device/display/Desktop-Space/app behaviour.
Dulche, MCP, models and AI-aware memory/resource controls are first-class OS settings and Dulche is always available without requiring a heavyweight model to remain loaded.
Common administration has friendly CUI workflows and Dangerous Terminal operations use warning -> authentication -> final confirmation.
Multiple users and enforceable administrator-managed profiles can restrict unapproved apps and other capabilities without trivial bypass through alternate launch surfaces.
All first-party 9to1 apps ship installed by default, update independently and integrate deeply with shared OS services including Automations.
System updates have GUI installation, verified recovery/rollback mechanisms and ordinary rollback does not rewrite firmware/bootloader code.
A friendly multi-provider package manager, System Log/crash diagnostics, Disk Management and donor-backed Task Manager/Settings are present as first-class CUI system utilities.
Go
Go is the universal Start/search/action surface for 9to1-OS. It combines the roles of a Windows-style Start menu, system-wide search, application launcher and contextual quick-action surface. Go is an OS primitive, not a separate heavyweight application, and the default taskbar places Go at the left/start position.
Default surface
Opening Go without a query presents a customisable home surface that can contain Pinned items, Recent items, Suggested/contextual items, All Apps, recent files/projects, quick system actions, account/session controls and power controls. Users can reorder, hide, resize or regroup supported sections and choose compact search-first, Start-menu-like or larger dashboard-oriented layouts.
All Apps is a first-class Go view containing installed applications/programs available to the current user/profile. It is separate from the Android-style Launcher app drawer. Go is the primary application-launcher replacement for the 9to1-OS desktop shell.
Search and AI modes
Go provides a Search / AI switcher. Search is deterministic universal search/navigation; AI routes natural-language intent through Dulche while using the same canonical Go providers and typed OS/app actions.
Examples of AI-mode requests include opening the project the user was working on, finding the setting that controls display scaling, launching a group of development tools or locating notes by context. AI mode MUST NOT fabricate applications, files, settings or entities that do not exist and MUST surface ambiguity when multiple plausible targets remain.
Universal provider model
Applications, frameworks and authorised extensions register typed GoProviders rather than requiring Go to hard-code product-specific databases. Providers may expose search, suggestions, recent items, result categories, previews, aliases, quick actions, indexing/change notifications and query-time-only results.
Go may search applications, files/folders, settings, people/contacts, LLM Spaces/conversations where authorised, Boards, Planner tasks/events, Maps places, Shelf items/collections, Stack repositories/branches, Dev projects, browser history/bookmarks where enabled, installed tools, Plugins/extensions and registered system actions.
Canonical identity
Go returns references to canonical entities owned by their source application/framework. Its local index may cache identifiers, search fields, aliases, presentation metadata, permissions and freshness state, but MUST NOT create a competing canonical copy of a file, document, project, place, person or other result merely because it is searchable.
Ranking and context
Ranking may combine exact/prefix/fuzzy match, aliases, keywords, recency, frequency, pins/favourites, current app, active project, current canonical object, Desktop Space, user-enabled Background Learning and provider relevance. Context can change ranking and available actions but never bypass access controls or change the canonical identity of a result.
Typed actions
Results can expose owner-provided typed actions such as Open, Reveal, Share, Navigate, New window, Pin, Create, Toggle, Open with or app-specific commands. Go may invoke these actions directly where appropriate but MUST NOT reproduce another app's private business logic.
Consequential actions remain subject to the underlying OS/app permission and confirmation requirements. Go and Dulche cannot use a quick-action surface to bypass security prompts.
Filters and previews
Go supports optional user-selectable filters/categories such as Apps, Files, People, Settings, Places, Projects and Actions plus provider-defined categories where useful. Results may expose compact CUI previews supplied from canonical provider data.
Indexing, privacy and freshness
Providers declare whether they are locally indexed, queried live or hybrid. They can push changed entities, invalidate deleted entities and request re-indexing. Search results MUST be permission-filtered before display, including for restricted folders/projects, managed user profiles and lock-screen contexts.
Users can disable sensitive providers/categories such as browser history, message contents or private project indexing. Stale/offline remote results must be marked with their freshness state and invalid/deleted results removed rather than accumulating as zombie entries.
Scoped reuse
The same Go framework may be embedded as a scoped picker/search surface in Launcher, Files, Shelf and other apps, and Dulche may query Go for authorised entity discovery. These are scoped views over the same provider contracts, not separate incompatible search engines.
Performance and failure isolation
Opening Go should be effectively immediate. Local providers should stream results incrementally; slow remote providers MUST NOT block applications, local files, settings or cached results. Failure of one provider is isolated and reported only for that provider.
Go acceptance requirements
Go acts as the primary 9to1-OS Start menu, universal search and quick-action surface, with Go at the default left/start taskbar position.
Pinned, Recent, Suggested and All Apps views are first-class and deeply customisable.
Search and AI modes use the same canonical entity/provider/action contracts; AI mode cannot hallucinate unavailable entities.
Search results remain permission-filtered canonical references rather than duplicate Go-owned objects.
Provider failures and remote latency do not block local search/launch functionality.
Universal Model Picker
On 9to1-OS, the Universal Model Picker is the OS-hosted presentation of the same canonical Dulche/Home model/provider state used by regular 9to1. Model identities, provider connections, ordered Model Routes, active/background routing, category overrides, fallbacks, permissions and usage state MUST remain interoperable across Home and 9to1-OS rather than becoming separate OS-only configuration.
The OS picker provides the same compact selection experience plus deeper integration with Settings → AI, system resource management, administrator policy and local-model lifecycle. It can expose local/cloud/remote identity, capabilities, reasoning/effort controls, aliases/nicknames, route order, fallback state, locality/privacy, loading/residency, RAM/VRAM fit and per-app/Agent/Desktop-Space overrides.
9to1-OS may host the picker natively while Windows regular 9to1 hosts it through Home, but both clients MUST read/write the same versioned routing contracts and Dulche model catalogue. A route configured in Home remains meaningful on 9to1-OS subject to device-local model availability, provider authentication, administrator policy and device-specific resource constraints.
OS resource and policy integration
When a selected local model requires additional memory, the picker integrates with the 9to1-OS resource broker to show required/available/reclaimable RAM/VRAM and may request permitted reclamation before declaring the model unavailable. It MUST distinguish Installed, Unloaded, Loading, Loaded, Offloaded/Partially loaded where supported and Unavailable due to resources.
Administrator-managed user profiles can restrict allowed models/providers, cloud use, model acquisition and routing fallback. Model ordering MUST never bypass those restrictions; policy-ineligible candidates are filtered before route selection.
Shared-routing invariant
Ordered model fallback is a shared 9to1 capability, not an OS-specific behaviour. Requests from regular 9to1/Home and 9to1-OS use the same eligibility-first routing semantics: determine required capabilities and policy constraints, filter the configured route, then choose the highest-priority eligible available model and fall through only on classified model/provider-routing conditions.
Wine/WinBoat Framework
The Wine/WinBoat Framework is the unified 9to1-OS compatibility platform for non-native application packages. It provides one coherent installation, routing, execution, lifecycle, permissions, diagnostics and shell-integration model across Windows applications and Android APK applications rather than exposing Wine, VM/container tooling or an Android runtime as unrelated expert-only subsystems.
Compatibility backends
A CompatibilityBackend is a typed implementation capable of installing/running one or more foreign application formats. Required backend classes include a Wine-compatible Windows runtime, a WinBoat-style Windows environment for applications needing a fuller Windows VM/container context, and an APK/Android compatibility layer for Android applications. Additional compatible backends MAY be registered later through the same framework.
The compatibility manager owns stable entities such as CompatibilityApp, CompatibilityPackage, CompatibilityBackend, CompatibilityEnvironment, CompatibilityRoute, AppRoutingRule, CompatibilityPermissionSet, CompatibilityHealth and CompatibilitySnapshot or equivalent contracts. Applications are identified by stable package/application identity rather than by the pathname of the installer that originally created them.
Automatic package routing
Opening or double-clicking a supported foreign application package MUST route through the compatibility framework automatically. Executable/package type should be determined from trusted file metadata/signature/MIME inspection where available rather than relying only on filename extension.
Windows .exe/.msi and equivalent supported installers are routed to an eligible Windows backend. Android .apk packages are routed to an eligible APK/Android compatibility backend. The normal user experience is Install/Open application, not manually invoking wine, configuring a prefix, running Docker/Podman/QEMU/RDP commands or issuing Android runtime commands in Terminal.
The router evaluates package type, known application identity, architecture, backend capability, existing environments, administrator policy, resource requirements, compatibility knowledge and user defaults. When there is one clear eligible default, routing should proceed without unnecessary questions. When multiple viable frameworks exist or the user requests control, the UI may ask which framework/backend to use.
Per-application framework defaults
Users can set a preferred/default CompatibilityBackend for each installed application or recognised application identity. A chooser can provide an explicit 'Always use this framework for this app' action. This preference is stored against stable app/package identity and survives moves/renames of the original installer.
A per-app default does not override hard incompatibility, missing backend capability, administrator policy or unavailable hardware. If the selected backend cannot satisfy the app, the framework reports why and may offer other eligible backends rather than silently executing through an unrelated path.
Users can change/reset the backend association later from the application's compatibility settings. Global defaults may exist for Windows packages and APK packages, but per-app rules take precedence where valid.
Windows: Wine path
The Wine backend manages Wine runtime/version, isolated prefixes/environments, application architecture, DLL/runtime dependencies, graphics/DirectX translation, environment variables, registry integration, drive mappings, fonts, file associations, launch arguments and per-app overrides through CUI.NET management surfaces.
Ordinary users MUST NOT need to manually run winecfg, winetricks, edit registry state or construct WINEPREFIX environment variables. Advanced views may expose equivalent controls and raw technical details when useful.
Applications SHOULD normally use isolated managed Wine environments so dependency/runtime changes, repair, backup and uninstall do not corrupt unrelated apps. Applications may deliberately share an environment when required, but that relationship must be explicit.
Windows: WinBoat-style environment path
The WinBoat-style backend provides a managed Windows VM/container environment for applications that need or work better with a fuller Windows installation. It may expose configurable CPU, RAM, storage, hardware acceleration, networking, shared folders, USB/device passthrough, graphics configuration and individual-app/RemoteApp-style window integration where supported.
The management experience hides Docker/Podman, QEMU, VM orchestration and RDP implementation details during normal use while retaining advanced diagnostics. Individual Windows applications should appear as normal 9to1-OS windows where technically possible; a full Windows desktop remains available as a fallback/advanced mode.
Android/APK compatibility path
9to1-OS MUST support Android APK applications through the same Compatibility Framework using an Android/APK compatibility layer. Installing an APK creates/registers a normal CompatibilityApp backed by the Android runtime rather than placing Android apps in a disconnected secondary launcher.
The APK backend is responsible for Android runtime/container lifecycle, package installation/update/removal, Android package identity, architecture/ABI compatibility, graphics acceleration, display/window integration, storage mappings, networking, clipboard, audio, microphone/camera, notifications, input, orientation, intents/file associations and other host bridges where supported.
Android applications should participate in Go, taskbar/taskbar layers, window switching, Desktop Spaces, notifications, Files/open-with/share flows, Shelf and other applicable 9to1-OS integrations. The Android compatibility layer MUST NOT require the user to launch a separate Android desktop merely to start an installed APK unless a full Android environment is explicitly requested.
If multiple APK-compatible runtimes/backends are available, the same automatic eligibility and per-app default framework rules apply. The user may choose a backend and persist it for that Android app; otherwise 9to1 selects the highest-priority eligible configured default.
Unified installation experience
Opening a supported .exe, .msi, .apk or other registered foreign package invokes a single compatibility installation flow showing detected application/package identity, recommended backend, destination environment, required permissions, storage/resource estimate and relevant compatibility warnings. Advanced settings expose backend-specific controls without requiring them for a normal install.
The GUI package manager may also install Windows software through Winget or other approved Windows sources and Android packages through approved configured package sources where supported. Package-source discovery does not bypass administrator policy, signing/trust requirements or compatibility permissions.
Native-feeling OS integration
Foreign applications remain subject to the same shell/platform integration expectations as native applications wherever technically possible: Go search/launch, taskbar and layers, Desktop Spaces, snapping, app switching, tray/status integration, Files/open-with, default associations, clipboard, drag/drop, audio/microphone, printing, notifications, shortcuts, recent items, System Log/crash diagnostics and resource management.
Compatibility apps may expose Automations/Dulche actions only through typed supported bridges. Running inside Wine, a Windows VM or an Android runtime does not give an application unrestricted access to the host Automation framework or other 9to1 capabilities.
Filesystem and host permissions
Host folder exposure is explicit and revocable. Compatibility environments receive only user/admin-authorised Files locations rather than unrestricted access to the entire Linux home directory by default. Shared-folder mappings identify the canonical host location and the guest-visible mapping.
Clipboard, microphone, camera, USB/devices, network modes, location and other sensitive bridges use the normal 9to1 permission/policy system where applicable. A locally running foreign application is not automatically trusted with unrestricted host resources.
Graphics, gaming and input
The framework exposes backend-appropriate GPU acceleration, Vulkan/DirectX translation, discrete/integrated GPU preference, fullscreen, controller/input support and relevant compatibility/performance settings. Windows or Android games can integrate with Gaming Desktop Space telemetry/controls where the backend exposes the required data.
Resource and lifecycle management
CompatibilityEnvironment lifecycle states include at least Starting, Running, Suspended, Stopped, Degraded/Error and backend-specific transitional states. The framework reports allocated and actual RAM/CPU/storage/GPU usage where available and participates in 9to1-OS memory/resource policy so idle VM/container environments can be suspended or stopped according to user policy.
Compatibility environments must preserve application/user state safely across suspend/resume and OS memory pressure. The OS MUST NOT simply terminate a managed environment and discard unsaved guest/application state to satisfy a memory target.
Snapshots, repair and updates
Backends supporting snapshots/checkpoints should expose them through the unified manager, particularly before major guest/runtime changes. Compatibility snapshots are separate from 9to1-OS system snapshots.
The framework manages or coordinates updates for Wine/runtime components, WinBoat-derived host integration, Android compatibility/runtime components and guest-integration tooling. Guest Windows/Android update behaviour remains explicit and must not be confused with host OS updates.
Repair/reset operations should be scoped to the selected app/environment and preserve unrelated environments. Destructive reset/uninstall flows explain whether app data, shared environment state or snapshots will be removed.
Diagnostics and recovery
The CUI compatibility manager normalises common failures such as missing Wine dependency, application crash, graphics translation failure, Windows guest boot failure, RemoteApp disconnection, Android runtime failure, incompatible APK ABI, insufficient RAM, unavailable hardware acceleration, broken shared folder or package-install failure into actionable health states.
Advanced diagnostics expose underlying Wine/runtime/VM/RDP/Android logs and environment details through System Log integration. Dulche may analyse these diagnostics and invoke typed repair/configuration APIs but should not replace a supported manager operation with arbitrary host shell automation.
Managed-user policy
Administrator policies can disable foreign-app compatibility entirely, restrict allowed backends, block arbitrary .exe/.msi/.apk installation, allowlist approved applications/package identities, restrict package sources such as Winget/Android sources, constrain host-folder/device/network bridges and lock per-app backend choices.
Launching through Go, Files, Shelf, Terminal, Dulche or another app MUST NOT bypass the same compatibility policy. Policy enforcement occurs in the routing/install/execution broker below the launch surface.
Compatibility Framework acceptance requirements
Double-clicking/opening a supported Windows installer/executable or Android APK automatically enters the unified compatibility routing flow rather than requiring Terminal.
Wine, WinBoat-style Windows environments and APK/Android compatibility are represented as typed backends under one manager.
The user may choose among eligible frameworks and can persist a default framework per application; valid per-app defaults are remembered and editable.
Installed Windows and Android applications integrate with Go, taskbar/window management, Desktop Spaces, Files, notifications, diagnostics and resource policy wherever technically possible.
Host files/devices and sensitive bridges remain explicit permission boundaries, not blanket compatibility-environment access.
Administrator policy applies regardless of which launch surface or compatibility backend is used.
Backend-specific complexity remains available for advanced users but is not required for ordinary installation, launch, repair or troubleshooting.
Pass 2: Terra-form
Pass 2 operating contract
Pass identity and model
Terra-form is the codename for this development pass only. It MUST NOT be interpreted as a model family, capability tier or instruction to use a model named Terra. All Terra-form implementation workers and the coordinator MUST use GPT-6.1 Sol wherever model selection is configurable. The intended execution shape is six parallel implementation workers plus the coordinator unless an external concurrency limit temporarily prevents it.
Hard deadline and outcome
By 21:00 Europe/London on 3 October 2026, the entire 9to1 application and OS MUST be feature-complete against the full active specification including the Terra-form tranche below, integrated, validated against the specification's required acceptance tests, and usable at release-level quality. The deadline does not permit fake implementations, hidden stubs, skipped required tests, weakened permission/security boundaries or silent regressions.
Pre-pass baseline, merge and user test drop
Before Terra-form feature implementation begins, the final accepted Astra la Vista head MUST complete its exact-head acceptance, then be merged into main while preserving history. Do not squash, force-push, destructively reset or discard accepted evidence. The resulting main commit is the Terra-form baseline.
Before the pass begins, build usable test artifacts for every currently shippable 9to1 product or platform target and deliver clearly named copies to the user's local PC. Include a manifest mapping each product to its artifact path, version, exact commit, cryptographic hash, platform/runtime requirements and launch instructions, plus a concise known-limitations record. An artifact that has not passed its required build/launch acceptance MUST be labelled honestly rather than represented as release-ready. User testing and feedback from this drop becomes a priority defect stream during Terra-form.
Scope expansion
All mandatory requirements from the existing specification remain in scope and MUST NOT regress. The previously deferred Files organisation, Link, Prototype, Paths, Replay and Variants tranche below is now mandatory Terra-form scope. There is no generic Future or out-of-scope escape hatch for these named features. Only concepts explicitly left OPEN, such as the separate Playgrounds naming/product question, remain non-committal unless the user explicitly expands scope again.
Implementation and evidence contract
At pass start, regenerate a requirement-by-requirement index from the entire authoritative specification and this Terra-form tranche. Track every requirement as VERIFIED, IMPLEMENTED-UNVERIFIED, MISSING or BLOCKED. A source file, authored test, worker statement or isolated draft does not establish completion. Completed cohorts MUST be integrated continuously through bounded source capture, owning tests, regression/resource/native checks where applicable, accepted-root integration and exact-head CI rather than saved for a final mega-merge.
Where a named Terra-form feature needs a low-level format or interface that is not explicitly specified, choose the narrowest coherent shipping contract consistent with the product behaviour below, document that decision and validate it. An unspecified technical detail is not permission to invent an additional product, weaken canonical ownership/permissions, or defer the named feature to another pass.
Android and Go release rule
Full Android/Go parity remains the target. If time is genuinely critical near the 21:00 deadline, complex newly added Terra-form surfaces MAY temporarily ship on Android/Go as responsive read-only or limited-editing experiences provided their canonical data formats, permissions and navigation remain compatible and all existing Android/Go functionality continues to work. Full authoring parity then continues overnight. This fallback does not apply to existing features that already had stronger mobile requirements.
Release exit gate
Terra-form is complete only when every in-scope feature is implemented and reachable through normal user-facing navigation; no demo-only or stub path stands in for production behaviour; required specification acceptance suites are green; required native, device and provider paths have been exercised; accessibility, performance, reliability, recovery and failure behaviour meet the specification; production authentication/backend integration works; release packages build, install and run cleanly; and the final evidence ledger shows effectively 100% verified coverage. If a genuine external prerequisite prevents one item, isolate and report that blocker explicitly while completing everything else.
Terra-form product and interaction contract
TF-01 — Scope, terminology and ownership
All requirements in this section are active Pass 2 shipping requirements, in addition to the full existing specification and the operating contract above. This is one consolidated specification: product definitions, UI behaviour, data rules, APIs and acceptance criteria below describe the same required implementation. Earlier terminology is not an alternative implementation path.
Files owns ten native organisation types: Folder, Project, Sheet, Tree, Smart, Timeline, Pipeline, Catalogue, Stash and Matrix. They are not ten separate applications. Link owns two authored document types: Flow and Binder. Sheet belongs to Files, not Link. Binder is the interconnected document previously called Flow; Flow now means the continuous reading document defined below. Prototype replaces the proposed name Models. Stash is the ordered collection. Variants is an integrated capability, not an app or Files organisation type. Project retains its Files meaning and MUST NOT silently become a separate Projects app.
Files owns storage, canonical file identity, providers, contextual organisation metadata, sync and filesystem operations. Link, Prototype, Paths and Replay own their respective semantic document/session models. Existing owning apps retain authority over embedded originals and app-specific edits. The distinction MUST be visible in the interface: arranging a file, editing that file, editing an authored block and creating an independent copy are different operations.
The new surfaces MUST reuse CUI, Home services, the Shared Productivity Engine, the registered preview/editor system and the Node Graph Framework for their applicable capabilities. Domain-specific nodes and objects extend those shared contracts; they MUST NOT create competing permission brokers, generic content-merge engines or parallel implementations of the same shared object. Existing donor-backed apps retain their donor-parity requirements. This section does not select an additional donor, paid dependency, external hosting service or overlapping product.
TF-02 — Shared UI, navigation and authoring behaviour
Link, Prototype, Paths and Replay MUST have functional launch screens: New, Open/import, Recent, Pinned, Shared with Me and search, backed by real artifacts and permissions. Link offers New Flow and New Binder; Prototype offers New Prototype; Paths offers New Path; Replay offers New capture and Open Replay. Templates use the existing template registry when compatible templates are available; an empty registry shows an honest empty state, not fictitious sample projects. Opening a specific artifact bypasses the launch screen. Returning Home MUST preserve saved work and session state.
Each editor MUST have a clear title/location area, save/sync state, history access, share controls and an explicit distinction between authoring and viewing/running. Use a compact contextual command bar, a central work area, a collapsible navigation/outline or asset panel where required below, and an inspector for the current selection. Tools belong near the relevant work, not in a permanent wall of unrelated forms. Panels MUST be resizable or collapsible, preserve useful user preferences and leave a usable work area at smaller sizes. A Properties panel MUST not be the only way to perform ordinary creation, navigation or editing.
Use the existing CUI typography, theme tokens, spacing, focus, menus, dialogs, tooltips, icons and persistent contextual AI bar. Labels MUST use the names in TF-01. Theme changes, reduced motion, contrast settings and scaling MUST apply to the actual editor, embedded content chrome and pop-ups. Product controls MUST not expose development jargon such as raw schema IDs, worker status or implementation notes as their ordinary labels. IDs and diagnostics belong in details/developer surfaces.
Pointer selection, multiple selection, keyboard focus, context menus, clipboard operations, undo/redo, rename and delete MUST follow the owning app and shared engine conventions. Provide visible menu/button alternatives to drag-only, hover-only and shortcut-only actions. Text-entry focus MUST prevent a canvas shortcut from deleting an object or moving the viewport while the user is typing. Selection and contextual toolbars MUST identify the active object and the scope of the next action.
Spatial surfaces MUST provide pan, zoom, fit-to-content, fit-to-selection and an accessible outline/list alternative. They MUST distinguish moving an item from panning the surface and selecting an object from opening it. Authoring mode supports selection handles and explicit Open/Edit actions; reader mode allows direct activation of openable items. Touch input MUST distinguish tap, long-press and drag, and provide a visible alternative to context menus. Moving between an overview, a child container and a document MUST preserve the relevant selection, scroll/zoom position and navigation history.
Inline and pop-up editors MUST visibly identify the source document and whether edits affect the original. Pop-ups require a title, Close, Open in owning app and permission/save state, plus Back or breadcrumbs when navigating within a nested container. Closing returns focus and the surrounding view to the originating item. Escape closes the innermost dismissible surface, not an unrelated outer editor; modal surfaces use the shared focus/inert contract. Dismissal MUST NOT discard uncommitted edits. Where a full-screen mobile view replaces a desktop pop-up, Back returns to the same contextual location.
All surfaces MUST distinguish Loading, Empty, No matching results, Read-only, Offline/unavailable, Permission denied, Unsupported capability, Missing source, Saving, Saved, Unsynced changes and Conflict where applicable. An empty state provides the relevant first action. A failed operation keeps the existing work intact, identifies the affected item and offers an appropriate retry, resolve or return action. A loading placeholder MUST NOT replace a recoverable draft or falsely represent an empty document.
TF-03 — Common data, source references and recovery
Every organisation object, document, authored block, placement, relationship, section, step, event, checkpoint and variant MUST have stable identity at its owning scope. Names, row positions, coordinates and file paths MUST NOT be identity keys. Persist content/layout separately from per-user viewport, panel state and reading position. Format/schema versions, current/base revision, owner, storage location and permission references MUST survive save, reopen, sync and export/import through the supported native route.
A source reference MUST identify the canonical file/artifact, owning app, optional stable sub-object/section selector and revision policy. Ordinary references follow the current authorised source by default; an explicitly pinned revision and every Replay checkpoint identify a specific historical revision. Repeated appearances MAY have different local layout or labels while referring to the same original. Renaming or moving a source MUST NOT detach references. Deleting a selected source section produces a visible missing-section state; the app MUST NOT silently substitute the whole document or a different section.
Access to a container or composed document MUST NOT grant access to its sources. Recheck source permissions when resolving previews, opening, editing, exporting, sharing, searching and providing AI context. Inaccessible references appear as locked/redacted placeholders without leaking prohibited names, thumbnails, counts or content. Missing, offline and denied states MUST remain distinguishable only to the extent the caller is entitled to know them. A share dialog MUST explain that referenced originals may require separate access; changing their grants is a separate explicit action.
Removing an appearance, connection or authored block removes that contextual object only. Deleting an original invokes the owning Files/app operation and its confirmation, Trash and recovery rules. Duplicating a placement or composed document preserves references by default; duplicating source content requires a separately labelled Make independent copy action, appropriate rights and an explicit destination. The UI MUST preview the difference before a consequential operation. Undo/redo MUST act on the same semantic operation and respect current revisions; it MUST NOT reverse unrelated collaborators' changes.
Mutations MUST be validated and committed atomically at the smallest user-visible boundary using stable operation identity and expected/base revisions. Real-time updates and offline journals inherit the existing Files and owning-app contracts. Concurrent incompatible edits produce recoverable conflicts, not silent last-write-wins. Invalid edits preserve the last valid state and the recoverable draft. Save failure MUST remain visible until durability is established. Content and referenced assets MUST not be evicted while they are the only unsynced copy.
Native export/import MUST preserve the organisation/document structure, supported authored objects, reference identities, revision policies and required dependency manifest. References are not silently flattened or copied. Portable exports that include source bytes require the source's export/copy permissions and MUST explain the resulting independent disclosure. Unsupported/missing dependencies remain explicit. Import validates schemas, quotas, references and permissions before commit and resolves identity collisions without overwriting existing artifacts. Static export is separately labelled and MUST disclose lost interaction; it is never a substitute for the native artifact.
Files — native organisation types
TF-F01 — Shared Files organisation shell and operations
The existing donor-parity Files sidebar, tabs, Back/Forward, breadcrumbs/address bar, toolbar, selection, previews, location management and grid/list/details views remain the shell. The New menu MUST expose the ten organisation types at compatible locations, alongside existing native document creation. Creation asks for type, name and storage/backing location, then opens an immediately usable empty organisation. A provider lacking native metadata MAY use the existing Files-owned metadata capability; unsupported storage or write permissions MUST be explained before creation rather than falling back to an ordinary folder without consent.
Every non-Folder type is a first-class versioned Files organisation object with a stable Files item identity, type, storage location, settings and local membership/layout records. A membership records its stable membership/placement ID, target FileID/FolderID or organisation ID and any type-specific section/stage/cell/order data. Contextual membership is not a second filesystem parent. New files created from a virtual view use an explicit Files destination, initially the organisation's configured backing location; the location MUST be inspectable/changeable before creation. The owning app creates the file, and Files then adds its appearance. An external file is imported through the normal transfer flow before a new managed reference is committed.
Organisation commands MUST include Add existing, New item, Rename, Open, Open in new tab/window, Show original location, Properties, Share, view/layout settings, Remove from this organisation and the separately labelled original-file delete action when permitted. Supported bulk actions show the selected scope and partial-success results. Dragging an existing item into a contextual collection adds a reference by default; the drop indicator MUST state Add reference, Move original, Copy original or Reorder as appropriate. The default MUST NOT unexpectedly move or duplicate source bytes.
All organisation types MUST support nesting with every other type, including ordinary folders, subject only to explicit provider capabilities and coherent containment rules. Nested organisation objects are openable as units, not flattened into their parents. Owned containment MUST be acyclic; reference resolution MUST detect recursion and avoid infinite expansion. Smart query results MUST not recursively ingest their own collection. A relationship that cannot be represented safely is rejected with its reason and an alternative, not silently converted to a different type.
A normal folder-style contents view MUST be available for every specialised type without converting its data. Changing the view does not erase sections, coordinates, relationships, filters, stages, metadata or ordering. View choice and viewport are per-user preferences; authored layout and collection settings are shared document state. Tree retains its stricter editor-only visual mode. Breadcrumbs MUST distinguish a contextual section/group from an actual filesystem folder, and Show original location MUST resolve the canonical storage location.
TF-F02 — Folder
Folder remains an ordinary filesystem/location hierarchy with its existing donor behaviours, sorting, grouping, views, folder colours, navigation, permissions and file operations. The new organisation types MUST NOT reinterpret existing folders, add mandatory grouping metadata or replace normal move/copy semantics. Files can store a new organisation object within a folder, and a contextual collection can reference a folder without creating a second physical parent.
Folder acceptance MUST verify ordinary create, rename, move, copy, delete/restore, colour, sort and nested navigation before and after adding organisation objects. A normal folder opened from a Project, Tree or Matrix MUST still behave as a folder, and returning to the parent context MUST restore that view without moving the folder.
TF-F03 — Project
Project is a folder-like view divided into visible named sections on the same page. For example, Homework shows Maths containing Mathshomework.pptx and Mathshomework2.pptx, and French containing Frenchlistening.docx. A Maths folder containing its own homework remains possible. Sections are not subfolders and assigning an item to a section MUST NOT change its underlying Files location.
The main view MUST show each section's title, authorised item count, collapse control, contextual menu and Add item entry point. A section contains the selected grid/list/details representation of its members. The toolbar provides Add section, Add existing, New item and view/sort controls. Sections support create, rename, reorder, collapse/expand, colour/label customisation through shared presentation controls and delete. A searchable section outline provides direct navigation for large Projects without forcing the user to open every section as a new page.
Each section has a persistent SectionID and addressable deep link. Moving an appearance between sections updates that membership only; source rename/edit actions remain visibly separate. New unassigned members appear in an Unsectioned area. Removing a section MUST offer to keep its members in Unsectioned or remove those appearances; neither option deletes originals. Sorting items within one section MUST not reorder the other sections unless the user applies a Project-wide sort. Per-user collapse state MUST not rewrite shared ordering.
Project acceptance MUST create the Homework example, add a nested folder and another organisation type, reorder and rename sections, follow a SectionID link after rename, move an appearance and delete a section while retaining originals. Reopen and a second authorised client MUST preserve authored section order/membership; viewer mode MUST allow reading and navigation without showing usable mutation controls.
TF-F04 — Sheet
Sheet is a Files-owned whiteboard-like workspace for arranging separate files and ideas. The canvas MUST support file/folder/organisation appearances, sticky notes, rich text, images, labelled connections, freehand drawing and shapes. These surrounding objects supply context; placing a file does not merge its contents into a new document. A Sheet can contain another Sheet, a Stash or a Link document as an openable item without spreading its contents over the parent canvas.
The editor MUST provide Select, Pan, Add files, Text, Sticky note, Image, Shape, Pen, Eraser and Connector tools. A contextual inspector exposes supported appearance, fill/stroke, text style, dimensions, position, layering and link/target properties. Multi-selection supports move, resize where compatible, align/distribute, group/ungroup, duplicate appearance and remove. Snap/grid controls, zoom, fit and an object outline MUST be available. Connectors attach to stable object IDs rather than being abandoned when an item moves; deleting a connected object previews and removes its affected contextual connections, not its source file.
File appearances MUST show a useful permission-safe name/type/preview and an identifiable open action. Each Sheet has a persisted File opening setting: Pop-up or Owning app, with Pop-up as the initial setting for a new Sheet. An item's explicit context command can choose the other route for that opening without silently changing the Sheet default. In authoring mode a click selects and the explicit Open action or normal activation gesture opens; in view mode activation opens directly. Pop-up editing uses only a safe registered owning editor and MUST identify that it changes the original; otherwise provide a read-only preview and Open in owning app.
Persist ObjectID/PlacementID, source reference, geometry, z-order, grouping, notes, drawing strokes, shape properties, connector endpoints and opening policy. Viewport and selection remain per-user. Moving or deleting a file appearance MUST not alter an unrelated appearance in another Sheet, while editing the canonical file MUST update every authorised live reference. Undo for local geometry MUST not roll back source edits performed through a different editor.
Sheet acceptance MUST combine a Write file, image, sticky note, labelled connection, freehand stroke, shape and nested Stash; arrange and group them; open and edit the same original from two contexts; close the preview and recover the prior canvas position; switch opening policy; and save/reopen with identical authored layout. Keyboard and touch users MUST be able to create, select, open and reposition items without precise pointer dragging.
TF-F05 — Tree
Tree is a structured Sheet connecting related files and groups. An editor can create a Maths group linked to Maths.pptx, Maths2.pptx and Algebra.pptx; activating Maths opens a pop-up containing its related contents and folders. The same actual file can appear in multiple Trees without unmanaged copies or separately created shortcut files. Tree relationship changes affect the Tree; source edits affect the shared original.
Editors MUST see a Tree / View switch. Tree provides a connected layout with Add group, Add existing, Connect, Disconnect, arrange, expand/collapse and fit controls, plus a searchable outline and a selected-node inspector. Nodes display accessible names and authorised previews/counts. Connections, parent/group relationships and collapsed branches MUST be explicit. Reparenting MUST preview its structural effect; a cycle is rejected. Changing arrangement MUST not change logical relationships or file identity.
View presents the contents using ordinary folder-style browsing. View-only users MUST receive View, not a disabled visual Tree. They can open authorised groups/files and navigate Back, but MUST NOT obtain the protected visual layout through a hidden route, embed or layout API. An editor switching to View sees the same accessible logical contents. Editing permission on the Tree does not imply edit permission on its referenced files, and source permissions remain independently checked.
Persist stable GroupID/NodeID/ConnectionID, memberships, hierarchy and authored layout. Removing a group or node MUST show whether children are being retained/reassigned or appearances removed and MUST never delete originals as an incidental graph operation. Tree acceptance MUST verify the Maths journey, one file in two Trees, rename/move stability, cycle rejection, editor/viewer mode differences, nested folders and no protected-layout leakage through APIs or Boards embeds.
TF-F06 — Smart
Smart is a rule-based collection of canonical originals from explicitly selected locations. The editor MUST show a readable rule builder, location/scope picker, All/Any condition grouping, supported operators and a live result preview. Required filter fields include tags, file type, work status and modification date where the source supplies them. Values that are unavailable MUST be treated as unknown, not silently replaced with false, zero or an empty string.
The command bar provides Edit rules, Add location, Refresh/reconcile, Pin item and view/sort controls. Each result exposes Why included, identifying the matching rule or manual pin. Pinned exceptions remain visible even when they stop matching; unpinning returns the item to rule-driven membership. Removing a dynamically matched appearance MUST explain that it will return while it matches and direct the user to adjust the rule or scope rather than pretending the source was removed from the collection. Original-file delete remains separate.
Optional AI setup converts a request into proposed visible rules and locations for review. It MUST not run an opaque classifier as the only explanation for membership or search private locations without permission. Membership updates use the Files change/index contracts, with visible freshness and partial/unavailable-provider state. A disconnected provider MUST NOT make its missing results look like confirmed non-matches. Nested organisations can be matched or pinned as whole objects under TF-F01.
Persist the versioned rule expression, selected location IDs, recursion policy, pins and view settings; cached results are not authoritative copies. Smart acceptance MUST demonstrate entry/exit after tag and date changes, All/Any conditions, a pinned non-match, a newly inaccessible location, an offline result set and an inspectable AI-generated rule proposal. No match operation may move, duplicate or widen access to an original.
TF-F07 — Timeline
Timeline positions files and nested groups along a chronology. The main surface MUST provide a labelled time axis, zoom between broad periods and individual dates, pan, date navigation, fit, an Undated area and a visible Date source selector: Created, Modified, Deadline or Assigned. Labelled periods can contain material and open their contents in a pop-up. A date range is drawn as a span rather than forced into a single point.
The inspector MUST show the effective date/range, source of that value, relevant timezone/date-only interpretation and any locally assigned value. Users can add, rename, resize and reorder labelled periods, open an item/group and filter the displayed contents. Dragging a file to change its chronological position is available for Assigned dates and changes Timeline-local data. Under Created/Modified/Deadline, the UI MUST explain the source rather than secretly rewrite it; explicitly editing a writable source date invokes its owning operation with permission and impact checks.
Files with no value for the selected date source remain in Undated. Overlapping items MUST remain discoverable through stacking/grouping, previews and the folder-style alternative. Live source-date changes reposition the appearance without changing the file's identity. Changing the selected date source MUST preserve authored assigned dates and periods for later reuse instead of deleting them.
Persist DateSource, assigned start/end values, period IDs/ranges, memberships and display settings. Timeline acceptance MUST cover all four date-source choices, an ongoing range, an undated file, overlapping files, a nested organisation, a period pop-up, timezone/date-only boundaries and a source modification that updates the view without rewriting unrelated dates.
TF-F08 — Pipeline
Pipeline represents progression through configurable stages, not a Project's static categories. The main view MUST show horizontally arranged stage columns, accessible stage titles/counts, item previews, Add stage and Add item. A compact list/grouped view remains available. Users can create, rename, reorder and remove stages, move appearances between stages and inspect an item's contextual process history without opening its source document.
The stage editor MUST support optional checklist requirements and reviewer approval. New personal Pipelines begin without mandatory gates. A transition preview identifies unmet requirements, approval status and any explicit shared-metadata mapping. An unmet mandatory gate blocks the transition with its reason; a request for reviewer approval becomes visibly pending and does not masquerade as a completed stage move. Reviewer identity and authority MUST be checked. Dragging, the Move to stage command and APIs enforce the same gates and revision checks.
Each membership has a stable EntryID and local StageID, order, checklist state and approval/transition records. Pipeline stage state is local to that Pipeline by default. A Mapping control may explicitly connect a selected field/stage to global file metadata, showing the target field, conversion, affected items, required rights and conflict behaviour before activation. No implicit mapping occurs. If the global update cannot be authorised or committed, the transition remains blocked or reports an explicitly declared partial result; it MUST not silently claim both succeeded.
Deleting a stage MUST require a destination for retained entries or explicit removal of appearances. Originals are unchanged. Pipeline acceptance MUST move an item by pointer, keyboard and API; reject an unmet checklist; obtain and revoke an authorised approval; handle a simultaneous transition; and prove that a stage change in one Pipeline does not change another Pipeline or source metadata without an explicit mapping.
TF-F09 — Catalogue
Catalogue is a file-centred collection with structured information attached to entries. It MUST provide Cards, Table and Grouped views, a field editor, sort/filter/group controls and an information panel that opens without launching the full source document. The file itself is the organised item; typing a filename into a disconnected table cell MUST NOT create a valid source reference.
Required configurable field kinds include text/description, person/owner reference, status/select, tags, date, number and rating. Each field declares its stable FieldID, type, source and validation. The UI MUST distinguish source metadata from Catalogue-local fields, and read-only source values from writable ones. Editing local notes or ratings MUST not alter another Catalogue. Editing an exposed global field invokes its actual owning operation and shows that broader scope. Changing a field type MUST preview incompatible values and preserve them until an explicit conversion is confirmed.
The entry panel MUST show the authorised source identity/location, available metadata, local values, Open, Show original location and Remove from Catalogue. Users can add/reorder/hide fields, resize columns, choose card preview fields, group results and edit compatible selections in bulk. Validation errors stay attached to the affected field/entry without dropping the rest of the user's edit. Removing a field previews affected local values and is recoverable through normal history; it does not delete source properties.
Persist EntryID-to-source mappings, the field schema, local values and authored view configuration. Catalogue acceptance MUST use the same file in two Catalogues with different local notes, change a true global property visibly, reject an invalid field value, preserve values during type changes, open the information panel in all views and retain canonical identity after source rename.
TF-F10 — Stash
Stash is a deliberately ordered collection for working through separate files one at a time. Its reader MUST show the current item, its position in the sequence, Previous/Next, an overview/filmstrip, Open in owning app and an optional Reviewed control. Keyboard and touch navigation MUST work. The sequence is persistent authored data, not an incidental filename sort, and files remain separate rather than forming Flow's continuous page.
Editors can add, remove and reorder entries through the overview, using drag and explicit Move earlier/later commands. A Compare action opens two selected entries side by side with independent source identity and navigation; changing one comparison slot MUST not silently advance the main reading position. On narrow screens comparison may switch between clearly labelled A/B views while retaining both selected entries. A Stash opened from a Sheet remains one contextual surface rather than expanding every entry onto the canvas.
Persist stable EntryIDs and sequence order. Reading position and optional reviewed state are per user, keyed to EntryID rather than numeric position, and survive restart. Reordering MUST retain the reader's current item when it still exists. Removing that entry moves to a clearly identified neighbouring position without deleting its original. The UI MUST distinguish Complete/reviewed status from actually changing a file's global work status.
Stash acceptance MUST save a non-alphabetical sequence, reopen at the same item, mark reviewed items, reorder from another authorised client, compare two files, handle a denied/missing source and return from a Sheet pop-up without changing the canvas or cloning files.
TF-F11 — Matrix
Matrix organises material by two authored dimensions. The main view MUST display user-defined row and column headings together, with sticky headings or an equivalent persistent orientation aid, cell counts/previews, Add row, Add column and view/zoom controls. Each intersection contains file/folder/organisation appearances. Users can open a cell group, a row's combined contents or a column's combined contents without traversing an invented outer-folder hierarchy.
Rows and columns support create, rename, reorder and remove. Each has a stable ID; a CellID is tied to those identities, not its visual coordinates or labels. Dragging an appearance between cells changes Matrix-local classification only. Keyboard navigation MUST identify the current row/column and provide explicit move/add/open commands. Large grids MUST remain navigable using filtering, scrolling and the normal contents view rather than shrinking every cell until its contents are unreadable.
Removing an axis previews the affected memberships and offers reassignment, retention in an Unassigned group or removal of appearances; it MUST not delete originals. A row/column combined view MUST not suggest that repeated appearances are independent copies: repeated canonical items are coalesced with visible placement context or clearly marked as repeated references. The authorised counts MUST correspond to the chosen displayed unit, not include hidden private entries.
Matrix acceptance MUST build Topic A/B/C rows and Writing/Data/Presentations columns, populate a cell with a nested folder, open cell/row/column groups, rename/reorder both axes, move an appearance, remove an axis safely and reopen without losing identity, classification or readable orientation.
Link
TF-L01 — Link shell, documents and shared content
Link connects work together through Flow and Binder. The launch screen and New menu MUST distinguish them by both name and preview: Flow is a continuous page; Binder is an explorable interconnected document. Creating a document asks for its type, name and Files destination. A document can itself be placed in any compatible Files organisation, opened from Spaces or included in Boards without changing its identity. Link MUST NOT offer Sheet as a third document type or use Boards as the name of Binder.
The editor MUST expose the current document type, outline/search, Insert, source management, preview/view mode, undo/redo, save/sync/history and sharing. Link-authored text, tables, images, media, drawings and other supported objects use the Shared Productivity Engine. Embedded originals use registered owning-app renderers/editors. A Sources panel lists authorised references, live/pinned policy, selected source section, availability and permission status, with Reveal placement, Change source/section and Open original actions.
Link owns its block/container structure, arrangement and directly authored information. Existing files stay independent originals. Authoring a note inside Binder does not require creating a new file; placing a Write document inside Binder does not silently import its text as Binder-owned content. The distinction MUST be visible in the inspector and destructive-action wording. Duplicate document copies its authored structure and preserves source references unless the user explicitly chooses independent source copies.
TF-L02 — Flow reading and authoring UI
Flow MUST render selected documents and other content inline in one chosen reading order, with one primary vertical scroll. It MUST not be a column of file icons, buttons to open pop-ups or permanently nested vertically scrolling document panels. The content width, typography integration and transitions MUST form a coherent page while preserving the owning source's meaningful content. Large tables may use local horizontal navigation; interactive media can retain their own controls, but normal document reading MUST remain continuous.
The author MUST have a reorderable block outline and an insertion affordance between blocks. Insert supports authorised whole documents or stable source sections, directly authored shared objects, images/media and a scoped report assistant. Each selected block shows Move, Duplicate placement, Remove, source/section selection and supported layout controls. Reordering by drag or outline commands changes only the Flow sequence. Duplicate placement can show the same original at a second point without cloning it. Source labels/chrome MUST be available on focus/selection or through the Sources panel without making the reading surface resemble a file-manager grid.
The Annual report example is mandatory: Report.data, then Report.write, then an image, then another authorised section/appearance of Report.data, then an AI assistant for questions about the report. Readers scroll through all contributions as one page. The assistant's context is the report and its authorised sources; it cannot silently search unrelated work or reveal a source the reader cannot access. AI unavailability MUST not block reading the report.
A live source change MUST update the correct block while preserving the reader's stable location as far as the underlying content permits. Explicit revision pinning MUST be visible. Missing sections, unsupported renderers, offline sources and denied access get bounded, accurately labelled placeholders without erasing the block or substituting another source. Navigation back from an original editor MUST return to the corresponding Flow position. Large documents use incremental layout/virtualisation without changing source identity or making the scrollbar repeatedly jump during ordinary reading.
Inline viewing is required for supported sources. Inline editing is available only through a safe registered owning editor, with an explicit Edit original state and ordinary source permissions, revision checks and audit. A reader with edit rights to Flow but not its source can rearrange the reference where permitted but cannot edit that source. Where embedded editing is unavailable, provide faithful read-only inline content plus Open in owning app; do not flatten, fork or invent a private editor. Formatting a Flow-owned heading MUST not unexpectedly restyle a source document.
Flow acceptance MUST build the Annual report example; use the same Data source twice with stable section selectors; edit the original through a permitted route; revoke source access; delete a referenced section; reorder and undo; reopen and resume reading; and verify a continuous primary scroll on desktop and mobile. No source copy or widened permission may be introduced by composition.
TF-L03 — Binder overview, containers and navigation
Binder is one authored interconnected document with an overview and layers of detail: one file, connected ideas, and explorable contents. Its authoring surface MUST be a freeform overview containing clickable notes, cards, physical-style folders, binders, tabs, stacks and connected sections. These are real authored document containers with nested content, not ordinary filesystem folders with decorative styling and not merely shortcuts to other files.
The palette MUST provide note/card, folder, tabbed binder, stack, section/connection and supported shared content objects. Authors can place, resize, group, layer and label objects, create/reorder tabs and stack contents, connect stable items and edit a selected container's contents. The inspector exposes title, accessible label, appearance, target/open behaviour and relevant container settings. The hierarchy/outline is searchable and supports the same add, rename, move, reorder and open operations without relying on spatial precision.
Opening a folder reveals its contained material. Opening a tabbed binder exposes named section tabs and the selected section. A stack exposes its ordered contents. A card or note can reveal writing, images, tables, audio and other supported material authored directly in Binder or referenced from an original. Containers can nest under the shared recursion safeguards. Visual physical metaphors MUST not conceal controls or require ornamental animations to finish before the content is usable; reduced motion preserves the same navigation.
Reader mode hides layout handles and authoring chrome while retaining accessible openable items, connections, breadcrumbs/Back, Close and search/outline. Closing a detail view returns to the same surrounding overview and focus. A stable item deep link opens the corresponding detail and a route back to its context. Readers choose what to explore; Binder MUST NOT force a fixed sequence or masquerade as a Paths progression system. Connections are navigation links between related parts, not an obligation to turn the document into a flowchart.
Persist stable object/container/section/tab/connection IDs, nested authored content, geometry, source references and intended overview. Reader viewport, currently open containers and selected tabs are per-user session state unless the author explicitly sets a default starting view. Deleting a Binder container previews its authored descendants; separately referenced files remain intact. Extracting authored content into another app requires an explicit owning-app create/export operation, not an implicit file for every note.
Binder acceptance MUST author a folder with rich content, a tabbed binder, a stack, a referenced original and a connection; read them in a non-linear order; close back to the same overview; find an off-canvas item through the outline; follow a deep link after rename; and open the Binder from a Sheet and as a Boards page. Directly authored information, source references and all nested content MUST survive reopen without being flattened or split into unwanted files.
Prototype
TF-P01 — Product boundary and editor layout
Prototype creates editable interactive systems: objects with typed properties, formulas, rules, relationships, adjustable inputs and visible outputs. Its scope includes simulations, calculations, interactive explanations and experimental tools, not only software-interface mock-ups or 3D geometry. It MUST be useful without AI and MUST NOT be renamed Models in menus, artifact types or launch screens.
The editor MUST provide a component/object library, an object hierarchy, a central Design surface, a Logic/relationships surface, a contextual property inspector and a Run/Preview surface. Users MUST be able to switch between Design, Logic and Run without losing work or creating separate copies of the model. A collapsible diagnostics area shows validation, formula errors and runtime problems with links to the responsible object/property. The contextual AI bar shares the selected model/object scope rather than creating an unrelated chat-only prototype.
The component library MUST include text/value outputs, numeric and text inputs, sliders, switches, buttons, selectors, tables/charts and reusable containers/components. The Design surface supports placement, size, grouping and shared layout controls. The inspector exposes accessible label, property type, default/current value, limits/options, units where declared, binding and event actions. Controls MUST be backed by typed properties and real behaviour; a visually plausible slider disconnected from the model is not implemented functionality.
TF-P02 — Typed model, logic and execution
The canonical model MUST contain versioned stable object/property/component/relationship/event/action IDs, types, defaults, constraints, formulas, dependency references, layout, assets and saved authoring revision. Bindings target stable identities rather than display labels. The Logic surface uses the shared Node Graph Framework for applicable typed ports, connections, comments/groups, pan/zoom, keyboard editing, validation and execution overlays. A readable formula editor remains available for expressions that are clearer as formulas than as large graphs.
Authors can create typed properties, bind controls to them, define formulas, connect object relationships, add events/actions and compose reusable components with explicit inputs/outputs.
